[p. 161]

**Surah 38: Sad**

It is Meccan, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas and others. It is also said to be Medinan, but this is not sound, as al-Dani said. It has eighty-eight verses according to the Kufan count, eighty-six according to the Hijazi, Basri and Shami counts, and eighty-five according to the count of Ayyub ibn al-Mutawakkil alone. It has been said that no one holds that *Sad* by itself is a verse, as has been said of the other letters at the beginnings of surahs, but this requires examination. The surah complements the one before it in that it mentions prophets, such as Dawud and Sulayman (peace be upon them), who are not mentioned in that surah. When God, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned earlier that the disbelievers said, ﴿If only we had a reminder from the former peoples, we would have been sincere servants of God﴾, and that they disbelieved in the Reminder when it came to them, He, mighty and majestic, began this surah with ﴿the Qur'an full of reminder﴾, and detailed what had been summarized there about their disbelief. There is considerable connection in this, and whoever examines closely will see other connections. And God Most High is the One who grants success.

[p. 161, continued]

**In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.**

**﴿Sad﴾** With a sukun (vowel-less) on the letter, as a pause (waqf) according to the majority. Ubayy, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu al-Simmal, Ibn Abi 'Abla, and Nasr ibn 'Asim read *Sadi* with a kasra on the *dal*. The apparent reason it is kasra is the meeting of two unvowelled letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn). It is one of the letters of the alphabet, like *Qaf* and *Nun*.

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Hasan that it is an imperative from *sada*, meaning "to oppose" or "to counter." From it comes *al-sada*, which is the echo that answers the first sound and returns it in the same way in empty places and hard, high bodies. The meaning is: "Counter the Qur'an with your deeds," that is, act upon its commands and prohibitions. 'Abd al-Wahhab said: "Present it to your deeds, and see where your deeds stand in relation to the Qur'an." It has also been said that it is an imperative from *sada*, meaning "to occur," so the meaning is "Let the Qur'an happen (to you)." This is also reported from al-Hasan, and it is close to the first meaning.

'Isa, Mahbub from Abu 'Amr, and a group read *Sada* with a fatha on the *dal*. Likewise they read *Qaf* and *Nun* with a fatha. It has been said that this is also due to the meeting of two unvowelled letters, sought for lightness. It has also been said that the fatha is an i'rab (grammatical vowel marking), with *Sad* being in the accusative governed by a hidden verb: "Mention *Sad*," or "Recite *Sad*." Or it is governed by a verb of oath after removing the preposition, because of the sense of glorification it carries, which takes a direct object, as in "By God, I will do it." Or it is in the genitive by implying the preposition of oath, and it is not declined (*mamnu' min al-sarf*) because of being a proper noun (*'alamiyya*) and feminine, on the basis that it is the name of the surah. Al-Sharif mentioned that when a named thing becomes well known through the use of a word for it, the named thing is considered within that word, and on this basis it is correct to consider the feminine gender in the name. Ibn Abi Ishaq, in one transmission, read *Sadin* with a kasra and tanwin. This is either because a triliteral word with a unvowelled middle letter may be declined (i.e., may take tanwin), indeed it has been said that this is the more preferred view; or because it is considered a name for the Qur'an, as is one of the possibilities concerning it. In that case the two reasons for non-declension are not both present, so it must be declined. The claim that it is named after the meaning of the surah and not its wording, so that there is no feminine form with the proper noun status, leaving two causes, is not free of doubt.

Ibn al-Sumayqa, Harun al-A'war, and al-Hasan in one transmission read *Sadu* with a damma on the *dal*. It seems it was considered a name for the surah, and treated as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "This is *Sad*." Regarding its meaning they hold various views, not limited to the reading of the majority, like the other letters at the beginnings of surahs. 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Abu Salih, who said: Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and Ibn 'Abbas were asked about *Sad*, and they said: "We do not know what it is." This is the view of many regarding its counterparts. 'Ikrimah said: Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas about *Sad*, and he said: "*Sad* was a sea in Mecca, and upon it was the Throne of the Most Merciful, when there was no night nor day."

Ibn Jubayr said: "It is a sea by which God Most High gives life to the dead between the two blasts." God Most High knows best the soundness of these two reports.

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Dahhak who said: "*Sad*: God has told the truth." Ibn Mardawayh reported from him that he said: "*Sad*, means: I am God, the Truthful." Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: "It is the key to the names of God Most High: *Samad* (the Eternal), *Sani' al-Masnu'at* (the Maker of creation), and *Sadiq al-Wa'd* (the Truthful in promise)."

It has been said that it is an allusion to the turning away of the disbelievers from the Qur'an. It has been said that it is a letter recited in the manner of a challenge, and many scholars of realization (*tahqiq*) inclined to this. It has been said that it is the name of the surah, and this is the view of al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and most scholars. It has been said that it is the name of the Qur'an. It has been said that it is other than these, according to some readings, as you have heard above. Among the strange views is that the meaning is "Muhammad (ﷺ) has won over the hearts of creation and attracted them until they believed in him." Perhaps the one who said this considered it a past-tense verb with a fatha or a sukun at the end for pausing. I do not say this, nor do I accept it as a valid interpretation. On some of these views it has no share in i'rab. On some it may be a sworn oath (*muqsam bihi*), an object of a hidden verb, or the predicate of an omitted subject. On some it is definitely a sworn oath. On some of the readings mentioned above, what can be derived is derived, which is not hidden from you.

In sum: if it is not taken as the thing sworn by, then the *waw* in His words, glorified is He, ﴿By the Qur'an full of reminder﴾, is the particle of oath. If it is taken as the thing sworn by, then the *waw* is for coordination with it. However, if it is an oath in the accusative, governed by omission and transitivity, then the coordination with it is in meaning and origin. Then the difference between the two may be real, as when the Qur'an as a whole is meant by it and *Sad* means the surah, or the reverse, or *Sad* means the sea that was mentioned above, and the Qur'an as a whole or the surah is meant by the Qur'an. It may also be a relative difference, as when the whole surah or the Qur'an is meant, according to what has been said. What the eloquence free of artificiality requires is not hidden.

[p. 162]

It has also been criticized to make the *waw* a particle of oath, based on the view of a group that the successive occurrence of two oaths on a single sworn-about matter is weak. The word *dhikr* (reminder), as Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, means honour (*sharaf*), and from it is His saying, ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾. Or it means remembrance and admonition for people, as reported from Qatadah and al-Dahhak. Or it means the mention of what is needed in matters of religion, such as laws and rulings, and other stories of the prophets (peace be upon them), accounts of the nations that passed, and promise and threat, as has been said.

The answer to the oath has been said to be mentioned. The Kufans and al-Zajjaj said it is His words: ﴿Indeed that is true: the dispute of the people of the Fire﴾. Al-Farra' objected to this, saying: "We do not find it suitable, because that is far too removed from the oath." Al-Akhfash said it is: ﴿There is none but that he denied the messengers﴾. Some people said it is: ﴿How many generations did We destroy before them﴾, and the *lam* was omitted, meaning "for you," because the speech was long, just as it was omitted from ﴿He has succeeded﴾ after His words, "By the sun." This was related by al-Farra' and Tha'lab. Al-Tabarsi objected to this, saying it is an error, because the *lam* does not enter on the object, and *kam* is the object.

Abu Hayyan said these views must be rejected. Al-Samarqandi reported from some of them that the answer is: ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve...﴾, etc., because *bal* (rather) negates what precedes it and affirms what follows it. So the meaning is: "Those who disbelieve are only in pride and dissension."

It is allowed that this speaker meant that *bal* is superfluous in the answer, or that the answer is linked to it because it is stripped of the meaning of affirmation. It has also been said that it is *Sad*, because its meaning is "God has spoken the truth," or "Muhammad (ﷺ) has spoken the truth." This is attributed to al-Farra' and Tha'lab, and it is based on the permissibility of placing the answer of the oath before it, and the belief that *Sad* indicates what was mentioned. Yet, even so, there is obscurity in whether *Sad* itself is the answer.

It has also been said that it is the whole phrase "This is *Sad*," meaning "the surah that defeated the Arabs." So it is as if it is said: "This is the surah that defeated the Arabs, and by the Qur'an full of reminder." This is like saying: "This is Hatim, by God," meaning "This is the one famous for generosity, by God." This too is based on the permissibility of placing the answer before it.

It has been said that the answer is omitted. Al-Hufi estimated it as "The truth has come to you," or similar. Ibn 'Atiyyah estimated it as "The matter is not as you claim," or similar. Some researchers estimated it as "He who disbelieved did not disbelieve out of a flaw he found, and this is indicated by His words, ﴿Rather, those who...﴾, etc." Another said: "It is indeed a miracle (*mu'jiz*), and this is indicated by the sense of challenge in *Sad*, on the basis that it is the name of a letter of the alphabet mentioned as a challenge and as a reminder of the miraculous nature." Or the sense in "I swear by *Sad*," or "this *Sad*," indicates it on the basis that it is the name of the surah, or that it is required to act upon, indicated by *Sad* on the basis that it is an imperative from *musadah*. Others estimated something other than this. In *al-Bahr* (the Sea of Tafsir): "It is appropriate to estimate here what was given as the answer to the oath by the Qur'an in His words, Most High: ﴿Ya-Sin. By the wise Qur'an, indeed you are among the messengers﴾."

This estimate is strengthened by the mention of warning here in His words, Most High: ﴿And they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves﴾, and there, in His words, glorified is He, "that you may warn a people." So the message includes warning and good tidings.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 2:

The "bal" (بَلْ) in His saying, ﴿Nay, but those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾, is used for transition (intiqal) from this oath and what is sworn upon, to mention the state of the disbelievers' haughtiness and their opposition in refusing to accept His Messenger ﷺ and to comply with what he brought. It is so in many of the previously mentioned aspects. It may also, in some of them, be taken as a retraction (idrab) from the answer, by saying for example: "Indeed it is inimitable (la-mu'jiz), but those who disbelieve are in arrogance from submitting to its inimitability," or "this is the surah which has defeated the Arabs, but those who disbelieve do not submit." Some of them made it a retraction from what is understood from what has been mentioned, and its like, that whoever disbelieves did not disbelieve due to a defect in himself. It is as if it were said: whoever disbelieves did not disbelieve due to a defect in himself, but rather he disbelieved out of pride against following the truth and obstinacy. This is more evident than making it a retraction from its explicit wording. And if something like this understood meaning is considered an answer, then the retraction from it is certain. In al-Kashf: this retraction is counted among the kind of ma'nawi retraction, as in: "Zayd is chaste and learned, but his people have belittled him," retracting from what the attributes necessitate of honour. As has been transmitted from some of them, it is a deviation from the apparent. It is possible that the answer from which the retraction is made is: "You are not remiss in warning those who disbelieve and in manifesting the truth to them," which the following verses also indicate, and the occasion of revelation that will be mentioned, if God wills. It is as if it were said: (Sad.) By the Qur'an, full of reminder, you are not remiss in warning those who disbelieve and in manifesting the truth to them; rather, those who disbelieve are remiss in following you and acknowledging the truth. The manner in which what is in the sublime composition indicates our saying "rather, those who disbelieve are remiss" etc. is evident. These are several possibilities before you, and the choice is yours. Peace be upon you.

The meaning of "izzah (honour/arrogance) here is what they display of haughtiness against the truth, not true honour, for true honour belongs to God, His Messenger ﷺ, and the believers. The root of shiqaq is opposition: your being on a side other than your companion's side, or from splitting the staff (shaqq al-'asa) between you and him. The meaning here is opposition to God the Exalted and His Messenger ﷺ. The indefinite form (tankir) indicates the intensity of both, and the use of fi (in) indicates their total immersion in them.

Hammad ibn al-Zibriqan and Sawrah on the authority of al-Kisa'i, Maymunah on the authority of Abu Ja'far, and al-Jahdari through the route of al-'Uqayli read "ghirrah" with a kasrah on the ghayn (marked) and an unpointed ra, meaning in great heedlessness of what they must consider. It is transmitted from Ibn al-Anbari that he said in his book refuting one who opposed the Imam: a man recited it thus, and said: it is more fitting with shiqaq, which is fighting with earnestness and striving; and this reading is a fabrication against God the Exalted. End of quote. And in it is what is in it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 3:

﴿How many generations We destroyed before them!﴾ This is a warning to them for their disbelief and arrogance, by showing what befell those of their kind. The word *kam* (how many) is the object (*maf'ul*) of ﴿We destroyed﴾, and *min qarnin* (from a generation) is a specification (*tamyiz*). The meaning is: We destroyed many generations of the past. ﴿Then they called out﴾ at the coming of Our punishment and the descent of Our vengeance, seeking help to be saved from it. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: they raised their voices in repentance when they saw the punishment, hoping to be saved from it. ﴿But it was no time for escape﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *nadaw* (they called out), and its returning pronoun is implied, though it is not obligatory, meaning *manasahum* (their escape). *Lat* here is the *la* that resembles *laysa* according to Sibawayh; the letter *ta'* of feminine (*ta' al-ta'nith*) was added to it to emphasize its meaning, which is negation, because adding to a word's form indicates added meaning. Alternatively, the *ta'* is for intensification, as in *'allamah*. Or it is to emphasize its resemblance to *laysa* by making it three letters with a silent middle. Al-Radi said: it is for the feminization of the word, so it serves to emphasize the feminine. It is specifically restricted to being followed by time-words (*ahyan*), and the word *hin* (time) is not necessarily fixed except according to some, and this is refuted by the attested use of it with its synonym, and by the verse of al-Mutanabbi:

*Indeed I have been patient until there was no more patience (lat musta bar),*
*and now I rush in until there is no more rushing in (lat muqtahim).*

If his matter does not concern us, it may be explained by taking *al-musta bar* and *al-muqtahim* as time-nouns (*ism zaman*), or by saying that *lat* enters on a *hin* implied after it, and they accepted the deletion of one of the two parts. The usual practice is to delete the nominative, as here according to the reading of the majority, meaning: the time is not a time of escape. The view of al-Akhfash is that *lat* is the *la* of generic negation that works like *inna*, with the *ta'* added to it, so ﴿hina manas﴾ (time of escape) is its subject and the predicate is omitted, meaning: for them. It is also said that *lat* is the *la* negating the verb, with the *ta'* added to it, and it has no governing function at all. If a noun in the nominative follows it, it is a subject whose predicate is omitted; or if it is in the accusative, as here, then a verb is implied after it that governs it, meaning: and you do not see a time of escape. Abu al-Simal read ﴿wa-lata hinu﴾ with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a *damma* on the *nun*. According to Sibawayh's view, *hin* is the subject of *lat*, and the predicate is omitted, meaning: the time of escape is not present for them. According to the last view, it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, and likewise according to al-Akhfash's view, since, as stated in al-Bahr, his position is that when the noun after it is nominative, it is in the state of a subject (*ibtida'*), meaning: so there is no time of escape existing for them.

[p. 164]

'Isa ibn 'Umar read ﴿wa-lati hinin﴾ with a *kasra* on the *ta'* along with the *nun*, as in the verse of al-Mundhir ibn Harmalah al-Ta'i al-Nasrani:

*They sought peace with us, but it was no time for a time (lat awan),*
*so we replied: no time for survival (lat hina baqa').*

This is explained either as: *lat* governs time-words just as *lawla* governs pronouns, as in *lawlaka* and *lawlahu* according to Sibawayh; or by assuming an implied *min* (from), as if it were said: *lat min hini manas* (it is not from a time of escape) and *lat min awani sulh* (it is not from a time of peace), just as they used the preposition with an implied *min* in their saying: *'ala kam jidh'in baytuka* (how many trunks is your house on), meaning: from a trunk, according to the more correct of the two opinions; and their saying: *alā rajulin jazahu Allahu khayran*, meaning: *ala min rajul* (is there not a man). The position of *min hinin manas* would be nominative as the subject of *lat* in the sense of *laysa* (is not), just as you say: *laysa min rajulin qa'iman* (there is no man standing). The predicate is omitted according to Sibawayh's view, and it is a subject whose predicate is omitted according to others. Al-Akhfash interpreted *wa-lat* or *anna* as having an implied *hin*, meaning: *wa-lata hina awani sulh* (and it was no time of the time of peace), so *hin* was deleted and *awan* was kept in the genitive. It is also said that *awan* in the verse is built on the *kasra*, and it is likened to *idh* in the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

*I forbade you from your pursuers, Umm 'Amr,*
*with a consequence, while you were then healthy (idh sahih).*

The point of comparison is that it is a time from which the genitive complement has been cut off, since the connection is *awan sulh* (a time of peace), and it has been compensated by tanwin, so it takes a *kasra* due to meeting of two unvoweled letters, being built like *idh*. Both share being built with a tanwin at their end as compensation, which requires the final letter to take a *kasra*. Even if the reason for building in *awan* is not *idh* but the similarity to the adverbs of place and time (*ghayat*), in that it is a time from which the genitive complement has been cut off while it is still intended, the compensatory tanwin does not prevent its assimilation to them, since they are built when there is no tanwin, because the cause of their building is their need for the omitted element, like the need of a particle for what completes it. This meaning exists whether tanwin is present or not, since the tanwin is a verbal, not a semantic, compensation, so there is no contradiction between compensation and building. However, it happens that they used tanwin as compensation only in the state of its inflection. It seems that this was so that it would not be purely for compensation, but would also carry the meaning of declension, so there is no conflict. The building is established in what we are discussing by the evidence of the *kasra*, and since the reason found in the adverbs of place and time existed, the building was attributed to it. It also happens that they used tanwin as compensation here in imitation of *idh*, since when it was cut off from the genitive construction it received tanwin, or to give the word its due form when the meaning's due was lost. The reading was explained by taking ﴿manas﴾ as *awan* in the verse, treating what the adverb was added to, which is ﴿hin﴾, as if it were the adverb itself, since the noun and the genitive complement are like one thing. So its adverbial character was considered, and it was originally *manasuhum* (their escape), then it was cut off and became like a built adverb cut off from the genitive construction and with tanwin because of its being cut off. Then what was added to it, which is ﴿hin﴾, was built with a *kasra* because it was added to something built supposedly and conventionally, which is ﴿manas﴾, similar to *awan*. It was objected that what was stated about treating it this way did not affect the thing treated itself, so how could it affect what is added to it? Moreover, there is much to be said about explaining the genitive in the verse by this method. How utterly strange it is that anyone would accept it! The *damma* on the *ta'* in the reading of Abu al-Simal and the *kasra* in the reading of 'Isa are for building. It is also narrated from 'Isa: ﴿wa-lata hinu﴾ with *damma*, and ﴿manasa﴾ with *fatha*. The author of al-Lawami said: if that is authentic, then perhaps *hinu* was built on the *damma*, likening it to the adverbs of place and time, and ﴿manas﴾ was built on the *fatha* with *lat*. In the sentence there is an inversion, meaning: *wa-lata manasa hina* (and no time of escape), but the *la* of generic negation only works on indefinite nouns attached to it, not separated from it even by an adverb. It may be that this has a meaning I do not know. The end of the quotation. What seems to me easier than this is that ﴿hin﴾ is inflected and genitive, governed by ﴿manas﴾, and the *fatha* is due to the proximity of the conjunction *waw* in the statement of the Most High: ﴿and they wondered﴾, similar to the *fatha* on the *ra'* of *min ghayr* in the saying of the poet:

[p. 165]

*It did not prevent them from drinking except that a dove spoke*
*among branches with a thick (ar-qal) clump*

according to one view. The more probable opinion is that this reading is not authentic. 'Isa also read like the reading of the majority, except that the *ta'* of *lat* was given a *kasra*. From these readings it is known that the *ta'* has three dialects. The scholars differed concerning how to stop on it. Sibawayh, al-Farra', Ibn Kaysan and al-Zajjaj said it is stopped on with the *ta'*. Al-Kisa'i and al-Mubarrad said it is stopped on with the *ha'*. Abu 'Ali said there should be no disagreement that stopping is with the *ta'*, because turning the *ta'* into a *ha'* is specific to nouns. Some claimed that the *ta'* is not attached to *la*, but is an addition at the start of what follows it. Abu 'Ubaydah chose this and mentioned that he saw in the Imam (the Uthmanic codex) ﴿wa-lataḥina manas﴾ with the *ta'* written merged with the beginning of *hin*. It cannot be objected that the script of the Qur'anic codex deviates from the regular rules of writing, since it does not occur elsewhere in the Imam written differently from this, so that one might say what is here deviates from analogy; the default is to consider it, except where evidence specifies otherwise. From here al-Sakhawi said in his commentary on the Ra'iyyah: I prefer stopping on *la* after I witnessed it in the codex of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him. We have heard them say: *idhhab talan wa-tahin* (go now and then) without *la*, and it is common in prose and poetry. From it is the saying:

*The ones who bend (al-'atifun) at tahin without a bending one,*
*and the ones who feed at a time without food (ma min mut'am).*

The origin of *al-'atifuna* is with the *ha'* of pausing (*ha' al-sakt*), and when it is affixed in continuous speech it turned into a *ta'*, which is not worth paying attention to. Yes, the preferable view is to consider the *ta'* with *la* because *hin* is well known, not *tahin*. Some said: *lat* is not the same as *laysa*; the origin of *laysa* is *lays* with a *kasra* on the *ya'*, so it was changed into an *alif* because it moved after a *fatha*, and the *sin* was changed into a *ta'*, as in *sitt* (six), whose origin is *sudus*. It was also said: it is a past verb, and *lat* means "he diminished," and it became rare, so it was used in negation like *qalla* (it was little). This is not a reliable view. *Al-manas* means refuge and escape. It is said: *nasahu yanusuhu* when it escaped him. Al-Farra' said: *al-nawsu* is withdrawal, *nasa 'an qarnihi yanusu nawsan wa-manasan*, meaning he fled and turned aside. It is said: *istanasa* means he sought refuge. Harithah ibn Badr said describing his horse:

*Thick-chested, when you shorten its rein,*
*by my hand it sought refuge and wished to run like the mule.*

According to the first meaning, some interpreted it here and said: the meaning is they called out and sought help seeking deliverance, while the situation is that it was not a time of escape and deliverance. From Mujahid: its interpretation is flight. Al-Tabari narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq said to him: tell me about the statement of the Most High ﴿but it was no time for escape﴾. He said: it is not a time of flight. He recited to him the verse of al-A'sha:

*I remembered Layla, but it was no time for remembrance,*
*and I had been far from her, and escape was distant.*

From al-Kalbi: he said, they, when they fought and were forced, some of them said to others: *manas* (escape), meaning flee. When the punishment came to them they said: *manas*. Then the Most High said: ﴿but it was no time for escape﴾. Al-Qushayri said: according to this, the implied meaning is: they called out "manas," so it was deleted because what follows indicates it, meaning: the time is not the time of your calling out for it. The apparent meaning of the sentence according to this interpretation is circumstantial: they called out for flight, while it was not the time of flight. Abu Hayyan, in establishing the circumstantial reading, said: they were in a state where there was no time of escape, meaning for them. Al-Jurjani said: meaning they called out at a time when there was no escape, that is, at an hour when there was no refuge and no escape. When he put *la* first and delayed *hin*, this required the *waw* just as the circumstantial clause requires it when it is made into a subject and predicate, like: *jaa Zayd rakiban* (Zayd came riding), then you say: *jaa Zayd wa-huwa rakib* (Zayd came and he was riding). So *hin* is an adverb for the statement of the Most High: ﴿they called out﴾. End of quotation.

As for the claim that the origin is that *hin* is an adverb for *nadaw* (they called out), it is a foreign assertion, contrary to the taste of Arabic speech, especially since this is the most eloquent of speech. I do not know what prompted him to that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 4:

﴿And they wondered that a warner had come to them from among themselves.﴾ This is a narration of their falsehoods, which branch out from what was in them of arrogance and opposition; that is, they wondered that a messenger had come to them from their own kind, i.e., a human being, or from their own type, namely those who are known for being unlettered (ummiyy), so the meaning would be: an unlettered messenger. The intended sense is that they regarded this as an amazing matter, beyond the bounds of possibility, and denied it with the utmost denial, not that they believed it had occurred and marveled at it. ﴿And the disbelievers said﴾ Here the apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun, out of anger at them, censure of them, and a notice that none would dare to say the like of what they say except those who plunge deep into disbelief and wickedness. ﴿This is a sorcerer﴾ in what he displays of things for which we cannot find an equal, ﴿a liar﴾ in what he attributes to Allah, glorified and exalted is He, of sending and sending down.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 5:**

﴿Has he made the gods into one God?﴾ That is, by denying divinity (*uluhiyyah*) to them and restricting it to one. The verb *ja'l* (making) here carries the sense of *tasyir* (rendering something into a state), but it is not a transformation in external reality, only in speech. The naming is as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, into females﴾. This does not belong to the category of denying the unity of existence (*wahdat al-wujud*) in any way, such that one would say that God, glorified is He, rebuked the unbelievers for that denial, so that the unity would be established. For he (peace be upon him) did not say that their gods were identical with Him, mighty and majestic is He, in existence. ﴿Indeed, this is a thing astonishing (*ujab*)﴾, that is, exceedingly amazing. *Fu'al* is a form of intensification, like *rajul tuwal* (a very tall man) and *suras* (very swift). The reason for their astonishment is that this was contrary to what they had found their fathers upon, who were unanimous in the plurality of gods and persistent in worshipping them. Their whole basis in all that they did and abandoned was imitation (*taqlid*), so they regarded what was contrary to their habits as strange, even impossible. It has also been said that the basis of their astonishment was their claim that the knowledge and power of one being could not suffice for many things. This would only hold if they attributed knowledge and power to their gods, and it is apparent that they did not attribute these to them: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "God."﴾

Ali, may God honor his face, as well as al-Sulami, Isa, and Ibn Miqsam, read *ujjab* with a doubled *jim*, and this is more emphatic than the unstressed form. Muqatil said: *ujjab* is the dialect of the tribe of Azd Shanu'ah.

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, and others narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When Abu Talib fell ill, a group of the Quraysh, among them Abu Jahl, entered upon him and said: 'Your nephew insults our gods, does such-and-such, and says such-and-such. So if you would send for him and forbid him.' So he sent for him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) came and entered the house. Between them and Abu Talib there was the space of a seat. Abu Jahl feared that if he sat beside Abu Talib, he (the Prophet) would be treated more gently by him, so he sprang up and sat in that place. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) found no seat near his uncle, so he sat at the door. Abu Talib said to him: 'O my nephew, what is the matter with your people? They complain about you, claiming that you insult their gods and say such-and-such.' He said: They pressed him with many words. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) spoke and said: 'O uncle, I want them to adopt one word which they would say, by which the Arabs would submit to them and by which the non-Arabs would pay them the poll tax (*jizyah*).' They were delighted at his word and his statement, and the people said: 'What is it? By your father, we will give it to you, and ten like it!' He said: 'There is no god but God.' So they rose up in alarm, shaking their garments, saying: ﴿Has he made the gods into one God? Indeed, this is a thing astonishing.﴾"

In another narration: they said, "Ask us for something other than this." The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Even if you brought me the sun and placed it in my hand, I would not ask you for anything other than it." They became angry, rose up in fury, and said: "By God, we will surely revile you and your God who commands you with this."

﴿And the chiefs among them set off﴾, that is, the nobles of Quraysh set off from the gathering of Abu Talib after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had rebuked them, and they witnessed his steadfastness in the religion and despaired of what they had been hoping to gain from him through his uncle, (upon him be prayer and peace). Among them were Abu Jahl, al-As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib ibn Abd Yaghuth, and Uqba ibn Abi Mu'it.

(Page 167)

Ibn Abi Hatim related, on the authority of Abu Mijlaz, who said: "A man said on the day of Badr: 'They are nothing but women.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Rather, they are the chiefs (al-mala'),' and he recited: ﴿And the chiefs among them set off﴾."

﴿Go on﴾. The apparent meaning is that it is a command to walk, in the sense of moving one's feet away from that gathering. The word *an* here is an explanatory *an* (*an mufassira*, the "an" that introduces an explanation of a preceding idea). It is said that there is an omitted element in the sentence which stands as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) describing the chiefs, meaning: the chiefs set off conversing with one another, and the explanation (*tafsir*) of that omitted element, which implies the sense of speech without its wording, is what follows. It is also said: there is no need to posit an omission, for setting off from a gathering of mutual talk customarily entails that those who depart discuss with one another what took place in it, and the explanatory element's implying the sense of speech, in a broader way than by direct indication and other ways such as concomitance, is sufficient for it. It is also said: *inṭilāq* (setting off) here means rushing into speech, so it implies the sense of speech by way of indication. Applying *inṭilāq* to this is, apparently, a well-known metaphor (*majāz mashhur*) treated as if it were a literal usage (*ḥaqīqa*). It is also permitted that the figurative usage lies in the attribution (*isnād*), its original form being "their tongues set off," and the meaning is: they began to speak this statement. Some said: the intended sense of *imshū* (go on) is "proceed along your path and persist in your way." It is also said: it derives from *mashat al-mar'a*, when a woman has many births, and from it comes *al-māshiya* (livestock), which was so named because it is characteristic of it to bear many young, or as an omen of that. The intended meaning is the necessary implication of that sense, i.e., "multiply and gather together." It is also said: it is a supplication for an abundance of livestock, which they opened their speech with as an honorific, as one says: "Be safe, O commander." They chose it from among the supplications because of the great importance of livestock to them. This was criticised as an error, because its verb is an augmented form (*mazīd*): one says *amshā* when one's livestock increases, so the initial hamza would have to be elided, whereas the recitation is otherwise; moreover, the intention of this meaning here is extremely remote. In any case, some of them said this to others. It is also said: the nobles said it to their followers and common people. And *imshū* was read without *an*, on the basis of an implied verb of saying rather than the implied *an*, meaning: saying, "Go on." ﴿And persevere in your gods﴾, that is, remain steadfast in their worship, enduring what you hear of them in the way of disparagement.

Ibn Mas'ud recited: "And the chiefs among them set off, walking, *an isbirū*" (that is, "that persevere"). So the clause *yamshūna* (walking) is circumstantial (*ḥāliyya*) or a new resumptive sentence (*mustaʾnafa*). The discussion of *an isbirū* is the same as that of *an imshū*, whether it is connected to *inṭalaqa* (set off) or to what follows it. ﴿Indeed, this is a thing that is intended﴾ is the rationale for the command to persevere, or for the obligation to comply with it. The reference is to what has occurred and what they witnessed of the Prophet's (ﷺ) matter and his steadfastness in the affair of monotheism and the negation of the divinity of their gods. That is: indeed, this is a great thing that is intended by him (ﷺ) to be carried out and enforced without doubt, without any deterrent that could turn him aside and no one who could bend him back, not a mere saying uttered by the tongue, nor a matter in which leniency may be hoped for through someone's intercession. So cut off your hopes of drawing him down to your desires, and persevere in the worship of your gods. It is also said: this matter is one of the calamities of time, aimed at us, so there is no remedy except to swallow the bitterness of patience. It is also said: what he claims concerning the matter of monotheism, or what he intends of leadership and exaltation over the Arabs and non-Arabs, is a thing that everyone desires or wants, but not everything one desires or wants comes to be; so persevere. It is also said: this, that is, your religion, is sought to be snatched from you and cast aside, or its nullification is intended. It is also said: the reference is to the patience understood from ﴿persevere﴾, that is, patience is indeed a thing that is required, because its outcome is praiseworthy.

Al-Qaffal said: this is a phrase used for threat and intimidation, and the meaning is that his purpose in this statement is not to establish the religion, but rather that he wants to take control over us and rule over our wealth and our children as he wills. So consider this carefully.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 7:

﴿"We have not heard of this"﴾ which he says, ﴿"in the last religion"﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb and Muqatil said: they meant the religion of the Christians. The description "last" is according to their belief, because they are the ones who do not believe in the prophethood of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Their meaning in saying "we have not heard of this," etc., is that we have heard the opposite of it, namely non-monotheism, for the Christians used to believe in the Trinity and claimed that this was the religion brought by ʿIsa (peace be upon him), and far be it from him. It is also reported from Mujahid and Qatadah that they meant the religion (milla) and creed (nihla) of the Arabs, upon which they had found their fathers. It is also permissible for "in the last religion" to be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the demonstrative noun, not connected to "we have heard" — meaning: "we have not heard of this which he calls us to, of tawhid, existing in the religion that will be at the end of time." They meant that they had not heard from the People of the Book and the soothsayers (kuhhan), who used to speak to them before the mission of the Prophet ﷺ, that with the appearance of a prophet, his religion would include tawhid. But they lied in this, for the report: "The prophet who will be sent at the end of time will break the idols and call to the monotheism of the All-Powerful King," was among the most famous matters before the (Prophet's) appearance. And if by this meaning they intended: "we have heard the opposite of that," then their lie is more ugly.

﴿"It is nothing but fabrication"﴾, i.e., invention and fabrication without any precedent of its like.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 8:

﴿Has the Reminder been sent down to him, of all people, from among us?﴾ That is, the Qur'an. ﴿From among us﴾, while we are the leaders and nobles of the people, as they said elsewhere: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to some great man of the two cities?﴾ Their intent is to deny that it is a Reminder sent down from God, the Exalted, just as they said: ﴿Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it.﴾ Such false statements are evidence that the basis of their denial is nothing but envy and a narrow focus on worldly trash. ﴿Rather, they are in doubt about My Reminder﴾, meaning the Qur'an which I have sent down to My Messenger, filled with monotheism, because of their inclination to blind imitation and their turning away from the proofs that lead to knowledge of its truth. They have no conviction in their belief that they could be certain of, so you see them attributing it to sorcery at one time and to fabrication at another.

It has been said that the particle "bal" (rather) here is for a turning away from everything that precedes it. However, the "bal" in God's words ﴿Rather, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ is a turning away from the two preceding statements together: the discourse on envy in His words "Has it been sent down…" and the discourse on doubt in His words ﴿Rather, they are in doubt﴾. That is, they have not yet tasted My punishment. When they taste it, the envy and doubt they have will be removed at that time, meaning that they will not affirm except when punishment touches them and they are compelled to affirm. Or it is a turning away from the preceding turning away, meaning: they have not yet tasted My punishment; when they taste it, their doubt will vanish and they will be compelled to affirm My Reminder. The first, according to what is in al-Kashshaf, is the correct view, and what follows of the verses fits it. It has also been said that the meaning is: they have not tasted My punishment promised in the Qur'an, and that is why they doubt it, but as you see, this is weak. And in the expression "lamma" (not yet) there is an indication that their tasting of the punishment is at the point of occurring.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 9:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they have the treasuries of the mercy of your Lord, the Almighty, the Bestower?﴾ It is in contrast to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has the Reminder been sent down upon him...﴾ etc., and it is its counterpart in refuting its counterpart: ﴿Or do they apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾ The "am" (or) here is disjunctive (munqati'ah), understood as being equivalent to "bal" (rather) with the hamza (interrogative), and what is meant by "indiyyah" (having, in one's possession) is ownership and disposal, not mere presence.

The fronting of the adverbial phrase ("'indahum", with them) is because it is the locus of the denial, meaning: "Rather, do they possess the treasuries of His mercy, the Exalted, and dispose of them as they wish, to the extent that they might grant them to whomever they wish and withhold them from whomever they wish, and exercise authority over them according to their own opinion, so that they might choose for prophethood some of their chieftains?"

The attribution of "Lord" (Rabb) to his pronoun (ﷺ) is for honour and kindness towards him, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him. "Al-'Aziz" is the Almighty, the one who prevails over His creation; "al-Wahhab" is the one of abundant gifts who places them in their proper places. The theme of might and dominance suits what they were upon of arrogance, rising above him (ﷺ) in prophethood out of haughtiness.

The intensification in "al-Wahhab" in terms of quantity suits His saying, exalted is He: "treasuries", and indicates a great deprivation for them. Within this is an implicit inclusion (idmaj) that prophethood is not, in reality, a single gift, but includes numerous gifts beyond counting. These are in terms of quality, alluded to by "placing them in their proper places", to indicate that the one deserving the gift and its recipient is the one who has been granted it, namely the Prophet (ﷺ). In the aforementioned attribute

there is also an indication that prophethood is a divine bestowal (mawhibah rabbaniyyah),

"And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they have the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them?﴾ is a reinforcement (tarshih) of what preceded, meaning: rather, do they possess the dominion over these celestial bodies and these lower bodies, so that they might speak about the divine affairs and exercise control over the divine arrangements which the Lord of Might and Majesty alone monopolizes? And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then let them ascend by the means﴾ is the answer to an omitted condition (shart mahdhuf), meaning: if they have the dominion that has been mentioned, then let them climb up by the ladders and the paths (al-ma'arij wal-manahij) by which one reaches the heavens, and let them manage them, and let them dispose of them, for they have no way to manage them or dispose of them except that. Or, if they claim the dominion that has been mentioned, then let them ascend and dispose of [affairs], until the truthfulness of their claim is presumed, for they have no sign of its truthfulness; so at the very least they should make that a sign.

Al-Zamakhshari and his followers said: meaning, let them ascend by the ladders and the routes by which one reaches the Throne, until they settle upon it, and manage the affairs of the world and the kingdom (malakut) of God Most High, and send down revelation to whomever they choose and approve of. This is appropriate to the context, but there is in it a certain evasiveness (daghdagha). In any case, in commanding them to do that there is a mockery of them that is not hidden.

The sabab (cause, means) originally is a connection made of a rope or the like.

From Mujahid: "The asbab here are the gates of the heavens." It was also said: "The heavens themselves, because God Most High made them asbab (secondary causes) of customary (ʿadiyya) effects upon the lower events."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 11:

﴿A host, there, routed, of the confederates.﴾ That is, they are a host, etc. So "jund" (a host) is the predicate of an omitted subject that is presumed to be placed first, as is the apparent reading. "Ma" is extra (mazidah). It has been said: it is for diminution and belittlement, like the phrase "I ate something (shay'an ma)." It has also been said: it is for magnification and abundance. This was objected to on the grounds that it does not suit "routed" (mahzum). It was answered that describing them with greatness and abundance is by way of mockery, so that by wording it is greatness and abundance, while in reality it is humiliation and paucity. It was preferred that the more common usage in their speech is that it is for magnification, as in: "For some matter, the short-nosed one had his nose slit," and "For some matter, whoever rules, rules."

And the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"The tale of the riders on the day of Hunan, and the tale of what, for all its brevity..."

Although the speech is for the consolation of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the good news of their defeat, and that is more complete on this reading. It has been said: the good news of the abasement of a small number may indicate humiliation and belittlement:

"Do you not see that the sword's worth diminishes when it is said that the sword is more forceful than the staff?"

But there is scrutiny in this. "Hunalika" is either an adjective of "jund" or an adverbial complement, and "mahzum" (routed) is the predicate. It is an indication of a distant place, and it is meant, according to one view, as the place where they conferred with the Messenger (ﷺ) with those earlier words, namely Makkah. This is taken as foretelling their defeat on the day of the Conquest. It has also been said: the day of Badr; this is narrated from Mujahid and Qatadah. You know well that if "hunalika" is an indication of Makkah and is connected to "mahzum," this is not possible unless by Makkah is meant what includes Badr. "Mahzum" is a predicate after a predicate. The root of hazm (routing) is pressing a dry thing until it breaks, like crushing a waterskin or crushing cucumbers and melons; from it comes "hazimah" (defeat), since it is expressed by breaking and shattering. The expression of what has not yet occurred by the passive participle, which signals occurrence, is (as in some commentaries on the Kashshaf) to indicate its extreme nearness, so that it is as if it were certain. "Min al-ahzab" is an adjective of "jund," meaning: they are a host, few and abased, or numerous and great, present there of the unbelievers who band together against the messengers, broken shortly; or a host of the confederates broken shortly in their place where they spoke with what they spoke. So do not be concerned with what they say, and do not mind what they babble.

Abu al-Baqa' said: "Jund" is a subject, "ma" is extra, "hunalika" is a qualifier, and likewise "min al-ahzab," and "mahzum" is the predicate. Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying that there is after it a shift (iltifat) away from the preceding speech.

Al-Zamakhshari took the sense as restriction, i.e., they are nothing but a host of the banding-together ones, routed shortly, not exceeding that military role to divine matters. This is good, except that there is disagreement about its source. It has been said: the host ought to have been definite since it is known, but it was made indefinite, driving the known as if it were unknown, as though nothing of them is known except this much, that they are a host of this description.

The author of al-Kashf said: it is the emphasis indicated by the indefiniteness, and the addition of "ma," which indicates generality and extreme magnification, since both indicate that the description is restricted to soldiery from among all other attributes, as if they have no description other than this. There is in this a clear objection. The words of the second scholar imply that "jund" is considered a predicate of an omitted subject placed first, because the context requires restriction. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

Al-Zamakhshari made "hunalika," which is set for indicating a distant place, metaphorically used for a rank of height and nobility, on the basis that it indicates the position in which they placed themselves in undertaking such a great saying, as in the saying of people to one who has been appointed to a matter that is not of his kind: "You are not there." This implies the reason for the blame. It was also permitted on this basis that "ma" be negative, i.e., they are a host who are not where they placed themselves.

This was criticised as something no one among the grammarians has said, and it does not suit the context. There is discussion in it. It was also permitted that "hunalika" be an indication of a distant time. It is, as Ibn Malik said, sometimes pointed to for that, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There every soul will know what it has sent before﴾. It is connected to "mahzum," and the speech is a foretelling of the unseen, either of their defeat on the day of the Conquest, or the day of Badr, as already related, or the day of the Trench. What is in it is not hidden. It has been said: it is an indication of the time of ascending by means. That is, these people are a host, routed when they ascend by means. This is not the preferred view. It has been said: "ma" is a relative noun, subject, and "hunalika" is in the position of the relative clause; "jund" is a fronted predicate; "mahzum" and "min al-ahzab" are two adjectives, and they are the intended ones for the benefit. "Wa ma hunalika" is an indication of Makkah, and what is meant by those in it are the polytheists. The expression about them by "ma" is because they are like cattle, nay, they are more astray. It has been said: the idols and their worshippers. The matter of expressing by "ma" is more evident, and what Abu Hayyan said about Abu al-Baqa's speech applies to it, with an addition that is not hidden.

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 38, verse 12:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Before them the people of Noah, and ʿĀd, and Pharaoh, the lord of the stakes, denied﴾, to the end of the verse, is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) that confirms the content of what precedes it by explaining the circumstances of the stubborn tyrants: what they did of denial, and what punishment was inflicted upon them. "Dhu al-awtad" (the lord of the stakes) is an attribute of Pharaoh, not of everything before it; otherwise it would have been said "dhawu al-awtad" (the lords of the stakes). Awtad is the plural of watad (stake, peg), which is well known. The vowelling of the tā' with a kasra is more common than with a fatḥa. It is said: watada (he staked) and wātid (one who stakes), just as it is said shaghala (he occupied) and shāghil (one who occupies). This is what al-Aṣmaʿī said, and he recited:

They reached the water, a tall stump driven in, and they were not disappointed by its promises.

It is also said: wadd, by replacing the tā' with a dāl and assimilation (idghām); and watt, by replacing the dāl with a tā', and in this there is inversion of the second letter for the first, which is rare. The origin of applying this term to the tent (bayt) is that it is pitched with its stakes, and it does not stand without them, as al-Aʿshā said:

A tent is not built except upon pillars, and there is no pillar if its stakes are not driven in.

It is said: here he likened Pharaoh, in the firmness of his kingdom and the solidity of his dominion, to a firm tent whose pillar is erected and whose stakes are fixed, a concealed comparison in the mind by way of the implicit metaphor (istiʿāra makniyya). He was described as "lord of the stakes" by way of imagery (takhyīl). The meaning, then, is: the people of Noah and ʿĀd denied before them, and Pharaoh, whose kingdom was firm and whose dominion was established, denied.

It is also said: he likened the firm kingdom, in respect of its firmness and solidity, to the lord of the stakes, which is the tent pitched with its stakes, and "the lord of the stakes" was borrowed for it by way of the explicit metaphor (istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya). It is said: this is clearer than what has passed. Its outcome is that he described Pharaoh with this in hyperbole, making him the very essence of his kingdom, and the meaning according to this description is the firmness of the kingdom, the solidity of the dominion and the soundness of his affairs.

Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās, in the narration of ʿAṭiyya, said: the awtad are the armies, who strengthen his kingdom as the stake strengthens a thing; that is, Pharaoh is "the lord of the armies." The metaphor in "the stakes" is then explicit. It is also said: it is a metonymic metaphor (majāz mursal) because stakes are bound to the army. It is also said: the great, firm structures. In this too there is metaphor. Ibn ʿAbbās, in another narration, and Qatada and ʿAṭāʾ said: he had stakes and wooden frames on which he was tormented (ʿalayhā al-laʿna, and he was cursed upon them, and they were played with for him and upon them). It is also said: he would stretch the one being punished between four ropes, each end of which was tied to a pillar, and he would drive into each a stake of iron, and leave him until he died. Its meaning is also related from al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid. It is also said: he would stretch him between four stakes in the ground, and send upon him scorpions and snakes. It is also said: he would bind him to four stakes, then raise a rock which would be dropped upon him, crushing him.

Upon these four views, the stakes remain firm in their literal sense,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 13:

﴿And Thamud, and the people of Lot, and the companions of the Thicket (al-Aykah). These are the factions.﴾ The companions of the Thicket (aṣḥāb al-ghayḍah), and they are the people to whom Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) was sent. They were named after a thicket (ghayḍah) in which they used to dwell. It was also said: al-Aykah is the name of a town belonging to them. ﴿Those﴾ are the deniers, ﴿the factions﴾, that is, the disbelievers who banded together against the Messengers (peace be upon them), the defeated. It is a subject and predicate (mubtada' wa-khabar). From this it is understood that the factions from among whom the defeated army was made up are those same people, and that they are the ones in whom denial was found, because the subject and predicate in such a construction are mirror images of each other head to head, not because ﴿those﴾ is a reference to the factions first and the factions second are the deniers.

Allah's words, ﴿There was not one of them but that he denied the Messengers﴾, are a resumptive sentence (istinaf) brought in to confirm their denial in the most emphatic manner and to prepare for what follows. The ﴿in﴾ here is a negative particle (nafiyah) with no governing effect, because the negation is cancelled by ﴿illa﴾ (except). ﴿Kull﴾ (each, every) is the subject (mubtada'), and the exception is an incomplete exception (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general category, which is the predicate (khabar). The meaning is: no party among the factions is described with any judgment except that it is described as having denied the Messengers, or reported about with any report except that it is reported about as having denied the Messengers. This is because each of the Messengers confirms all the others, and they all agree upon the truth, so denying any one of them is a denial of all of them.

It is also permissible that this be a case of matching a plural with a plural, meaning: none of them is described with any judgment, or reported about with anything, except as one who is judged or reported as having denied his Messenger. The restriction (hasr) is an intensification, as if all their other attributes, in comparison with what is affirmed of them, are equivalent to nothing. This indicates that they went to extremes in denial. Their extremism in it is also indicated by the repetition of the denial, this time connected to the Messengers, and by the arrangement of the two sentences into an exceptive nominal sentence and other than it, namely His words ﴿The people of Noah denied before them﴾ and so on. Each group is treated as one that denied all of them, according to the first way of reading. This records against them that they deserve the most severe punishment. For this reason His words ﴿So My punishment was justly due﴾ are placed after it, meaning: My punishment, which their crimes required in its various kinds of penalties, became established and fell upon each of them. So He drowned the people of Noah, destroyed Pharaoh by drowning, the people of Hud by the wind, Thamud by the blast, the people of Lut by the sinking of the earth, and the companions of the thicket by the punishment of the cloud.

It is also permissible that ﴿Those are the factions﴾ be a substitute (badal) for the groups mentioned, and the sentence after it is then a new sentence, explaining what you have heard. It is also permissible that it be a subject (mubtada'), with the sentence after it as its predicate, with the returning pronoun deleted, meaning: indeed each of them, or all of them, none but denied the Messengers. Both of these are contrary to the apparent meaning. As for what has been said, that the predicate is His words ﴿And 'Ad﴾ and so on, or His words ﴿And the people of Lut﴾ and so on, this is among the things by which the sanctity of the Revelation must be held free.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 15:

﴿And they await not but one blast; there will be no pause for it﴾. This begins the explanation of the punishment of the Meccan unbelievers, following the explanation of the punishment of their like. The preceding speech is of the kind that makes the listener eager to hear its explanation. The verb *nazar* here means "to await", and it is used metaphorically (*majaz*, figurative usage) by treating the event as certain to occur, as though it were something awaited by them. The demonstrative *hā'ulā'* ("these") is used to belittle them. The "one blast" is the second blast (*al-nafkhah al-thāniyah*), by which the Hour will be established. So the meaning is: these contemptible unbelievers, who are like those destroyed nations in unbelief and denial, await nothing but the second blast by which the Hour arises. This is the view of Qatadah. The intended meaning is not that the blast itself is the punishment for them, since it encompasses the righteous and the wicked of all nations. Rather, the intended meaning is that between them and what has been prepared for them of punishment there is nothing but this blast, which postpones their punishment until the Hereafter. This is because punishment by total annihilation, in the manner they deserve, does not apply while the Prophet (ﷺ) is present, outside the divine custom founded on manifest wisdom, as indicated by Allah's saying: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾. The meaning of "while you are among them" is his existence (peace be upon him), not merely his dwelling among them, as some have imagined. Hence, it is said, the verse does not prove the impossibility of such punishment after the Hijrah, since that contradicts the well-known interpretation.

It was also said that the blast mentioned is the first blast. This has been criticised as having no basis at all, because he (ﷺ) does not witness it, and no one is struck senseless by it except those alive at the time it occurs. Their promised punishment does not follow immediately after it, nor is general punishment postponed until it. Rather, punishment befalls them from the moment of their death.

It was also said that the intended blast is one by which they will be destroyed in this world, as Thamud was destroyed. It is not hidden that this is punishment by annihilation, which does not occur, as you have heard, and so it would not be something awaited.

Abu Hayyan said: "The blast" is what befalls them of killing, captivity, and defeat, just as you say: "Time has cried out at them" (*ṣāḥa bihimu al-dahr*). It is thus a metaphor for evil, as in their saying: "They await nothing but like the cry of a woman in labour," meaning an evil that will quickly overtake them. But this is far-fetched.

It is permissible to take *hā'ulā'* as referring to the confederates (*al-aḥzāb*), since they were mentioned earlier. Repetition here emphasises that they are present in the mind of the addressee. The mental existence is thus treated as external and perceptible, and they are indicated with the demonstrative used for something present and seen. The possibility of belittlement remains, and the expression *ulā'ika* (those) does not contradict it, because distance in reality, though it may also be intended for belittlement, is not contrary to this. The speech explains what they will arrive at in the Hereafter of punishment, after the punishment that already befell them in this world. Their being described as awaiting it is because the punishment of annihilation that befell them is not the result of the evil deeds they committed, since it is insignificant compared with the terrors that lie ahead. So this is a warning to the unbelievers of Quraysh and an admonition to whomever the discourse is addressed to. Therefore there is no basis for what Abu al-Su'ud said, that this is not within the realm of possibility at all, because awaiting, whether literal or mocking, is conceivable only regarding those upon whose deeds their consequences have not yet been established. Having explained the punishment of the confederates and their total annihilation, nothing remains of the punishments intended to be explained that is still awaited. This differs from the unbelievers of Quraysh, who committed what they committed and have not yet met anything. This was said by al-Khafaji. It is not hidden that what comes to mind first is the first possibility, which is what is transmitted from the early generations (*al-salaf*).

*Al-fawāq* is the interval of time between the two milkings of the milker, and between the two sucklings of the suckling child. The milk that gathers in the udder between the two milkings is called *fīqah*, and its plural is *afwāq*, while *afāwīq* is the plural of the plural. The phrase is elliptical with two implied nouns, meaning: "they await nothing but one blast, which has no pause of the measure of a *fawāq*"; or it mentions the cause (*al-malzūm*), which is *al-fawāq*, while the intended effect (*al-lāzim*) is the measure of a pause. This is a well-known metaphor. The meaning is that when the time of the blast comes, it will not be delayed even by this measure of time.

From Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatadah, it is reported that it means "return" and "repetition". This is a metaphor in which the cause is used and the effect is intended, since in the interval between the two milkings the milk returns to the udder. The meaning is that it is one blast only, not repeated and not reiterated. Thus the clause, on this reading, is a descriptive clause emphasising the singleness of the blast.

Al-Sulami, Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Talhah read the *fā'* with a *ḍammah*. It is said that both forms have one meaning, the same as *qiṣāṣ al-sha'r* and *quṣāṣuh* (the trimming of hair), meaning what was mentioned above. It is also said that the form with *fatḥah* is a verbal noun (*ism maṣdar*) from *afāqa al-marīḍ* (the sick person recovered), *ifāqatan* and *fawāqatan*, when he returned to health. To this meaning belongs the explanation of Ibn Zayd, al-Suddi, Abu Ubaydah, and al-Farra', who interpreted it as recovery and rest. The form with *ḍammah* is the name of the time when the milk returns to the udder.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 16:

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Our Lord, hasten to us our share (qitt) before the Day of Reckoning."﴾ This is a report of what they said when they heard that their punishment was being deferred to the Hereafter. That is, they said, mockingly and derisively: "Our Lord, hasten to us our portion (qist) and our share of the punishment with which You threaten us, and do not defer it to the Day of Reckoning, whose beginning is the Blast mentioned above." The introduction of their supplication with the aforementioned address (rabbana) is for the sake of intensifying the mockery, as if they were calling upon that with complete desire and supplication. The speaker, according to what is narrated from ʿAtaʾ, was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn ʿAlqama ibn Kalada, and he is the one about whom God, exalted is He, said: ﴿A questioner asked about a punishment that will surely befall﴾. And according to what is narrated from Qatada, it was Abu Jahl. Those remaining agree with both opinions, which is why the plural pronoun was used.

Al-qitt means a piece of something, from qattahu, meaning "he cut it," and the document of a reward is called qitt, because it is a piece of paper. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Nor the king al-Nu'man, the day I met him, who with his bounty gives out the qutut (documents of reward) and releases [prisoners]."

It is said that this is its more common usage. Abu al-ʿAliya and al-Kalbi interpreted it here as such, meaning: "Hasten to us the record of our deeds, so that we may look into it." This is also a report from al-Hasan. Another report from him states that they meant their share of Paradise.

This was also narrated from Qatada and Ibn Jubayr, because they heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) mention God's promise of Paradise to the believers, so they said in mockery: "Hasten to us our share of it, so that we may enjoy it in this world."

Al-Samarqandi said: The strongest of the interpretations is that they asked that the bliss which the one (ﷺ) promised to whoever believed in his saying be hastened for them, since they said "Our Lord." Had it been as the commentators understood, namely a request for punishment or the book in mockery, they would have addressed the Messenger of God and not their Lord. There is a discussion on this which is known from what has passed just above.

﴿Be patient over what they say﴾: over the futile and hurtful statements of this kind that keep recurring. ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud (David)﴾: that is, recount to them his story, peace be upon him, to magnify the act of disobedience in their eyes and to alert them to the extreme ugliness of what they have dared to do. For he, peace be upon him, despite his lofty rank and having been given prophethood and kingship, when he committed something that was contrary to what was preferable, there befell him what befell him, and his grief and regret persisted. So what then of these wretched disbelievers who have continually persisted in the greatest of major sins? Or, "remember his story" means within yourself, and be on guard against committing what would bring reproach. It has also been said that Allah, exalted is He, commanded him, peace and blessings be upon him, to recount the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them, who encountered what they encountered, and who were patient until Allah, exalted is He, relieved them and granted them a good outcome, in order to encourage him toward patience and to ease his task, and as an indication that he would attain what he desires by this. But that, as you see, is weak. It has also been said that He commanded him to be patient and to mention the stories of the prophets so that this would serve as proof of the truthfulness of his prophethood, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The "remembrance" (al-dhikr) on this view and on the first view is verbal, while on what lies between them it is mental, and this is what is meant by those who interpreted ﴿remember (udhkur)﴾ in this sense as "reflect (tadhakkar)." ﴿Possessor of strength (dhā al-ayd)﴾: that is, possessor of power. It is said: "So-and-so is ayyid, and dhū ayd, and dhū ād, and ayyād," all with the same meaning. The ayyād (support) of everything is that by which it is strengthened.

﴿Indeed he was awwab (one who turns back)﴾: that is, one who returns constantly to Allah, exalted is He, and to His obedience. Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) transmitted from Ibn Abbas and Mujahid that they both said: "The awwab is the one who glorifies (Allah) (al-musabbih)." And it is related from Amr ibn Shurahbil that it means "the one who glorifies" in the language of Abyssinia.

Al-Dailami transmitted: "From Mujahid, who said: I asked Ibn Umar about the awwab, and he said: I asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, about it, and he said: It is the man who remembers his sins in private and then seeks forgiveness from Allah, exalted is He."

If this is authentic, it should not be departed from. The clause is a justification for his being dhā al-ayd, and whatever meaning awwab carries here indicates that the intended meaning of ayd is religious strength, namely strength in worship, as Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Hasan and others said. For the justification would not be fitting if the strength were taken to mean physical strength. Yes, he, peace be upon him, was also physically strong, but that is not intended here. In calling him "Our servant," in describing him as possessor of strength, and in the justification mentioned, there is an indication of his abundant worship and great obedience.

Al-Bukhari, in his Tarikh, transmitted from Abu al-Darda, who said: "Whenever the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, mentioned Dawud and related about him, he would say: He was the most devout of mankind."

Al-Dailami transmitted from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: It is not befitting for anyone to say, 'I am more devout than Dawud.'"

It is narrated that he would fast one day and break his fast the next day, and that he would stand in prayer for half the night.

This is an indication of his strength in worship, since each of the fasting and the standing mentioned involves forgoing a comfort that you will mention shortly.

[Page 174]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 18:

﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify [God] along with him﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining his story, peace be upon him. It has also been permitted that it be a causal clause explaining his strength in religion and his being constantly turned back (awwabiyyah) to God, Mighty and Majestic. The phrase "ma'a" (with) is connected to "sakhkharna" (We subjected), and its being preferred over the lam (for/to) is because the subjecting of the mountains to him, peace be upon him, was not by way of delegating full disposal over them to him, as with the subjecting of the wind and other things to Solomon, peace be upon him. Rather, it was by way of following him in the worship of God, Exalted. The adverbial phrase mentioned is placed after "al-jibal" (the mountains), whereas in surah [al-Anbiya'] it is placed before it, where it is said: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify along with David﴾. Some of the learned have said: because David and Solomon are mentioned there, the phrase was placed first for the sake of quick specification; this is not the case here. It has also been permitted that it be connected to the words of God, Exalted: ﴿glorify﴾, and this is closer in relation to the verse of al-Anbiya'. Their glorification (tasbih) is sanctification (taqdis) by tongue, befitting them, like the glorification of the pebbles heard in the palm of the Prophet ﷺ. It has also been said: it is sanctification by the tongue of state (lisan al-hal). Restricting it to the two times mentioned afterward rejects this, since their state-glorification is not specific to those two times; likewise, it is not specific to their being with him. It has also been said: the meaning is that they travel with him, on the reading that "yusabbihna" derives from "sibahah" (swimming), and the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "al-jibal." The shift from "musabbihat" (glorifying, in the feminine plural active participle form) although the original form for a circumstantial clause is the singular is to indicate the renewal of glorification state after state, similar to what is in the words of al-A'sha:

By my life, many eyes have indeed gazed toward the light of a fire on a height, blazing.

It has also been permitted that it be a resumptive clause explaining the manner of the subjecting, and that its being contrasted with "mahshurah" (gathered) here is as if it specifies the circumstantial sense. ﴿In the evening﴾ is, as al-Raghib said, from the decline of the sun until the morning, meaning they glorify at this time; and this is not explicit in encompassing the entirety of the time with glorification. ﴿And at sunrise﴾, i.e., at the time of sunrise. Tha'lab said: it is said "shariqat al-shams" when the sun rose, and "ashraqat" when it shone and became clear; so the time of ishraq is the time when it rises above the eastern horizon and its rays become clear, and this is the early forenoon (al-dahwah al-sughra).

It was narrated from Umm Hani' bint Abi Talib that "the Prophet ﷺ prayed the forenoon prayer and said: this is the prayer of ishraq."

'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from 'Ata' al-Khurasani that Ibn 'Abbas said: "There remained in my soul something concerning the forenoon prayer until I read this verse: ﴿They glorify in the evening and at sunrise﴾." In another narration from him as well: "I did not know the forenoon prayer except through this verse." The basis of the scholar's (al-habr) understanding of it from the verse is that every glorification mentioned in the Qur'an, unless it is meant as an expression of wonder, and tanzih (declaring God free of imperfection) in the sense of prayer, is according to him; since there was a prayer of David, peace be upon him, and it was related in the manner of praise, its legitimacy is thereby known.

In al-Kashf: its basis is that the verse indicates his, peace be upon him, specifying those two times for glorification, and it is known from the narration that he used to pray glorifying during them, so what he used to do is recounted in the Qur'an, even if its manner is not mentioned; thus the verse contains mention of the forenoon prayer, which is the aim. Or we say: the glorification of the mountains is other than the glorification of David, peace be upon him, because the first is metaphorical, so the glorification of David is also taken as metaphorical, because metaphor is more fitting. End.

It has been criticized: if it is known from the narration, how can it be said that he took it from the verse? And metaphor should be minimized as much as possible. This is based on the premise that "ma'ahu" is connected to "yusabbihna," so that he himself is glorifying, i.e., praying; otherwise the glorification of the mountains has no indication of prayer. Even so, there is then a combination of two metaphorical meanings, unless it is said to be so, or it is taken to mean "yu'azzimna" (they magnify), and the magnification of each is understood according to what suits it. After this "lutayya wa-llati" (this and that), it is not free from turbidity. Al-Khafaji preferred the first, and I see it is also not free from turbidity.

Al-Jalabi said regarding this: it may be said that specifying these two times by mention indicates their being distinguished by extra nobility, so that nobility is suitable as a cause for designating them for prayer and worship, for the excellence of times and places has an effect on the excellence of the acts of worship performed in them. This, in my view, is clearer than what came before, and it is suggested by what al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I used to pass by this verse, ﴿They glorify in the evening and at sunrise﴾, and I did not know what it was until Umm Hani' related to me that the Messenger of God ﷺ prayed on the day of the Conquest of Makkah eight rak'ahs of the forenoon prayer." Ibn 'Abbas said: "I had thought that this hour has a prayer, because of His words, Exalted: ﴿They glorify in the evening and at sunrise﴾."

Now, they have a lengthy discussion concerning the forenoon prayer, and the truth is that it is Sunnah. Ibn al-'Iraqi said that many sound and well-known hadiths have been transmitted about it, to the extent that Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: they have reached the level of tawatur (mass transmission).

Among them is the hadith of Umm Hani' in the two Sahihs. One who claimed that this prayer was a prayer of thanks for that great conquest, which coincided with that time, and not an act of worship specific to that time apart from the reason for its time, was making up for what had occupied the Prophet ﷺ that night of his wird; there is disagreement with the apparent sense of the preceding report about it.

Likewise, what Abu Dawud narrated through Kurayb from her, that she said: "He, peace and blessings be upon him, prayed the subha of the forenoon."

Muslim, in the Book of Purity, through Abu Murrah from her also, in which is: "Then he prayed eight rak'ahs, the subha of the forenoon."
