Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in al-Tamhid through 'Ikrimah ibn Khalid, that she said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ came to Makkah and prayed eight rak'ahs. I said: what is this prayer? He said: this is the prayer of the forenoon."

Those who held the negation argued with the hadith of 'A'ishah: "The Messenger of God ﷺ would indeed leave an action while loving to do it, fearing that people would do it and it would be made obligatory upon them. And the Messenger of God ﷺ never glorified with the subha of the forenoon, though I glorify with it." Narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, and Abu Malik. The affirmers interpreted it as negating her seeing him do it, because Muslim, Ahmad, and Ibn Majah narrated from her: "The Messenger of God ﷺ used to pray the forenoon four rak'ahs, and add what God wills."

It has also been witnessed that he, peace and blessings be upon him, used to pray it, according to what al-Hakim said, from Abu Dhar al-Ghifari, Abu Sa'id, Zayd ibn Arqam, Abu Hurayrah, Buraydah al-Aslami, Abu al-Darda', 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa, 'Utban ibn Malik, 'Utbah ibn 'Abd al-Sulami, Nu'aym ibn Hammam al-Ghatafani, Abu Umamah al-Bahili, Umm Hani', and Umm Salamah. Among the well-known principles is that the affirmer is given precedence over the negator, although the narrations of affirmation are far more numerous than those of negation, and their interpretation is easier than the interpretation of those.

The Shafi'is mentioned that it is the best of supererogatory prayers after the regular sunnah prayers. However, al-Nawawi in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab placed the tarawih prayer before it, making it in merit between the regular sunnah prayers and the forenoon prayer. The school's position from them is that it was obligatory upon him, peace and blessings be upon him, and that this is among his particularities, peace and blessings be upon him. It is argued for by what Ibn al-'Arabi narrated with his chain from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of God said: sacrifice was prescribed for me and not for you, and I was commanded to pray the forenoon prayer and you were not commanded to it." Al-Daraqutni also narrated it. Shaykh of the Huffaz Abu al-Fadl ibn Hajar said: this has not been established in a sound report, and among the reports there is what contradicts saying so. It is mentioned that its minimum is two rak'ahs.

For the report of al-Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah, that he, peace be upon him, enjoined him to observe them and not to abandon them. Its minimum perfection is four, because it is established: "He, peace be upon him, used to pray the forenoon four rak'ahs and add what he wills." Then six, then eight. Its maximum is twelve rak'ahs, based on a weak report which is acted upon in such matters. Most scholars held that the maximum is eight.

They mentioned that it is better than twelve, and that a small action may exceed a large one; so what your reward requires according to your exertion is generally the case.

Ibn Hajar al-Haytami, may God have mercy on him, explicitly stated the difference between the forenoon prayer and the prayer of ishraq. He said: Among what is not sunnah in congregation is two rak'ahs after ishraq, after the time of disliked prayer has ended, and it is other than the forenoon. What preceded for you indicates their unity, and other reports indicate it, and the designation "salat al-awwabin" for the forenoon prayer is sound, just as it is applied to the well-known prayer after maghrib. This and the complete discussion of it are in the books of jurisprudence and hadith.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 19:

﴿And the birds﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to ﴿the mountains﴾, according to what is apparent.

﴿Gathered together (maḥshūrah)﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "the birds", and the operative element is "We subjected" (sakhkharnā). That is: and We subjected the birds, being gathered together. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that when (ʿalayhi al-salām) [Dawud] glorified God, the mountains would respond to him with glorification, and the birds would gather to him and glorify along with him; and that is their gathering (ḥashr).

The circumstance is not expressed by a present-tense verb as in the preceding circumstances, in order to indicate a sudden gathering (ḥashr dafʿī), which is more indicative of power, and this is because of its placement in opposition to the verb; or because the sudden (dafʿiyyah) is the default when there is no indication to the contrary.

Ibn Abi ʿAblah and al-Jahdari read "wa-al-ṭayru maḥshūrah" with both in the nominative, as subject and predicate. Perhaps the sentence in that case is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in yusabbiḥna.

﴿Each one of them is oft-returning (awwāb) to Him﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf) that confirms the content of what precedes it, explicitly stating what was understood generally from the glorification of the birds. The lām is causal (taʿlīliyyah), and the pronoun refers to Dawud: that is, each one of the mountains and the birds, for the sake of his glorification, returns to glorification. The word awwāb is placed in the position of "one who glorifies" (musabbiḥ): either because they would repeat the glorification, and one who repeats is a rajjāʿ, since he returns to his action again and again; or because awwāb is the one who turns (tawwāb) much to God Most High, as is the well-known meaning, and it is part of his habit to increase remembrance and persist in glorification and sanctification. It has been said: it is permissible that what is meant is each one of the birds, so the sentence is to make explicit what was understood. Likewise it is permissible that what is meant is each one of Dawud (ʿalayhi al-salām) and of the mountains and birds, with the pronoun referring to God Most High, that is: each one of Dawud, the mountains and the birds is oft-returning to God Most High, that is, glorifying and repeating the glorification,

﴿And We strengthened his kingdom﴾: We strengthened it with awe, victory, a large number of soldiers, and an abundance of blessings. Some scholars limited it to awe, and al-Suddi limited it to soldiers. Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim transmitted from him that he had four thousand guards protecting him every day and night.

It is also related that around his prayer niche (mihrab) there were forty thousand armored men guarding him. This is extremely far-fetched in ordinary terms, since such a man (peace be upon him) would not need such protection. The first opinion is likewise (open to doubt), as is clear to any fair-minded reader.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: A man from the Children of Israel brought a claim before Dawud (peace be upon him) against another man concerning a cow. The accused denied it, so (Dawud) asked for evidence, but there was no evidence. He (peace be upon him) said to them both: "Stand aside until I consider your matter." So they rose from his presence. Then Dawud was shown in a dream, and it was said to him: "Kill the man who was accused." He said: "This is only a dream, and I will not hasten." Then on the second night he was shown again, and it was said: "Kill the man." He did not do it. Then on the third night he was shown, and it was said: "Kill the man, or punishment from Allah the Exalted will come upon you." So Dawud (peace be upon him) sent for the man and said: "Allah the Exalted has commanded me to kill you." The man said: "You would kill me without evidence or proof?" He said: "Yes. By Allah, I will carry out the command of Allah the Mighty and Majestic concerning you." The man said to him:
صفحة 177
"Do not hasten against me until I inform you. By Allah, I was not seized for this sin, but I had secretly killed this man's father, and for that I was seized." So Dawud (peace be upon him) ordered that he be killed, and thereby his awe grew among the Children of Israel, and his kingdom was strengthened by it.

Ibn Abi Abla read (the verb) with a shadda on the dal.

﴿And We gave him wisdom﴾: prophethood, perfection of knowledge, and excellence in action. It is said: (wisdom here means) the Psalms (Zabur) and knowledge of the laws. It is also said: every speech that agrees with wisdom is wisdom.

﴿and decisive speech﴾: that is, the decisive judgment in disputes, by distinguishing truth from falsehood. Thus "fasl" is in its verbal-noun sense, and "khitab" means dispute, since it involves it, or because it is one of its types and was singled out for it, since it is what needs deciding. Or (it means) the speech that separates the sound from the corrupt, the true from the false, and the correct from the erroneous, which was his (peace be upon him) speech in cases, judgments, the management of the kingdom, and consultations. So "khitab" is the speech addressed, and "fasl" is a verbal noun in the sense of an active participle. Or (it means) the speech that makes the addressee aware of the intended meaning without ambiguity, observing where to separate and where to connect, the places of coordination and resumption, pronouns and omissions, repetition, and similar features. So "khitab" again means the speech addressed, and "fasl" is a verbal noun, either in the sense of an active participle, meaning that which separates and distinguishes the intended meaning from others, or in the sense of a passive participle, meaning the intended meaning, that which has been separated from among the parts of speech by being made clear and by observing what was mentioned, or that whose parts have been separated from one another and not made confusing or mixed.

It is also permitted that "fasl al-khitab" means the direct speech which contains neither harmful brevity nor tiresome excess, as was said in the description of the speech of our Prophet (ﷺ): "Neither too little nor too much."

So "khitab" means the speech addressed, as already stated, and "fasl" is either in the sense of "that which separates," because the middle course, the moderate, separates between the two extremes, which here are the harmfully brief and the tiresomely lengthy; or because separation and distinction between the intended meaning and others is more evident in moderate speech, since in either extreme there is a defect, in the one a deficiency and in the other a tedium that leads to neglecting part of the intended meaning. Or (it means) "that which is separated," because the speech in question is separated and distinguished for the listener from both the deficient and the tiresome, by being free from both deficiency and tedium. The construction in the first sense is the verbal noun with its object, and in the other senses it is an attributive construction with its noun.

What is reported from Ali, may Allah honor his face, and al-Sha'bi, and which al-Tabrisi related from most scholars, is that "fasl al-khitab" is his saying: "The evidence is upon the claimant, and the oath is upon the one who denies." It is said this falls within "fasl al-khitab" in the second sense, for it involves separating the claimant from the defendant, which is part of separating truth from falsehood. Some narrations say it is: requiring evidence from the claimant and an oath from the defendant. Perhaps the intended meaning is that "fasl al-khitab" in the first sense, namely the decisive resolution of disputes, was by this, and he made it as himself by way of exaggeration.

What is reported from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Suddi, that it is judging between people, truth, correctness, and understanding, is nothing beyond what was mentioned first.

Ibn Jarir, from al-Sha'bi, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Daylami, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, transmitted that the "decisive speech" which he (peace be upon him) was given is "amma ba'du" (as for what follows), and Abu Musa mentioned that he (peace be upon him) was the first to say it. It is said this falls within "fasl al-khitab," but "fasl al-khitab" is not restricted to it, for it separates the intended matter from what precedes it as introduction, such as praise and blessing, or from the mention of Allah the Exalted in general. Its apparent meaning is to take "fasl al-khitab" in the sense of speech that makes the addressee aware of the intended meaning, and so on as already mentioned. The practice of some people implies that it is included in it according to the second meaning of "fasl al-khitab," but that cannot be fulfilled. Interpreting the report as restrictive is not appropriate, since giving this expression is not a great favor. Moreover, the apparent meaning of "amma ba'du" is what performs its function among expressions, not this exact word itself, because it is an Arabic word, and Dawud was not of the Arabs, nor was their prophet, nor even among them. So it is apparent that he did not speak in Arabic. What appears more likely to me is that "fasl al-khitab" means the decisive resolution of disputes. This depends on further knowledge, understanding, and making things understood, and so on. Giving him this includes giving everything on which that depends, and there is in it as much favor as there is, and it fits it most perfectly.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Has there reached you the news of the litigants?﴾ is an interrogative (*istifham*, a question) intended to express wonder and to arouse eagerness to hear what follows it, since it signals that this is one of the remarkable reports that ought to spread among everyone present and absent. It is said that the clause is conjoined (*'atf*) to ﴿Indeed, We subjected [the mountains]﴾ as a conjunction of one story to another story. It is also said that it is conjoined to the imperative "Remember" (*udhkur*).

*Al-khasm* (the litigant) is originally a verbal noun from *khasamahu*, meaning he disputed with him or overcame him. It is used to mean the one who disputes, and it is applied to the singular, the masculine, and their derivatives. Here it is used in the plural, according to some scholars, because of the plural pronouns that follow it. It is sometimes made dual or plural as *khusum* and *akhsam*. The root sense of *al-mukhasamah* (dispute), according to al-Raghib, is that each party takes hold of the other's side, or that each one pulls the opponent's side of a sack from one direction.

﴿When they scaled the prayer niche﴾: that is, they climbed over its wall (*sur*) and came down into it. The form *tasawwara* here denotes ascent, according to its original pattern, as in *tasannama al-jamal* (he mounted the hump of the camel, i.e., rose to its hump) and *tadharra al-jabal* (he ascended the summit of the mountain). *Al-sur* is the wall surrounding an elevated place. *Al-mihrab* is the upper chamber, which is a raised room. The *mihrab* of a mosque is named after this, either because it is set apart from what is around it, or because of the elevated status (*shurfah*) of the house's upper part, as al-Khafaji stated. Al-Raghib said: "As for the *mihrab* of the mosque, it is said it was named so because it is the place of fighting (*muharabah*) against Satan and desire. It is also said that it is because a person's right in it is to be intent on it (*harib*), free from worldly concerns and from the scattering of the mind. And it is said that the origin of it is that the *mihrab* of a house is the seat of honor in a gathering. Then, when mosques were built, its front part was called by this name." It is also said: "Rather, the *mihrab* originally belongs to the mosque, and it is a term specially applied to the front of a gathering place; then the front of a house was called *mihrab* by analogy with the mihrab of the mosque, and this seems most correct," end of quotation. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti explicitly stated that the mihrabs found in mosques in their well-known form today did not exist in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he has a treatise on verifying this.

(*Idh*, "when") is connected to a suppressed noun governing the word "litigants", meaning: the news of the litigants' contention, when they scaled [the niche]. Or it is connected to "news" on the understanding that what is meant is the event that took place in the time of Dawud (peace be upon him). The attribution of "has reached" to the news is by ellipsis of a noun, meaning: the story of the news of the litigants. It has also been permitted to connect it directly to "has reached" without ellipsis, by making the attribution of arrival to it figurative. Or it may be connected to "litigants", which is originally a verbal noun, and the adverbial phrase is a sufficient container that needs only the aroma of the verb. Al-Hufi claimed that it is connected to "has reached", but this can hardly be correct, because the arrival of the news of the litigants did not occur at the time they scaled the niche.

**Page 179** (page marker from the source)

﴿When they entered upon Dawud﴾. Here "idh" is a substitute for the first "idh", a substitution of the whole for the whole (*badal kull min kull*). This is so that the time of climbing over the wall and the time of entering are treated, because of their closeness, as if they were one time. Or it is a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*), so that extension (of time) is considered. Or it is an adverbial complement of *tasawwuru* (they climbed over), with the extension of its time taken into account, since otherwise the climbing did not take place at the time of entering. It is also permissible that "entering" means his intention to enter, but this is strained, because even though it is a metaphor, the statement of Allah the Exalted, ﴿So he was frightened of them﴾, is not built upon it, and so it would need to be built upon the climbing, which is also, as you see, (strained). It has also been allowed that it is connected to *udhkur* (remember), understood as an implied verb. *Al-fazaʿ* (fear) is a contraction and aversion that befalls a person from a frightening thing.

It is narrated that Allah the Exalted sent to him two angels in the form of two men. It is said: they were Jibril and Mika'il, peace be upon them both. They asked to enter upon him, and they found him on the day of his worship, so the guards prevented them. They then climbed over the sanctuary (*al-mihrab*) to him, and he did not perceive them until they were sitting before him.

Dawud, peace be upon him, as is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, divided his time into four parts: a day for worship, a day for judgment, a day for attending to his own personal affairs, and a day for all the Children of Israel, so he admonished them and made them weep. As for the cause of the fear, it is said: they descended from above the wall, and on the day of seclusion the guards were around him, not allowing anyone who wished to enter upon him. So he, peace be upon him, feared that they would harm him, especially since it is related that it was at night. It is also said: the fear was because he thought that the people of his kingdom had come to hold him in contempt,
**Page 179**
to the point that some of them had abandoned seeking permission. Thus it would in reality be a fear of corruption of conduct, not of those entering. Abu al-Ahwas said: he was frightened of them because they entered upon him while each of them was holding the head of the other. It is also said: he was frightened of them when he saw that their climbing was to a very high place, which could not be reached after months even with helpers and great numbers. The apparent meaning is that his fear was nothing but an anticipation of harm due to the violation of what is customary. So when they saw that he had become frightened, ﴿they said: Do not fear﴾. This is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*), coming as an answer to a question arising from the report of his fear, peace be upon him, as if it had been said: "What did they say upon seeing his fear?" So it was said: they said to him, to remove his fear: "Do not fear." ﴿Two adversaries﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "We are two adversaries." Here "two adversaries" means two groups, not two disputing individuals. It has already been mentioned that *al-khasm* (adversary) can include the plural, so it agrees with all the pronouns mentioned before. What supports this, according to what has been said, is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿one of us has wronged the other﴾, for this kind of expression is more common in the speech of groups. The reading of some (*bagha baʿduhum ʿala baʿd*, "one of them has wronged the other") is more evident as support. This does not prevent the dispute from having occurred only between two, since each of them may have been accompanied by someone who supports him, and custom applies the term "adversary" to the disputant and to his supporter even if he does not actually dispute. It is also permitted that the intended meaning is two, and the plural pronouns are used to refer to the dual, so they agree. This is supported by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, this is my brother﴾. It has also been said that it is permissible to supply *khasmani* (two adversaries) as a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "among us are two adversaries." But this, as you see, is (weak). The apparent view is that the clause ﴿one of us has wronged...﴾ and so on is in the position of a qualifier (*sifa*) of "two adversaries", and that the clause "We are two adversaries" and so on is a resumptive sentence in the position of a reason for the prohibition, so it is connected to "do not fear". It has also been allowed that they had said "Do not fear" and then were silent until they were asked, "What is your matter?" and they said: "Two adversaries, one of whom has wronged the other," meaning: one of us has oppressed the other. The objection to this statement, on the view that they were angels, is that it is a report about themselves of something that did not occur from them, and that is a lie, and the angels are free of it. It is answered that it would be a lie only if they had intended it as an actual report. But if it was a hypothetical case they formed in their own minds in order to make a point, they would not have come in the form of humans, just as a scholar, when he formulates a problem for someone, does so. Or it was an implicit and allusive reference to what happened from Dawud, peace be upon him, and then there is no objection. Abu Yazid al-Jarrar related from al-Kisa'i the reading "*khisman*" with a kasra on the *kha'*.

﴿So judge between us with truth and do not exceed (the bounds)﴾, meaning: and do not go beyond it. Abu Raja', Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Qatada, al-Hasan, and Abu Haywa read "*wa la tashtit*" from *shatta* in its triliteral form, meaning: "and do not stray far from the truth." Qatada also read "*tushit*" with assimilation from *ashatta* in its quadriliteral form. Zirr read "*tushatit*" with a damma on the *ta'* and an *alif*, on the pattern of *tufaʿil*, unassimilated. Also from him: "*tashtut*" from *shatata*. The meaning in all of these is: do not deviate in the judgment. They intended by this command and prohibition to show their eagerness for the truth to become apparent and their contentment with it, without any doubt that he, peace be upon him, judges by truth and does not deviate in judgment. One of the two adversaries may say something like this to hint that he is the one in the right, and he may say it as an accusation against the judge, and in that case it contains a certain harshness. According to what we mentioned first, there is some harshness in it. In Dawud's, peace be upon him, bearing of this from them is an indication that it is fitting for a judge to tolerate something like this from litigants, especially when he is one who has the truth with him. The condition of a person at the time of dispute is not hidden.

It is remarkable that a judge, or an arbitrator, or one to whom litigants have some recourse, such as a mufti, how can he not follow this penitent prophet, peace be upon him, in this matter? Rather, he becomes extremely angry at the slightest word that comes out, even a slip from one of the two litigants, from which a belittling of his status might be imagined. If he reflected within himself, he would know that in comparison with this penitent prophet, by the Great God, he is not worth the wing of a fly. O Allah, grant us success in the best of characters and protect us from errors, ﴿and guide us to the even path﴾, meaning: the middle of the way of truth, by restraining the oppressor from the path of injustice that he has taken, and guiding him to the course of justice.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 23:

﴿Indeed, this is my brother﴾, etc. is a resumed sentence explaining what the dispute concerns. By "brotherhood" is meant either brotherhood in religion, or brotherhood of friendship and affection, or brotherhood of partnership and association, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, many of the partners [in business] wrong one another﴾. Each of these kinds of brotherhood carries a right that prevents transgression and wrongdoing. It has also been said that it is brotherhood by lineage, and that the two litigants were brothers from the Children of Israel, sharing a father and a mother. It is not hidden that the well-known view is that they were angels; indeed, it has been said that there is no disagreement on this.

"My brother" is an explanatory apposition according to Ibn 'Atiyyah, and a substitute or predicate according to al-Zamakhshari. Perhaps the intended benefit on the second view is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe﴾. The "ewe" (na'jah) is the female of the wild cattle, of sheep, and of the mountain goat, and it is used metaphorically for a woman, as the ewe often is, as in the words of Ibn 'Awn:

"I am their father, three they are, and a fourth in the house, the youngest of them,
And my ewes, five, you must provide for them — is there not a sleek young man who will feed them?"

And the words of 'Antarah:

"O ewe, whatever is hunted is lawful to the one who takes it; you are forbidden to me, would that you were not forbidden."

And the words of al-A'sha:

"I shot, in a moment of carelessness, at his eye beside his ewe, and struck her heart and her spleen."

The apparent reading is to keep it in its literal sense here, and it may be meant as a female sheep; but it is also permissible that it means a woman. What relates to this will come, God willing, later.

al-Hasan and Zayd ibn 'Ali read (tis'un wa tis'una) with a fatha on the tā' in both places. The verbal noun (fi'l) occurs often with the same meaning as the form (fa'l), as in al-sikr and al-sakr; this is not far-fetched for "tis'" (nine), especially since it borders on "'ashr" (ten). Al-Hasan and Ibn Hurmuz read (ni'jatun) with a kasra on the nūn, which is a dialect of some of the Banu Tamim. Ibn Mas'ud read "wa-li ni'jatun unthā" (and I have one female ewe). al-Zamakhshari explained this by saying that one says "imra'atun unthā" of a beautiful and graceful woman, and the meaning is describing her as having the softness and languor of femininity; this is more graceful for her and adds to her coquetry and her swaying gait. Do you not see how they describe her as lazy and indolent, and as in his words:

"Languid in standing, curt in speech, lethargic at evening when she has not slept,"

and the words of Qays ibn al-Khutaym:

"She sleeps from the weight of her affairs, and when she rises slowly, she is nearly toppling over."

In the statement about it there is a fulfilment of the right of both parts, I mean what returns to the wrongdoer and what returns to the wronged one, as if it were said: despite his great wealth and my severe need, he wronged me of my right. This is evident if the ewe is used metaphorically; otherwise, the fitting thing is to emphasize the femininity by saying that she is complete in it, so that she is more abundant in milk and more productive of what is sought from her. Moreover, there is in it an allusion to what has been related about him: ﴿So he said, "Entrust her to me"﴾, meaning, "Make her mine," and its literal sense is, "Make me responsible for her as I am responsible for what is under my hand." Ibn Kaysan said: "Make her my share (kifl)," that is, my portion. From Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud: "Transfer her to me." This is an explanation of the meaning and more closely related to the aspect of the metaphor. ﴿And he overpowered me﴾, that is, he prevailed over me. There is a proverb: "Whoever is mighty plunders," that is, whoever prevails takes spoil. The poet said:

"A sandgrouse whom a snare has overpowered spent the night pulling at it, while its wing was caught."

﴿In speech﴾, that is, in his addressing me in argument, by bringing an argument I could not repel. al-Dahhak said: that is, if he spoke he was more eloquent than I, and if he fought he was more forceful than I. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: he was more distinguished than I and stronger; when I addressed him, his speech was stronger than mine, and his power greater than my power. It was also said: that is, he prevailed over me in his contest with me concerning the betrothal, the verb "khatabtu" (I proposed) and "khatabahā" (he proposed to her) being used, so that "khātabanī khitāban" means he competed with me in the proposal, and so he overcame me by marrying her without me. This is the view of those who take the ewe as a metaphor. Sahib al-Kashf objected to this, saying: interpreting "khitab" as competition in proposing to women does not suit the eloquence of the revelation, because the imagery is far removed from it, given the remoteness of His saying: ﴿and I have one ewe﴾ from that meaning, and likewise His saying: ﴿entrust her to me﴾, since on that reading he should be addressing the guardian of the woman proposed to. Unless the first is made a metaphor for what the situation will come to by supposition, the condition for its appropriateness being the certainty of its outcome, as in ﴿I am pressing wine﴾; and the second is a metaphor for his abandoning the proposal. The complications in both are not hidden. Moreover, its explicitness contradicts the purpose of the parable, which is to draw attention to the magnitude of what came from him, peace be upon him, and that it is a matter one would be ashamed to uncover, together with keeping it veiled and preserving his dignity. End of quotation; so consider it carefully.

Abu Haywa and Talhah read "wa-'azani" with the zāy lightened. Abu al-Fath said: one of the two zāys was dropped for lightness, just as one of the two sīns is dropped in the verse of Abu Zubayd: "Be good to him, for they are fierce toward him," and it is related likewise from 'Asim.

'Abd Allah, Abu Wa'il, Masruq, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan, and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read "wa-'azzani" with an alif after the 'ayn and the zāy doubled, meaning: and he overcame me.

"He said: 'He has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe be added to his ewes.'" (﴿قالَ لَقَدْ ظَلَمَكَ بِسُؤالِ نَعْجَتِكَ إلى نِعاجِهِ﴾) — the answer to an omitted oath, intended to emphasize the denial of the act of one who has many ewes and to censure his greed. This was not an initial statement from Dawud (peace be upon him) after the claimant finished speaking, nor a legal verdict based on the outward meaning of his words before the matter became clear to him. Thus it is said: this is on the presumption of ﴿لَقَدْ ظَلَمَكَ﴾ "if what you say is true." It is also said: there is an omitted statement, meaning: the defendant acknowledged, so he said: ﴿لَقَدْ ظَلَمَكَ﴾ etc. The Qur'an does not relate the defendant's acknowledgment, because it is known from all the revealed laws that a judge does not rule except after the defendant has answered.

It is reported in a narration that when he (peace be upon him) heard the plaintiff's words, he said to the other: "What do you say?" He acknowledged, so he said to him: "You must return to the truth, or I will break what is in your eyes," and he said to the second: ﴿لَقَدْ ظَلَمَكَ﴾ etc. At that they smiled and departed, and he did not see them at that moment.

It is also said: they went toward the sky in his sight. Al-Halimi said: he (peace be upon him) saw in the claimant signs of weakness and oppression, so he took his matter to be that he was wronged, as he said, and this led him to not ask the defendant, so he hastened with his words: ﴿لَقَدْ ظَلَمَكَ﴾. It is not hidden that this is a weak statement that is not relied upon, because signs of truthfulness often appear in a liar, and deceit is more than can be counted, in past and present times. What occurred with the brothers of Yusuf (peace be upon him), who were not prophets according to the more correct view, removes reliance in this matter. Some ignorant people went toward something like this and claimed that the sin of Dawud (peace be upon him) was only that he confirmed one of them against the other and wronged him before asking him.

The word "su'al" (asking/demanding) is a verbal noun added to its object, and its transitivity to another object with "ila" (to) is because it includes the meaning of addition, as if it were said: ﴿لَقَدْ ظَلَمَكَ﴾ by adding your ewe to his ewes in the manner of asking and demanding, or: "he has certainly wronged you by demanding your ewe be added to his ewes."

﴿وإنَّ كَثِيرًا مِنَ الخُلَطاءِ﴾ — "Indeed, many of the partners," i.e., the associates who mix their property; the singular is "khalit," and "khilta" is the mixing, which has become predominantly used for livestock. There is a discussion among the jurists about its ruling, some of which al-Zamakhshari mentioned. ﴿لَيَبْغِي﴾ — "surely oppress," i.e., transgress, ﴿بَعْضُهم عَلى بَعْضٍ﴾ — "one against another," not observing the right of partnership and companionship.

﴿إلا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ﴾ — "except those who believe and do righteous deeds" among them, for they avoid oppression and transgression. ﴿وقَلِيلٌ ما هُمْ﴾ — "and they are very few," i.e., they are very few indeed. So "qalil" is a predicate placed first, and "hum" is the subject, and "ma" is extra. Emphasis on fewness has come through the indefiniteness and the addition of the indefinite "ma," which implies wonder; when a thing is emphasized, it becomes a cause for wonder at it, as if it were said: "How few they are!" The sentence is a concluding parenthetical statement.

It was read as "liyabghiya" with a fatha on the ya', on the assumption of the omission of the light nun, its original form being "liyabghiyan," as Tarafa ibn al-Abd said:

اضْرِبَ عَنْكَ الهُمُومَ طارِقَها ضَرْبَكَ بِالسَّيْفِ قَوْنَسَ الفَرَسِ

He means "idribann," and it would be on the presumption of an omitted oath, and that oath and its answer are the predicate of "inna." On the reading of the majority, the lam is the one that falls in the predicate of "inna," and the clause "yabghi" etc. is the predicate. It was also read as "liyabgh" with the ya' omitted for lightness, as in His saying: ﴿واللَّيْلِ إذا يَسْرِ﴾ and the poet's saying:

مُحَمَّدٌ تَفْدِ نَفْسَكَ كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ∗∗∗ إذا ما خِفْتَ مِن أمْرٍ تَبالا

The apparent meaning is that His saying: ﴿وإنَّ كَثِيرًا مِنَ الخُلَطاءِ﴾ etc. is from the words of Dawud (peace be upon him), a continuation of what he mentioned first. Here he considered what the situation of the dispute was, as the apparent expression "al-khulata'" indicates, for it is predominant among partners who mixed their property in livestock. The example of the ewe was made, by way of metaphor, an initial illustration that did not consider the situation of the dispute, as if it were said: "Indeed, oppression is a matter found among those who are in contact with one another." He specified the partners because it is most common among them, so there is no wonder at what has arisen between you. It results in the intention of good admonition, and encouragement to adopt the custom of those partners who are judged to be few, and to make them dislike the oppression and transgression that most of them practice, together with regret over their condition, and to console the one wronged for what befell him from his partner, and that he has in most partners a model. Or it is as if it were said: "This matter that has occurred between you, O two partners, often occurs among partners, so it should be considered according to the particular circumstances of you two." Al-Kashf said: "The more apparent interpretation is this."

On both estimates, it is a concluding statement from which what was mentioned follows. Then he said: "Perhaps the more apparent is to take 'al-khulata'' as referring to those who are acquainted and opposed, and their like, among whom there is strong contact and mingling, as in the saying: 'Indeed the partner, they hastened the separation, so they departed.' The predominance in the partners who mixed their property in the usage of the jurists, so mention of 'al-khulata'' does not contradict mention of wives, since 'khilta' was not intended." End of quote. You know that although this does not contradict mention of wives, the priority of not intending wives, and keeping "ewe" in its literal meaning, is something about which two rams should not butt heads.

﴿وظَنَّ داوُدُ أنَّما فَتَنّاهُ﴾ — "And Dawud thought that We had only tested him." "Zann" (thought) is used metaphorically for inferential knowledge, because of the clear resemblance between them. In al-Bahr: since the predominant opinion approaches knowledge, it was borrowed for it. So the meaning is: Dawud knew and was certain, from what happened in the session of judgment, that Allah had tested him. It is said: when he judged between them, one of them looked at his companion and laughed, then they ascended to the sky in front of his face, so he knew by that that Allah had tested him. It is also permitted to keep "zann" on its literal meaning. Ibn Atiyya denied the use of "zann" after certain knowledge and said: "We do not find it in the speech of the Arabs; it is only a pause between two beliefs one of which overcomes the other, and the Arabs use it for knowledge not through the senses, since that is complete certainty. But people confuse this and say: 'zanna' in the sense of 'aqqana'," and so on at length. It is understood from this that the application of "zann" to inferential knowledge is a literal usage, whereas the well-known view is that it is metaphorical. The apparent sense of what follows is that here it means knowledge. As for "anna" with a fatha, some eminent scholars have verified that it does not indicate restriction as "inna" with a kasra does. Whoever says it indicates restriction, by analogy with the kasra form, as al-Zamakhshari did, does not claim that this is consistent. So the intended meaning here is not to restrict the test to him (peace be upon him), because that would require the separation of the pronoun, nor to restrict what was done to him to the act, because every act resolves into general and specific: the meaning of "I struck him" is "I performed his striking." Moreover, the meaning would be "We did to him nothing but test him," as Abu al-Su'ud said, because according to what is said, that is far-fetched and obscure. Whoever claims consistency must accept the second of the two negated restrictions, and must deny that what was mentioned is far-fetched and obscure.

Umar ibn al-Khattab, Abu Raja', and al-Hasan (with a variant from him) read "fattannahu" with the tashdid on the ta' and nun for emphasis; al-Dahhak read "iftannahu," as in the verse which al-Jawhari quoted from Abu Ubayda:

لَئِنْ فَتَنْتَنِي لَهي بِالأمْسِ افْتَنَّتْ ∗∗∗ سَعِيدًا فَأمْسى قَدْ غَوى كُلُّ مُسْلِمِ

Qatada and Abu Amr in one narration read "annama fatanahu" with the dual pronoun, referring to the two litigants. ﴿فاسْتَغْفَرَ رَبَّهُ﴾ — "So he asked his Lord for forgiveness," after he knew that what had come from him was a sin. ﴿وخَرَّ راكِعًا﴾ — "and fell down bowing," i.e., prostrating, the bowing being a metaphor for prostration, because it leads to it, so it was treated as its cause, and then the term was used for it figuratively; or it is a metaphor for its resemblance to it in bending and humility. The Arabs say: "a bowing palm tree" and "a prostrating palm tree." A poet said:

فَخَرَّ عَلى وجْهِهِ راكِعًا ∗∗∗ وتابَ إلى اللَّهِ مِن كُلِّ ذَنْبِ

It is also said: i.e., he fell down for prostration, bowing, i.e., praying, the bowing meaning prayer, because the figurative use of it for prayer is well known; and supplying an object for "kharra" is indicated by the predominance of its context, because it means "fell to the ground," as in His saying: ﴿فَخَرَّ عَلَيْهِمُ السَّقْفُ مِن فَوْقِهِمْ﴾.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: i.e., he fell from his bowing, that is, he prostrated after having been bowing; its apparent meaning keeps bowing in its literal sense, and "kharra" is taken to mean "sajada." The majority hold the view we previously stated. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, and his companions cited this verse as evidence that bowing takes the place of prostration in the prostration of recitation; this is also the view of al-Khattabi from the Shafi'is. There is no difference in this between prayer and outside it, as in al-Bazzaziyya and others. In al-Kashf, the Hanafis said: analogy requires that bowing take the place of prostration, because the Lawgiver made it bowing, and one of the two is used figuratively for the other since it stands in its place and suffices for it. They supported this by saying that prostration was not commanded for its own sake, and therefore was not legislated as a goal in itself of drawing near to God, but for humility, which is achieved by bowing. "If you say": Dawud's prostration was a prostration of gratitude, and the discussion concerns the prostration of recitation. I say: No, that does not matter to me, because I did not argue from Dawud's act, but from the Lawgiver's making it sufficient in place of prostration. The Shafi'is, our companions, may dispute that the relationship for metaphor is what they mentioned; rather it is the general inclination away from the humility shared between them, or because it is a prelude to it, as al-Hasan said: "One does not prostrate until one bows." Or "he fell down praying." What is considered is the utmost humility, and that is not in bowing. End.

It is not hidden that what is known of the Prophet ﷺ is prostration, and we have not found in any report that he (peace and blessings be upon him) bowed instead for recitation, even once, nor did his companions (may Allah be pleased with them). The analogy mentioned is not strong, so the safest course is to do what is transmitted and nothing else. Indeed some Shafi'is said: the statement of the companions that bowing does not take the place of prostration apparently indicates the permissibility of bowing, but this is far-fetched, and analogy indicates its prohibition. What the author of al-Kashf meant by what was mentioned in the question, that Dawud's prostration was a prostration of gratitude, is that it was likewise from our Prophet ﷺ.

For al-Nasa'i and Ibn Mardawayh reported with a good chain from Ibn Abbas that the Prophet

(ﷺ) prostrated in (Sad) and said: "Dawud prostrated for it as repentance, and we prostrate for it as thanksgiving." That is, [it was in thanks] for the acceptance of the repentance of Dawud (peace be upon him) for acting against what is better (khilaf al-awla), despite his lofty rank. He (peace be upon him) suffered in this matter an unsettling anxiety that no one else suffered, as you will learn, God willing. Adam (peace be upon him), although he also faced a great matter, was afflicted with grief over leaving Paradise. For that he was recompensed with the command for this Community to recognize his station and that Allah bestowed upon him a blessing that demands continued thanksgiving until the Hour. In some narrations, his story bears a resemblance to what happened to our Prophet (ﷺ) in the story of Zaynab, which called for rebuke upon him through the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿And you were concealing within yourself﴾, and so on. So mentioning it reminds him (ﷺ) of that and of what occurred and what the matter ended in, which is higher and greater. It seems that this demanded continued thanksgiving by showing prostration to him. Perhaps this is the reason for singling out Dawud with this, although the like of it occurred for other prophets (peace be upon them), so reflect on this. And do not overlook that the surah is Meccan according to the correct view, while the story of Zaynab (may Allah be pleased with her) is Medinan. The difficulty is resolved by holding that the prostration was after the story, so let it be settled. According to the Hanafis, it is one of the obligatory prostrations of recitation (sajdat al-tilawah, prostrations made upon reciting or hearing certain verses), as mentioned in the books of jurisprudence. As for those who interpreted ﴿and fell down bowing﴾ as "fell down to prostrate while praying," they held that what occurred from Dawud (peace be upon him) was a prayer containing prostration, and it was for seeking forgiveness. In our law, it has been prescribed to pray two rak'ahs upon repentance. However, we have not found in any report anything indicating that what is mentioned here should be understood as Dawud's (peace be upon him) prayer for that purpose. We have only found that he prostrated and turned back (anaba), meaning he returned to Allah, the Exalted, in repentance.

﴿So We forgave him that﴾; that is, We did not forgive him for what he sought forgiveness for.

Ahmad and Abd ibn Humayd related, from Yunus ibn Hibban, that Dawud (peace be upon him) wept for forty nights until the grass grew around him from his tears. Then he said: "O Lord, my forehead has been wounded, my tears have dried up, and my sin is still upon me as it was." So it was called out to him: "O Dawud, are you hungry so that you should be fed? Or thirsty so that you should be given drink? Or wronged so that you should be given victory?" Then he let out a great sob, and the greenery that had grown around him withered, and at that moment he was forgiven.

In the narration of Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in the Zawa'id al-Zuhd, from Mujahid, it is related that he prostrated himself for forty nights, until from the tears of his eyes there grew herbage that covered his head. Then he said: "..." etc.

It is also related that he did not drink water except that a third of it was from his tears. He exerted himself, longing for God Most High to pardon him, until he almost perished. He was preoccupied with this and neglected his kingdom, until a son of his called Iyasha (Ishba) rose up against his rule and called people to himself. The people of deviation from among the Children of Israel gathered around him. When Dawud was forgiven, he fought him and defeated him.

Ahmad related, from Thabit, that he (peace be upon him) made seven mattresses and filled them with ashes until he had soaked them with tears. He never drank a drink without mixing it with the tears of his eyes. Also related from Wahb: he withdrew from women and wept until he trembled, and the tears left furrows on his face. His fear and anxiety did not cease, peace be upon him, even after the forgiveness. Ahmad, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Jarir related, from Ata al-Khurasani, that Dawud carved his sin into his palm so that he would not forget it, and whenever he saw it his hands would tremble.

Ahmad and others related, from Thabit, from Safwan, and Abd ibn Humayd by way of Ata ibn al-Sa'ib, from Abu Abd Allah al-Jadali: "Dawud did not raise his head to the sky after the sin until he died." ﴿And indeed he has with Us a station of nearness﴾, meaning closeness after the forgiveness.

﴿And a good place of return﴾; that is, a good place of return in Paradise. Abd ibn Humayd related, from Ubayd ibn Umayr, that he said concerning the verse: he draws near to his Lord, glory be to Him, until He places His hand upon him. This, if it is authentic, belongs to the mutashabih (the ambiguous verses whose meaning is not to be taken literally).

Ahmad in the Zuhd, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, from Malik ibn Dinar, that he said concerning it: On the Day of Resurrection Dawud, peace be upon him, will be brought forward to the Throne's leg, and then the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, will say: "O Dawud, glorify Me today with that beautiful, melodious voice with which you glorified Me in the world." He will say: "O Lord, how, when You have taken it away?" He will say: "I will return it to you today." Then he will burst forth with a voice that overwhelms the bliss of the people of Paradise.

This is the matter. There is disagreement over the origin of his story, upon which what has been built has been built. It is said: he (peace be upon him) saw the wife of a man called Uriya, one of the believers of his people; in some reports he was his vizier. His heart inclined to her, so he asked him to divorce her, but he was too shy to refuse him, so he did so, and Dawud married her. She was the mother of Sulayman. This was permissible in his shari'a (divine law; the religious law given to a prophet) and customary among his people, not compromising manliness, since some of them would ask others to give up their wives to them when they found them attractive. Indeed, a man among the Ansar in the early period of Islam after the Hijra, if he had two wives, would give up one of them to whoever among the Muhajirun he made his brother. But because of his great station, his elevated rank and his exalted status, he (peace be upon him) was admonished through this example that it was not fitting for him to undertake what the individuals of his community undertake, and to ask a man who had only one wife to give her up so that he could marry her, despite having many wives. Rather, it was obligatory upon him to oppose his natural inclination, to subdue his self, and to be patient with what he was tested with.

It is also said that he secretly intended that if Uriya were killed, he would marry her. Ibn Hajar inclined to this view in his Tuhfa.

It is also said: Uriya had not married her, but had proposed to her, and then he (peace be upon him) proposed himself, and her family preferred him. So his sin was that he proposed upon the proposal of his believing brother. In some reports it is said that he did this without knowing about his brother's proposal, and so he was reproached for not asking whether anyone had proposed to her or not.

It is also said: in his shari'a, if a man died and left a wife, his guardians had more right to her, unless they were unwilling to marry her. When Uriya was killed, Dawud proposed to his wife, supposing that his guardians were unwilling, but when they heard, his awe and majesty prevented them from proposing to her.

It is also said: he was engaged in worship when two people came to him, a man and a woman, seeking his judgment. He looked at the woman in order to recognize her, and this is a permissible look. But his self inclined naturally toward her, and he was distracted from some of his supererogatory devotions, and for this he was reproached.

It is also said: he did not verify the matter in judgment and wronged the defendant before asking him, because of the fear that had seized him. The dispute between the two litigants was between two humans in reality, either according to the apparent meaning of what is related, or by taking "the ewe" in it as a metaphor for the woman. This is reported from Abu Muslim. The most acceptable of these views is that which is furthest from undermining the rank of prophethood. The storytellers (qussas) have a well-known account which almost cannot be sound, because it contains great undermining of his rank, peace be upon him.

For this reason Ali, may God ennoble his face, is reported in some books to have said: "Whoever narrates the story of Dawud, peace be upon him, according to what the storytellers relate, I will flog him one hundred and sixty times," and that is the prescribed punishment for slander against the prophets, may God's blessings and peace be upon them all.

This was Ali's own ijtihad (independent legal reasoning), may God ennoble his face. The reason for doubling the punishment compared to the punishment for free persons is that they, peace be upon them, are the masters of masters. This is a commendable view, except that al-Zayn al-Iraqi mentioned that the report itself was not authenticated from the Commander of the Faithful, may God ennoble his face.

Abu Hayyan said: What we hold to is what the apparent meaning of the verse indicates: that those who scaled the sanctuary were humans, who entered upon him by a way other than the proper entrance and at a time other than when he sat for judgment. He was frightened of them, supposing that they meant to assassinate him, since he was alone in his sanctuary worshipping his Lord, Mighty and Majestic. When it became clear to him that they had come for a judgment, and two of them stepped forward to litigate, as God Most High related, Dawud, peace be upon him, had supposed their entry upon him at that time and from that direction to be a trial from God Most High, that they would assassinate him. But what he had supposed did not happen, so he sought forgiveness for that supposition, since it was proven false, and it could not have come to pass as he imagined. He fell down in prostration and returned to God Most High. Glory be to Him forgave him that supposition, for He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So We forgave him that﴾, and nothing preceded it except His saying: ﴿And Dawud thought that We had only tested him﴾. We know with certainty that the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected from sins, and it is impossible for them to fall into any of them, by necessity; for if we permitted any such thing concerning them, the shari'a (divine law) would collapse, and nothing that they say is a revelation from God Most High could be trusted. What God Most High related in His Book passes as He intended, and what the storytellers related that contains a diminishment of the rank of messengership we reject.

And we, as the poet said:

"We prefer the judgment of reason in every doubt, when the ignorant storytellers prefer reports."

End of quotation. Something close to this from one aspect has been said: that a group intended to kill him, peace be upon him, so they scaled the sanctuary and found people with him. They feigned a litigation like the one God Most High related, and he knew their purpose, so he intended to take revenge on them. He thought this was a trial from God Most High and a test for him, whether he would become angry for his own self or not. So he sought forgiveness from his Lord for what he had resolved upon of revenge against them and punishing them for his own right, because he had turned away from the forgiveness that was more fitting for him. It is also said: the seeking of forgiveness was for the one who attacked him, and God Most High's saying ﴿So We forgave him﴾ means: So We forgave him on account of it. This is far-fetched (ta'assuf), even though it occurs in some books of kalam (theology). In my view, abandoning the reports entirely regarding the story is something a fair-minded person can hardly accept. Yes, what is not acceptable from them is whatever involves undermining the rank of prophethood, and an interpretation that removes that is not accepted. It must be said that from him, peace be upon him, there was nothing except leaving what is better befitting his exalted station, and seeking forgiveness for it, and this does not undermine infallibility ('ismah, the protection of prophets from sin).

[p. 185] [p. 186]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 26:

﴿O David, indeed We have made you a khalifah (vicegerent) on the earth﴾. This is either a narration of what he (peace be upon him) was addressed with, showing his nearness to Him (glory be to Him, the Mighty and Majestic). Or it is a continuation of an implied statement that is conjoined to (We forgave), or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to its agent, meaning: "And We said to him," or "saying to him: O David, indeed We have made you a khalifah on the earth," that is, "We have appointed you as a successor (istakhlafnāka) to rule over it and to judge among its people." Or, "We have made you a khalifah from among the prophets who came before you, who stood upright with the truth." On the first reading, it is like "So-and-so is the khalifah of the ruler," when he is appointed by the ruler's authority to carry out what he wills. On the second reading, it is like "This son is a khalifah for his father," that is, one who fills his place and carries out what he used to do, without regard to life, death, or other such things. The first reading is more evident, and the favour in it is greater. Thus he (peace be upon him) is the khalifah of God, Exalted, in the sense you have heard.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is not said 'khalifat Allah' (the khalifah of God, Exalted) except for His Messenger. As for the caliphs, each one of them is a khalifah on behalf of Him. What comes in poetry of calling one of them 'khalifat Allah' is a figurative usage (tajawwuz), as Qays al-Ruqayyat said:

*Khalīfatu-llāhi fī bariyyatihi*
*jaffat bi-dhāka al-aqlāmu wa-al-kutub*

("The khalifah of God over His creation: the pens and the books have dried up with that.")

The Companions said to Abu Bakr: "Khalifat Rasul Allah" (khalifah of the Messenger of God), and he was called by this until he died. When 'Umar came to rule, they said: "Khalifat khalifat Rasul Allah" (khalifah of the khalifah of the Messenger of God), then this was abandoned in favour of the brevity of "Amir al-Mu'minin" (Commander of the Faithful)."

The Greatest Shaykh, Muhyi al-Din (may God sanctify his secret), held that the khalifah among the messengers is the one to whom legislation (tashri') has been delegated. Perhaps this is among his own technical terms, and there is no dispute over terminology.

Some scholars used this verse to argue that the earth needs a khalifah from God, Exalted. This is the view of those who make it obligatory upon God, Exalted, to appoint an imam, because it is among the grace (lutf) that is incumbent upon Him, glory be to Him. The Jama'ah (the Sunni majority) do not say this; for them the imamate is among the subsidiary matters (furu'), even though they mention it in books of creed. There is nothing in the verse that necessarily implies this, as is not hidden. The verification of this matter belongs in its proper place.

﴿So judge between the people with the truth﴾ which God, Exalted, has legislated for you. Truth (al-haqq) is the opposite of falsehood, and the article (al-) in it is for a known reference (li-l-'ahd). It has been permitted that it may mean one of His names, Exalted, that is, "by the judgement of the Truth," meaning God, Exalted, since it is known that the essences (dhawat) are not what is judged by. It has been objected that its being contrasted with desire (hawa) rejects this; perhaps the one who holds this view takes the contrasted term to be an omitted genitive construction (muḍāf maḥdhūf), and the contrast is in terms of the fact that the judgement of God, Exalted, is never except with the truth. The command to judge with the truth is made consequent upon what has preceded, because khilafah in both senses requires just judgement, especially on the first meaning, because it is evident that his being a khalifah for Him, Exalted, requires that his judgement not oppose the judgement of the one who appointed him, but rather that it be in accordance with His will and His pleasure.

It has been said: what is consequent is the absolute judgement, because it is evident that it is consequent upon his being a khalifah. He mentioned "the truth" because it is by it that his rectitude lies. It has also been said: that was made consequent because khilafah is a great blessing, whose thanks is justice.

[Page 187]

In al-Bahr al-Muhit (the Ocean Surrounding): this is a command to constancy, and an admonition to others who have been put in charge of the affairs of people, that they should judge among them with the truth. Otherwise, he, being infallible (ma'sum), judges only with the truth. In my view, the prohibition in His saying, glory be to Him and Exalted: ﴿and do not follow desire﴾ is to be interpreted in this same manner, for following desire is something that hardly occurs from one who is infallible. The apparent context indicates that what is meant is: do not follow the desire of the self in judgements. Some generalised, saying: that is, in judgements and in other matters of religion and worldly affairs.

It is supported by this prohibition what has been said: that his sin (peace be upon him) was hastening to believe the claimant and wronging the other before questioning him, not inclining towards the wife of Uriah. So it is as if it were said: "Do not follow desire in judgement as you followed it at first." In this there is the objection that following desire and judging by other than what God, Exalted, has legislated for him is not fitting for his station, especially since God, Exalted, informed, before mentioning the matter of the two litigants, that He had given him judgement and decisive speech. Therefore this is nothing but guidance towards what the station of khilafah requires, and an admonition to one who is below him (peace be upon him).

The root of hawa (desire) is the inclination of the soul towards appetite, and it is said of the soul that is inclined towards it. It may also mean the object of desire, as in the saying:

*Hawāya ma'a al-rakbi al-yamāniyyīna musȃʻidun*
*janībun, wa-juthmānī bi-Makkata muwthaqu*

("My desire goes up with the Yemeni riders, a companion who is led away, while my body is bound in Makkah.")

Some interpreted it here in this sense, saying: that is, do not follow what the souls desire.

﴿lest it lead you astray from the way of God﴾: it is in the accusative (naṣb) on the basis that it is the answer (jawāb) to the prohibition. It has also been said that it is in the jussive mood (majzūm) by conjunction with the prohibition, and is vowelled with a fatḥah because of the meeting of two sukun (ending consonants), that is: so that desire, or following it, becomes a cause of your going astray from its proofs which He set up upon the truth. These proofs are more general than the rational (ʿaqliyyah) and the transmitted (naqliyyah) proofs. Turning away from these proofs is either due to failure to understand them, or to not acting upon what they require.

His saying, exalted: ﴿Indeed those who go astray from the way of God, for them is a severe punishment﴾ is a reason (taʿlīl) for what precedes, by explaining its outcome. Stating "the way of God" in the place of the pronoun is for the increase of the affirmation, and to signal the complete abomination of going astray from it. The predicate of inna is either the clause ﴿for them is a punishment﴾, with "for them" as a fronted predicate and "punishment" as a delayed subject; or the adverbial phrase, with "punishment" raised as an agent by what is contained in it of the sense of being established.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan (with a variant transmission from them), and Abu Haywah read ﴿yudallūna﴾ with a damma on the yā'. Abu Hayyan said: this reading is more general, because none goes astray except one who is himself astray; but the reading of the majority is clearer, because what is meant by the relative clause is those whom the following of desire has led astray, and who, after it has led them astray, have become astray.

His saying, exalted: ﴿bi-mā nasū﴾ (because they forgot) is connected to the stable/established predicate, the bā' is causal (sababiyyah), and mā is verbal-masdar (maṣdariyyah). His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿yawm al-ḥisāb﴾ (the Day of Reckoning) is the object of "nasū" according to what is most apparent, meaning: that punishment is established for them because of their forgetting, and their not remembering the Day of Reckoning. On this reading it is an explicit reason for the establishment of the severe punishment for them, because of forgetting the Day of Reckoning, after the indication of the causality of what it entails and necessitates, namely going astray from the way of God, Exalted, for going astray from it necessitates complete forgetting of the Day of Reckoning; rather, this is one instance of it.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ikrimah that the speech is in inversion (taqdīm wa-ta'khīr), meaning: "for them on the Day of Reckoning is a severe punishment because they forgot." Thus the Day of Reckoning is an adverbial of time for His saying, exalted: ﴿for them﴾. The forgetting is made a metaphor for their going astray from the way of God, by the relation of causality; and it necessarily follows that the object of forgetting is the way of God, Exalted. On this reading the explicit reason is the same as the implied reason, not different from it in essence but only in its expression. So reflect.

Page 188

﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain.﴾ That is, a creation in vain. So it is in the accusative as a substitute for the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq, the cognate accusative), like the phrase *kul hanian* ("eat with enjoyment"), meaning *aklan hanian* ("an enjoyable eating"). Al-batil ("the vain") is that which has no wisdom in it. It is also permitted for it to be a circumstantial accusative (al-hal) of the subject of *khalaqna* ("We created"), with an omitted modifier, meaning "possessors of vanity." Al-batil may also mean play and frivolity, that is, "We did not create that while being idle and playful," as in His saying, ﴿And We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾ It is also permitted for it to be a circumstantial accusative of the object, with this same interpretation. In any case, the statement is a new sentence (al-kalam al-mustanaf) confirming what precedes it about the Return and the Reckoning. The creation of the heaven and the earth and what is between them of created things, containing striking wisdoms, profound secrets and abundant benefits, is the strongest proof of the greatness of power, and that the matter of the Return and the Reckoning is not beyond it. For creating these things in this way indicates that He, mighty and majestic, does not leave people, when they die, neglected (sudan), but returns them and calls them to account. This is perhaps the better view.

It is also permitted for the sentence to be in the position of a circumstantial accusative relative to the subject of *nasu* ("they forgot"), brought to make the forgetting of the Day of Reckoning seem more terrible, as if it were said: "They forgot the Day of Reckoning although there is that which points to it." This, as you see, is far-fetched. It is also permitted for *batilan* ("vain") to be an object, explained as the opposite of truth, and meaning the following of desire, as if it were said: "We did not create this world for the vanity which is the following of desire, but for the truth which is what the proof requires of monotheism and adherence to the Law," like His saying, ﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they worship Me.﴾ Its remoteness is not hidden. On this view the sentence is a new sentence establishing the prohibition of following desire. It has also been said that it is a conjunction with what came before in meaning, as if it were said: "Do not follow desire, for it will be a cause of your misguidance, and because He, exalted, did not create the world for the sake of following desire, but created it for monotheism and holding fast to the Law. So do not be heedless."

﴿That﴾ refers to the denial that He created what was mentioned in vain. ﴿is the assumption of those who disbelieved﴾: that is, their supposition, so that the predication is valid, or one supposes an omitted modifier, meaning "that assumption is the assumption of those who disbelieved." For their denial of the Return and the recompense amounts to saying that the creation of what was mentioned is devoid of wisdom and is merely vain. Therefore He, glorified, said: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ Or, their denial of that amounts to denying the greatness of power, which is a denial of its proof, namely the creation of what was mentioned containing striking wisdoms and secrets. This is according to the first view in explaining the confirmation, and it is, as you see, far-fetched.

﴿So woe to those who disbelieved﴾: a subject and predicate (mubtada' wa khabar). The fa' ("so") serves to indicate that the establishing of woe for them follows from their false assumption, just as placing the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) in the place of their pronoun indicates, through what is in the relative clause (al-silah), that their disbelief is the cause of it. There is no contradiction between the two, because their assumption is one form of their disbelief, so the force of the causal indication is strengthened. The *min* ("from") in His saying ﴿from the Fire﴾ is either inceptive (ibtida'iyyah, indicating origin), or explanatory (bayaniyyah), or causal (ta'liliyyah), as in His saying ﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written﴾ and its like. On this last reading it indicates that the Fire is the cause of woe being established for them, explicitly, after the indication that what leads to it, namely their assumption and disbelief, is the cause. That is: woe to them because of the Fire that results from their assumption and disbelief. It has been said that the statement on this reading involves an omitted modifier, meaning "from entering the Fire."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 28:

﴿Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous deeds the same as the corrupters on earth?﴾ "Am" (أم) is disjunctive (munqati'ah) and is taken to mean "bal" (rather) together with the interrogative hamzah. The hamzah is for the denial of equality between the two groups and the negation of it in the most emphatic and forceful manner. "Bal" marks a transitional turn (al-idrab al-intiqali) from establishing the matter of resurrection and reckoning, by means of what has already passed concerning the negation that the world was created in vain, to establishing and confirming it by denying that the two groups are equal. The meaning is: "Rather, shall We treat the believing reformers like the disbelieving corrupters on earth, the earth which was made their dwelling place?" This is what the absence of resurrection would require, and what follows from it of recompense, since the two groups would be equal in enjoying the life of this world. "Rather, most of the disbelievers have a greater share of it than most of the believers." However, that making (of equality) is impossible (muhal) and contrary to wisdom (hikmah), so resurrection and recompense are necessarily required, in order to raise the first group to the highest of the 'Illiyyin and to return the latter to the lowest of the lowest. So they said. Its apparent sense is that the impossibility of making the two groups equal is a wisdom that requires the necessity of the bodily return (al-ma'ad al-jismani). This is obscure. The apparent view is that spiritual return (al-ma'ad al-ruhani) suffices for what wisdom requires, namely rewarding the first group and punishing the latter. So the rational proof to which the verse points clearly establishes a return, but only after refuting metempsychosis (al-tanasukh). This is sufficient in refuting the disbelievers of the Arabs, for they do not hold to any return at all, and metempsychosis never occurred to them. The establishment of bodily return has another well-known method among the theologians (al-mutakallimun), and making this rational proof a means of establishing it requires reflection. So reflect.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Shall We treat the God-fearing like the wicked?﴾ is a turn and transition (idrab wa intiqal) from establishing what was mentioned by means of the impossibility of equality between the two groups mentioned in general, to establishing it by means of what is more evidently impossible, namely equality between the pious believers and the wretched disbelievers. Taking "al-fujjar" (the wicked) to mean the wicked among the believers does not fit the context. It is possible that the two groups here are the same as the first two, and the repetition is by reference to two other attributes which are more emphatic in denying equality than the first two attributes. Whatever the case, the plural forms in the two places do not refer to specific individuals. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said: "The verse is general, encompassing all Muslims and disbelievers."

It has been said: it was revealed concerning specific people among the polytheists of Quraysh who said to the believers, "We will be given good in the Hereafter that you will not be given," so it was revealed. You know that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion of revelation. In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas, related by Ibn 'Asakir, he said: "Those who believed are 'Ali, Hamzah, and 'Ubaydah ibn al-Harith, may God be pleased with them, and the corrupters on earth are 'Utbah, al-Walid ibn 'Utbah, and Shaybah, who are those who fought in single combat on the day of Badr." Perhaps he meant that they were the cause of the revelation.

[Page 189]

Al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 38, verse 29:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A Book﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, which refers to the Qur'an or to the surah. On the second view, it may be estimated as masculine, meaning "it" or "this," and according to a group this is preferable, out of regard for the predicate (khabar). It may also be estimated as feminine, out of regard for the referent (marji'). His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We have sent it down to you﴾ is its attribute (sifah). His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿blessed﴾, meaning abundant in religious and worldly benefits, is a second predicate of the subject, or an attribute of "Book" according to those who permit placing a descriptive attribute (wasf sarih) after a non-explicit one (ghayr sarih). It has also been read as ﴿blessed﴾ in the accusative (mubarakan), as a circumstantial state (hal) of the object of "sent down," and it is a permanent state (hal lazimah), because blessing never departs from it. May God Most High place us within its blessings and benefit us with its noble verses. His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿that they may ponder its verses﴾ is connected to "We have sent it down." It is also permissible that it be connected to an omitted verb that indicates it.

Its original form is liyatadabbaroo, with a taa' after the yaa' (the first letter of the verb's form), and 'Ali, may God honor his face, read it in this original form. That is: We sent it down so that they may reflect on its verses, among which is this verse that expresses the secrets of creation and legislation, so that they may know what it arranges (yudabbir) and follow its outward meanings, which include sublime meanings and fitting interpretations. The pronoun of the subject (wa-damir al-raf') refers to "people of understanding" (ulu al-albab) by the method of tanazu' (competition between two verbs for a common complement) with the second verb being operative (i'mal al-thani), or it refers to the believers only, or to them and to the corrupters. Abu Ja'far read it as litaddabbaroo with the taa' of address and the dal lightened (tadhdif), and similarly it is reported from 'Asim and al-Kisa'i with a difference of transmission from them. The original is litatadabbaroo with two taa's, one of which is elided according to the disagreement about it: is it the taa' of the present-tense prefix or the taa' that follows it? The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the scholars of his community by the method of taghlib (prioritizing the masculine/addressee), meaning: let you and the scholars of your community reflect. ﴿And that people of understanding may take heed﴾: that is, that those with pure intellects, free from defects, may be admonished by it; or that they may recall what is almost fixed in their minds, owing to their great firmness in knowing it through the proofs set up for it. For the sending of messengers and the sending down of books is for clarifying what is known only through revelation (shar'), such as the obligation of the five daily prayers, and for guiding to what reason can grasp independently, such as the existence of the Eternal Creator, exalted is His majesty and widespread His bounty.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verses 30–31:

﴿And We gave to David Solomon; how excellent a servant he was.﴾ It is read as "نِعْمَ" (ni'ma) in its original form, and the object of praise is omitted, meaning "how excellent a servant he is," that is, Solomon, as indicated by its being placed after David even though it is the explicit object of "We gave." Another reason is that His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿Indeed, he was one who turned back (awwab)﴾, meaning one who returns to God, the Exalted, in repentance, as the context suggests, or who returns to glorifying (tasbih), or to His good pleasure, the Mighty and Majestic, is a justification for the praise. This (the praise) comes from his own state, because the pronoun in the genitive in His, the Glorified's, saying ﴿when there were displayed before him﴾ refers to him, peace be upon him, certainly. "Idh" (when) is in the accusative, governed by "udhkur" (remember). What is meant by mentioning the time is the mention of what occurred in it. Or it is an adverbial complement of "awwab," or of "ni'ma." The adverbial complement is flexible, but it is objectionable on both views that the restriction detracts from the perfection of the praise, so the first is preferable. It is like evidence that he is awwab, meaning: remember what proceeded from him when there were displayed before him ﴿in the late afternoon﴾ etc., for it bears witness to that. "Al-'Ashiyy" (late afternoon), according to al-Raghib, is from the decline of the sun until dawn; some said it is from that until the end of the day. The two adverbial phrases are attached to "'uridat" (were displayed). His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿the poised (al-safinat)﴾ is the deputy subject, and its being placed after them is, as has been mentioned more than once, to create anticipation for what is delayed. "Al-safin" among horses is the one that raises one of its two forelegs or hind legs and stands on the tip of its hoof. Al-Zajjaj recited:

He became accustomed to standing poised, so that he is always, as it were, standing on three legs much of the time.

Abu 'Ubayda said: it is the one that brings its two forelegs together and levels them. As for the one that stands on the edge of the hoof, it is "al-mutakhayyim." According to al-Tahdhib and Matn al-Lugha, it is "al-mukhayyim." Al-Qutaybi said: "al-safin" is the one standing among horses and other things.

In a hadith: "Whoever is pleased that people stand for him in ṣufūn, let him take his seat in the Fire."

That is, they continually stand for him. Qutrub related this, and he recited for al-Nabigha:

We have a tent pitched in its courtyard, with noble she-camels and poised horses.

Al-Farra' said: "I have seen the Arabs upon this, and their poetry indicates that it is standing specifically."
