The well-known meaning of ṣufūn is what has preceded, and it is among the praiseworthy attributes of horses, which hardly come to be realized except among the pure Arabs. ﴿The swift (al-jiyad)﴾ is the plural of "jawad," for the masculine and feminine alike. It is said: "jada al-faras" (the horse became broken in), meaning it became trained, "yajudu juwdatan" with a dammah, and it is "jawad." It is also pluralized as "ajwad" and "ajawid." Some said: it is the plural of "jawd," like "thawb" and "athwab." It has been explained as the one that is quick in its walking, and it has been said: it is the one that is generous in running. It has been said: they were described with ṣufūn and swiftness to show that they combined the two praiseworthy attributes, standing and running; that is, when they stood they were still and calm in their positions, and when they ran they were swift and light in their running. Horses are praised for stillness in standing just as they are praised for speed in running. From this is the saying of Muslim ibn al-Walid:

And when its saddle-bow is tied with its reins, it gnaws the bit until the visitor departs.

It has also been said: "jayyid" is like "kayyis," the opposite of "radi'" (inferior), and it is pluralized as "jiyadat" and "jayaʼid." This was deemed weak, because mentioning it together with ﴿the poised﴾ would then be useless, and because it would forfeit praising the horses in respect of their two states, and because "jiyad" is more general, so mentioning it would be a generalization after a specification, which is open to question.

In al-Bahr it is said: "al-jiyad" are those with long necks, from "al-jid," which is the neck. I am in doubt about the authenticity of this. In al-Qamus it says: "al-jid" with a kasra is the neck or its necklace, or its front; its plural is "ajyad" and "judud." With a fathah it is its length or its thinness together with length, and the masculine form is "ajyad," the feminine "jaydā'," and "jaydāna," and its plural is "judad." End of quote. I consulted other sources and found nothing further on this, so let it be settled. It may be said that "al-jiyad" is an irregular plural of "ajyad," "jaydā'," or "jaydāna," or that it is the plural of "jayad" with a fathah, like "jamal" and "jimal," and by "jayad" is meant "ajyad" or something similar, as "al-khalq" (creation) is used to mean "al-makhluq" (the created). God, the Exalted, knows best. In any case, the two attributes may be applied to male and female horses alike, and the plural with the suffix "-āt" (ʼalif and tā') is not specific to the feminine. So there is no need, after saying that what was displayed included both male and female horses, to go on to say that the feminine is given precedence over the masculine in "al-safinat," and that this is permissible though rare. "Al-jam'" here is meant to indicate abundance. According to al-Kalbi, these horses were a thousand horses that Solomon, peace be upon him, took when he raided Damascus and Nusaybin and acquired them. This report has been challenged on the grounds that spoils (ghanā'im, goods seized in war) were not lawful for anyone other than our Prophet ﷺ, as stated in the sound hadith.

It was answered that they may be fay' (property obtained without fighting) rather than ghanima, and according to Muqatil: they were a thousand horses that he inherited from his father David, peace be upon him, and David had taken them from the Amalekites, who are the children of ʻImlīq ibn ʻAwṣ ibn ʻĀd ibn Iram.

This report has been challenged, in addition to the first, on the grounds that prophets, peace be upon them, are not inherited from, as stated in the hadith narrated by Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, in which he argued in the matter of Fadak and al-'Awali in the presence of the Companions, who are those whom the blame of any blamer does not deter in God's cause.

It was answered that what is meant by inheritance is the seizing of disposal, not ownership. He slaughtered them as an act of drawing near to God, according to the views on the verse below. It also occurs in some reports, which does not imply ownership. Awf said: "It has reached me that they were horses with wings, brought out for him from the sea, which were not possessed by anyone before him or after him." This is also reported from al-Hasan. Ibn Jarir and others related from Ibrahim al-Taymi that they were twenty thousand winged horses. There is nothing in this except astonishment. Since no attention is paid to reports on this matter, because none of them is a sound marfu' report (traced to the Prophet ﷺ), nor anything of the same status on which one may rely, as far as I know, we may say: they were horses that he had, like the horses kept by kings, which came to him through some means of acquiring kingship; he reviewed them, and they continued to be displayed before him until the sun set. It was said: and he neglected the afternoon prayer. Al-Tabarsi related this from ʻAlī, may God honour his face, and from Qatada and al-Suddi. Then he said: "In the reports of our companions, it is that he missed the beginning of the time." Al-Jubba'i said: "The obligatory prayer did not escape him; rather, what escaped him was a supererogatory prayer he would perform at the end of the day."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 32:**

﴿So he said: "Indeed, I have preferred the love of good things over the remembrance of my Lord"﴾. He, peace be upon him, said this as an acknowledgment of the distraction that had come from him, as a sign of regret for it, and as a preparation for the command that follows it, to return the horses and hamstring them, according to the well-known view. The word *khayr* (good) has commonly been used for wealth, and from this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿if he leaves behind khayr (wealth)﴾, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And whatever good (khayr) you spend, indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾, and His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And indeed, he is intense in his love of khayr (wealth)﴾. Some scholars said: wealth is not called *khayr* until it is abundant and from good (lawful) means, as it is narrated that Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, entered upon a freedman of his and said: "Shall I not make a bequest, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "No, because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿if he leaves behind khayr (wealth)﴾, and you do not have much wealth."

It has been narrated that its interpretation here as wealth is from al-Dahhak and Ibn Jubayr. Abu Hayyan said: by *khayr* is meant horses, and the Arabs call horses *khayr*. This is also related from Qatada and al-Suddi. Perhaps this is because *khayr* is attached to them. In a report: "Horses have goodness (*khayr*) tied to their foreheads until the Day of Resurrection."

As for *ahbabtu* (I have loved/preferred), according to what is transmitted from al-Farra', it is implicitly (*mudammin*) containing the meaning of preferring (*al-iithar*), and this is treated as a literal usage because of its fame in that sense. The apparent statement of some of them is that it is literal in this sense. It is of those verbs that are construed with *ʿalā* (on), but here it is construed with *ʿan* (from) because it is implicitly containing the meaning of turning away (*al-inaba*). *Hubba al-khayr* (the love of good) is the direct object: that is, "I preferred the love of good, turning away from the remembrance of my Lord," or "I turned away from the love of good, preferring it."

It has been permitted that *hubb* be in the accusative as an analogical (comparative) verbal noun (*al-masdar al-tashbihi*), and the object of *ahbabtu* would then be omitted, meaning: "I loved the swift horses or their presentation with a love like the love of good, turning from that remembrance of my Lord." Here *khayr* does not refer to horses. Abu al-Fath al-Hamdani mentioned that *ahbabtu* means "I kept to/stayed (*lazimtu*)," from the line of verse: "The evil camel struck when it stayed (*ahabba*)." This was objected to: this meaning of *ahabba* is strange and occurs only in this line, and the strangeness of a word indicates awkwardness of usage, while the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is exalted above that. Moreover, *luzum* (keeping to) is not construed with *ʿan* unless it is implicitly containing a meaning that is construed with it, or it is used figuratively in that sense. So there is no benefit in deviating from the well-known meaning, even though it is also correct by implicit meaning. Some scholars took *al-ihbab* from the very beginning to mean sitting back and being detained (*al-taqaʿud wa al-ihtibas*), with *hubba al-khayr* as an object for the sake of which (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*): that is, "I sat back and was held back from the remembrance of my Lord because of the love of good." It was objected that what the lexicographers indicate about *ahabba* is that it means staying in place due to fatigue, sickness, or the like, so it does not fit the sitting back of idleness and diversion in which he, peace be upon him, was engaged.

As for the statement of some eminent scholars: after conceding the permissibility of using the restricted (*muqayyad*) in the unrestricted (*mutlaq*) sense, since staying in place out of love for horses was contrary to the pleasure of Allah the Exalted, he made it one of the diseases that need to be treated with their opposites, and for this reason he hamstrung them. Thus in *ahbabtu* there is a subsidiary metaphor (*isti'ara taba'iyya*), whose beauty is not hidden, and its suitability to the context is nothing, because this very metaphor is obscure and its indicator is not apparent. In sum, what Abu al-Fath mentioned is not something that should be opened as a door of approval among those who have knowledge (*dhawi al-irfan*). It has also been permitted to take *ahbabtu* in its apparent sense without considering its implicit meaning of what is construed with *ʿan*, and to make *ʿan* attached to an implied word such as "turning away" (*muʿridan*) or "distant" (*baʿidan*), which is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *ahbabtu*. It has also been permitted that *ʿan* be causal (*taʿlīliyya*), as will come, Allah willing. The *dhikr* (remembrance) is annexed (*mudaf*) to its object, and it has been permitted that it be annexed to its subject. It was also said: the annexation is in the sense of *al-lam* (the possessive/ for), and *dhikr* is not meant in its verbal-noun sense, but rather it means the prayer (*al-salat*), so the meaning of "from the remembrance of my Lord" is "from the prayer of my Lord which He legislated." This, as you see, is far-fetched.

Some who took *ʿan* to mean causal explained the Lord here as His Book, the Exalted, which is the Torah, meaning: "I loved the horses because of the Book of Allah the Exalted, which is the Torah, for it contains praise for keeping them tied." This was narrated from Abu Muslim. Abu Ja'far, Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr read *"inni ahbabtu"* with the *ya'* of the first person pronoun vowelled with fatha. ﴿until she was hidden behind the veil﴾ is connected to the statement of the Exalted: *ahbabtu*, with regard to the continuation of the love and its lasting according to the continuation of the presentation. That is: "I turned away from the love of good from the remembrance of my Lord, and that continued until the sun set," comparing its setting in its place of setting to the hiding of what is concealed by its veil, by way of subsidiary metaphor (*isti'ara taba'iyya*). It may also be that there is a veiled metaphor of imagination (*isti'ara makniyya takhyiliyya*) there. In any case, what Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ka'b, who said: "The veil is a veil of green emerald surrounding the creation, from which the sky has turned green," and what was said: that it is a mountain beyond Qaf, a year's distance, behind which the sun sets—its status is not hidden. People differ regarding the existence of Mount Qaf between one who affirms it and one who denies it. Al-Qarafi says: it has no existence, and to this I incline, even though those who affirm it have said what they said. The *ba'* (in *bil-hijab*) is for location (*zarfiyya*), or for instrument (*isti'ana*), or for accompaniment (*mulabasa*). The return of the pronoun to the sun without prior mention is due to the indication of *al-ʿashiyy* (the evening) upon it.

The pronoun attached to the verb in Allah's words ﴿Bring them back to me﴾ refers to "the swift horses" (al-ṣāfināt), as many commentators have said.

The apparent sense of their statements is that it refers to the "swift horses" (al-ṣāfināt) mentioned in the verse. Perhaps you may prefer that it refers to "the horses" (al-khayl), which is indicated by the present state that is witnessed, or to "the good" (al-khayr) in his words ﴿Indeed I have loved the love of good﴾, because ﴿bring them back﴾ is part of his speech, peace be upon him, while "the swift horses" are not mentioned in his speech but in the speech of Allah, the Exalted, to our Prophet (ﷺ). According to al-Zamakhshari, the discourse is on the assumption of an implied "saying" (qawl), meaning: he said, "Bring them back to me." The sentence is a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf) of an explanatory kind (bayānī), as if it were said: "What did Sulayman say?" It was answered: "He said: Bring them back." Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying that it does not need an implied element, since the sentence falls under the reporting of speech in Allah's words ﴿So he said, "Indeed I..."﴾ and so on. The "fa" (then) in Allah's words ﴿so he began to pass his hand﴾ is an explanatory "fa" (fā' faṣīḥa), revealing a sentence that has been omitted, relying on the situation to indicate it and to announce the extreme speed of compliance with the command, as in Allah's words ﴿So We said, "Strike the stone with your staff," and there gushed forth from it twelve springs﴾, meaning: so bring them back to him, then he began and so on.

"Ṭafiqa" is among the verbs of beginning (af'āl al-shurūʿ), its subject is the pronoun of Sulayman, and "masḥan" (passing the hand) is an absolute object (maf'ūl muṭlaq) of an implied verb which is its predicate, meaning: he began to pass, passing. It is not a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) construed as "māsḥan" (one passing), as Abu al-Baqa' permitted, since "ṭafiqa" must have a predicate, and this is not one of the cases where the circumstantial clause takes its place. Zayd ibn ʿAlī read "misāḥan" on the pattern of "qitāl". ﴿With the shins and the necks﴾, meaning: with their shins and their necks, on the basis that the definite article is for a prior reference, and that the "al" stands in place of the possessive pronoun that is added. The preposition "bi" (with) is connected to the "masḥ" (passing), with the meaning: he began to pass the sword over their shins and necks. A group said that it is superfluous (zā'ida), meaning: he began to pass over their shins and necks with the sword. And "masaḥtuhu bi-l-sayf" (I passed it with the sword), as al-Raghib said, is a metaphor for striking.

In al-Kashshaf: "He passes the sword over their shins and necks", meaning he cuts them. You say "masaḥa ʿilāwatahu" when he struck his nape, and "masaḥa al-musfir al-kitāb" when he cut its edges with his sword. It is also reported from al-Hasan: "He cut their hamstrings and struck their necks," intending by "kasf" the cutting. From this comes "al-kasf" in the names of the prosodic modifications (zaḥāf) and the metrical feet (ʿarūḍ). Whoever said it with the dotted "sh" (kashf) is mistaken. That the intended meaning is cutting has been indicated by some reports.

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, al-Isma'ili in his Mu'jam, and Ibn Mardawayh, with a good chain (sanad), reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "From the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said regarding Allah's words ﴿so he began to pass his hand over them with the shins and the necks﴾: he cut their shins and necks with the sword."

By that act he, peace be upon him, made them an offering (qurbān) to Allah, the Exalted, and bringing horses near as an offering was legislated in his religion. Perhaps the cutting of the hamstrings was so that their slaughter would be easy. It has been said that he, peace be upon him, had detained them in the way of Allah, the Exalted, and that this passing which he performed was a branding (wasm) of them, so that they would be known as horses detained in the way of Allah, the Exalted. This is similar to what is done today of branding with fire, and there is no harm in it in our law, so long as it is not on the face. Perhaps he, peace be upon him, saw branding with the sword as less harsh than branding with fire, so he chose it, or it was the known practice among them in those times. It is narrated that when he, peace be upon him, did that, the wind was subjected to him as a honour from Him. It has also been said that he, peace be upon him, intended by that to destroy them, since they had distracted him from the worship of his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, and his heart's attachment to them became a cause of his neglect. Al-Shibli, may his secret be sanctified, derived from this the permissibility of burning his garments with fire when they distracted him from his Lord, the Majestic in His majesty. But this is a false statement that should not be given any heed, and God forbid that the Prophet of Allah should destroy valuable property merely because he was busied with it from a worship. He had a way to remove it from his ownership with a benefit that is among the most excellent means of drawing near to Him, the Mighty and Majestic. Moreover, he, peace be upon him, had not acquired those horses and reviewed them out of arrogance or boasting, God forbid that, but he acquired them to benefit from them in the obedience of Allah, glorified is He, and he reviewed them to observe their condition, so that he might amend whatever aspect of them needed amendment, and all of that is worship. So the most that could be necessary is that he, peace be upon him, neglected one act of worship because of his occupation with another act of worship. Therefore al-Shibli's inference, may his secret be sanctified, is not valid. ʿAbd al-Wahhab al-Shaʿrani, from the Sufi masters, also pointed out its invalidity in his book (al-Yawāqīt wa-l-Jawāhir fī ʿAqāʾid al-Akābir), but he interprets the verse according to another understanding. What we have mentioned regarding its interpretation and explanation is what is well known among the majority, though they have other statements about it.

It has been said: the pronoun in ﴿bring them back﴾ refers to the sun, and the address is to the angels, peace be upon them, who are entrusted with it. They said: he requested its return when he had missed the afternoon prayer due to his occupation with the horses, so it was returned to him until he prayed the afternoon prayer. This view has been reported from ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face. It was also stated by al-Khafaji and al-Tabarsi. Al-Razi objected to this, saying that the One capable of moving the spheres and the stars is Allah, the Exalted, so it would have been necessary for him to say: "Return it to me", not "Bring them back" with the plural pronoun. If they say that it is for glorification, as in ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾, we reply: the word "rudduhā" (bring it back) indicates the greatest kind of humiliation, so how does honouring fit with this word? Moreover, if the sun had returned after sunset, it would have been witnessed by all the people of the world, and if that were so, the motives to transmit it would have been abundant. Since no one transmitted it, its falsehood is known.

The one who holds that the sun was returned to Sulayman holds that it was likewise returned for Yusha' (Joshua), and returned for our Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of the caravan and on the day of the Trench, when he was occupied from the afternoon prayer, and returned for ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face and be pleased with him, by the supplication of the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace.

It has been reported "from Asma' bint ʿUmays that the Prophet (ﷺ) was receiving revelation while his head was in the lap of ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, and he did not pray the afternoon prayer until the sun set. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Did you pray, O ʿAlī?' He said: 'No.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'O Allah, he was in Your obedience and the obedience of Your Messenger, so return the sun to him.' Asma' said: 'I saw it set, then I saw it rise after it had set, and it fell upon the earth. That was at Al-Sahba' in Khaybar.'"

[p. 194] The soundness of this report is disputed. Ibn al-Jawzi mentioned it in al-Mawdūʿāt (the fabricated reports) and said: it is undoubtedly fabricated. Its chain includes Ahmad ibn Dawud, who is abandoned in narration (matrūk al-ḥadīth), a liar, as al-Daraqutni said. Ibn Hibban said: he used to fabricate hadith. Ibn al-Jawzi also said: Ibn Shahin narrated this hadith, then he mentioned it and said: this is a false hadith. Among the blunders of its fabricator is that he looked at the appearance of a virtue, without noticing the absence of benefit in it, and that the afternoon prayer, when the sun sets, becomes a qaḍāʾ (prayer performed after its time), and the return of the sun does not make it an adāʾ (prayer performed within its time). End of quotation.

Ibn Taymiyya devoted a work to refuting the Rafidites (Rawāfiḍ), in which he mentioned the hadith with its routes and its narrators, and that it is fabricated. Imam Ahmad said: it has no basis. Al-Tahawi and Qadi ʿIyad authenticated it. Al-Tabarani narrated it in his al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr with a good chain, as Shaykh al-Islam Ibn al-ʿIraqi related in his commentary on al-Taqrib, from Asma' as well, but with a different wording. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Abu Hurayra. Ahmad ibn Salih used to say: it is not befitting for one whose path is knowledge to neglect memorizing the hadith of Asma', for it is one of the signs of prophethood. Likewise, there is disagreement regarding the hadith of the return on the day of the Trench: some said it is weak, some said it is fabricated. The scholar Ibn Hajar al-Haytami claimed its authenticity. As for the hadith of the caravan, I think they also disagreed about its soundness, and in any case it is not explicit about the return. The wording of the report is that when the Prophet (ﷺ) was taken on the night journey (isrāʾ), and informed his people about the caravan, its company and the sign that was on the caravan, they said: "When will it come?" He said: "On Wednesday." When that day came, the Quraysh climbed up to look, and the day had already passed and it had not come. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) supplicated, so an hour was added to the day for him, and the sun was held back for him.

Holding back is not the same as returning. Had there been a return, the Quraysh would have witnessed it and would have said about it what they said about the splitting of the moon, but it was not transmitted. It has been said: that was perhaps a blessing in time, similar to what the Sufis mention, which they express as "the expansion of time" (nashr al-zamān), even if many do not comprehend it. Likewise, what happened for Yusha', peace be upon him.

For in the sound hadith it came: "The sun was not held back for anyone except Yusha' ibn Nun." The story is well known. This sound hadith is, according to all, in opposition to everything previously mentioned. Its interpretation as meaning "it was not held back for anyone of the prophets other than me except for Yusha'", or by the necessary implication that the speaker is not included in the generality of his words, even after granting its acceptance, does not remove its contradiction to the report of the return for Sulayman, peace be upon him, since by its apparent meaning it requires the denial of the return, which is greater than holding back, for him, peace be upon him.

In sum, the claim that the sun was returned for Sulayman, peace be upon him, is not established. My not holding that view is not due to the impossibility of return in itself, as the philosophers claim, but because it is not established according to me. Sound taste rejects interpreting the verse in that way, for the reasons al-Razi and others gave, and because of the sequence of the request for the return followed by Allah's words ﴿so he began﴾ and so on. Then, what we have already quoted regarding the afternoon prayer being performed after the return as a qaḍāʾ is the view held by some.

In the Tuḥfa of the scholar Ibn Hajar al-Haytami: "If the sun returns after sunset, the time returns" (ʿād al-waqt), as Ibn al-ʿImad mentioned. The statement of al-Zarkashi seems to contradict this, and that if its setting was delayed beyond its customary time, its setting is assumed at that point, and the time has passed, even if it is still visible. End of al-Zarkashi's statement. What he mentioned last is remote, and so is what he mentioned first. The more likely position is the statement of Ibn al-ʿImad. That its return is a miracle for him (ﷺ) does not harm this, because the miracle is the return itself, while the continuation of the time by its return is a ruling of the Sharia. For this reason, when it returned, ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, performed the afternoon prayer as an adāʾ. Indeed, its return was for nothing but that. End of quotation.

I do not presently have what our Ḥanafī companions hold on this matter. However, I have seen in the margins of al-Baydawi's commentary by Shihab al-Din al-Khafaji, who is among the great of our companions, the claim that the apparent meaning is that the prayer after the return is an adāʾ. Then he said: The jurists have discussed it at length, but this is not the place for it.

It has been said: the pronoun in ﴿tawārat﴾ (until it was hidden) refers to the horses, as does the pronoun in ﴿bring them back﴾, and a group chose this. It was said: "al-ḥijāb" (the veil) is their stables, meaning until they entered their stables. It was also said: until they were hidden during the race by something that screened them from sight. Some of those who held that the pronoun returns to the horses made "ʿan" (from) causal, and did not take the passing with the shins and necks in the earlier sense. A group said: the horses were presented to Sulayman while he was in prayer, so he gestured to them: "I am in prayer," and they removed them from him until they entered the stables. Then when he finished his prayer he said: ﴿Indeed I have loved the love of good﴾, meaning, the good that is mine with Allah in the Hereafter because of the remembrance of my Lord, as if he were saying: "That distracted me from seeing the horses until they entered their stables. Bring them back to me." So he began to pass his hand over their manes and shins out of love for them and honouring them. It is also reported that the passing was for this reason, from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Zuhri and Ibn Kaysan, and al-Tabari preferred it. It was also said that it was washing with water. It is not hidden that the application of this group of the verse to what they say is extremely weak.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 33 (part 2 of 3):

Al-Razi said: Most scholars (al-Akthharun) say: he (peace be upon him) missed the afternoon prayer (salat al-'asr) because of his preoccupation with looking at the horses, so he took them back, and he struck their shanks and necks (ʿaqara suqahā wa-aʿnāqahā) out of nearness to Allah, the Exalted. In my view, however, this is far-fetched, and several points indicate this.

The first is that if "wiping" (masḥ) the shanks and necks meant cutting them, then the meaning of His words, ﴿And wipe over your heads﴾, would be "cut them," and no sensible person would say this. Rather, if it were said, "He wiped his head with the sword," it might be understood from it as striking the neck; but if the word "sword" is not mentioned, nothing of that sort is understood at all.

The second is that those who hold this view attribute to Solomon several kinds of blameworthy acts. The first of them is abandoning the prayer. The second is that preoccupation with love of the world overcame him to the point that he forgot the prayer, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Love of the world is the root of every sin." 

The third is that after committing this great sin, he did not occupy himself with repentance and turning back (to Allah). The fourth, on the view that the pronoun in ﴿Return them﴾ refers to the sun, is that he addressed the Lord of the worlds with a word that a wise man would not use except with a base servant. The fifth is that he followed these sins by hamstringing the horses' shanks and necks, and a prohibition has been reported against slaughtering animals except for eating them. These are kinds of major sins which they attribute to Solomon (peace be upon him), although the wording of the Qur'an does not indicate any of them. The sixth is that the mention of this story, and likewise the preceding one, after the command to bear patiently the folly of the disbelievers, requires that they include righteous deeds, noble character, patience in obedience to Allah the Exalted, and turning away from desires and pleasures. As for their including the commission of great sins and grave transgressions, that is far removed from what the context (al-ta'qib) requires. Thus it is established that the Book of Allah the Exalted calls the aforementioned view false.

The correct position is to say: the tethering of horses was recommended in their religion, just as it is so in the religion of our Prophet (ﷺ). Then Solomon needed to go out to war; he sat down, ordered the horses to be brought, ordered them to be made to run, and said: "I do not love them for the sake of this world or the satisfaction of the self; I love them only for the command of Allah the Exalted and the strengthening of His religion." This is what is meant by His words, ﴿out of remembrance of my Lord﴾. Then he (peace be upon him) ordered them to be driven away and moved on until they were hidden by the veil, that is, they went out of his sight. Then he ordered the trainers to bring those horses back to him. When they returned to him, he began to wipe their shanks and necks, and the purpose of that wiping is several things.

The first is honouring them and showing their dignity, since they are among the greatest helpers in repelling the enemy. The second is that he wished to show that in governing and ruling he humbles himself to the extent of attending to most matters personally. The third is that he had greater knowledge of the conditions, illnesses and defects of horses, so he would examine them, wiping their shanks and necks, until he knew whether there was in them anything indicating sickness. This interpretation is the one to which the wording of the Qur'an fits in a suitable manner, and it does not oblige us to attribute any of those abominable and forbidden things to any of the prophets, peace be upon them. Then he said: I am extremely astonished at people, how they accepted what spread of the flimsy views, although reason and transmission both reject them, and they have no doubt in establishing them, let alone proof. The wording of the verse does not indicate any of those views which the majority mention, as has become clear beyond any doubt for the intelligent. Even granting the indication, it may be said: the many proofs have established the infallibility (ʿiṣmah) of the prophets, peace be upon them, and no proof has indicated the soundness of those narratives; and the reports of single narrators (riwayat al-ahad) are not fit to oppose strong proofs. How then (can one accept) narratives about peoples who are not regarded and whose statements are not heeded? End of his words.

The same merciful scholar had objected to the view that the pronoun in ﴿hidden﴾ refers to the sun rather than the swift horses, on the ground that the swift horses are mentioned explicitly while the sun is not, and that returning a pronoun to something mentioned is preferable to returning it to something implied. Also, he said: ﴿Indeed I loved the love of good out of remembrance of my Lord until it was hidden by the veil﴾, and its apparent meaning indicates that he was repeating and reiterating his saying, "Indeed I loved the love of good out of remembrance of my Lord," until it was hidden by the veil. So if what was hidden is the sun, it would necessarily follow that he repeated that from the afternoon until sunset, which is far-fetched. If it is the swift horses, the meaning is that when his gaze fell upon them while they were being displayed, he kept saying that until they went out of his sight, and this is appropriate. Also, those who hold the return to the sun maintain that he abandoned the afternoon prayer, and the saying "Indeed I loved..." rejects this, because if that love was out of remembrance of Allah the Exalted, he would not have forgotten the prayer or left the remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. I say: what the majority hold is more worthy of acceptance, and what he has mentioned of objections against them is not to be paid attention to nor relied upon. As for his saying that if wiping the shanks and necks meant cutting, then "wipe over your heads" would be a command to cut them, the reply is that this follows only if it were said that wiping, whenever mentioned, means cutting; but that is not said. Rather, they say that wiping in the verse means cutting, and this was indeed said by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as came in a fair (hasan) report, which we have already quoted for you from al-Tabarani, al-Isma'ili and Ibn Mardawayh. There is no saying after the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him), and such a report suffices for a matter of this kind, since there is nothing in it that contradicts reason or a stronger transmission, as you will know, God willing.

This meaning of wiping has also been mentioned by al-Zamakhshari, and he is among the eminent scholars of this field; and its transmission from a group of the early generations (al-salaf) is sound. Al-Khafaji said: using wiping (al-masḥ) in the sense of striking the neck is a metaphor (istiʿarah) that occurred in their speech in earlier times. Yes, that it needs a qarinah (contextual indicator) is beyond doubt, and the qarinah according to those who claim it here is the context and the return of the pronoun in ﴿hidden﴾ to the sun, which is almost decisive, as will become clear to you, God willing.

As for his saying that they attributed to Solomon several kinds of blameworthy acts, this is a fabrication without doubt (fariyyah min ghayr miriyah). And as for his saying: the first of them is abandoning the prayer, the reply is that the blameworthy abandonment is that which is deliberate, and they do not hold that; what they hold is abandonment through forgetfulness, which is not blameworthy, since forgetfulness does not fall under obligation. Moreover, that what was abandoned was an obligation is something on which not all of them agree. And as for his saying: the second is that preoccupation with love of the world overcame him to the point that he abandoned the prayer, the reply is that this was preoccupation with the horses of jihad, which is itself an act of worship.

And as for his saying: the third is that after committing this great sin he did not occupy himself with repentance and turning back, the reply is that we do not concede that he (peace be upon him) committed a sin in reality, let alone a great one. Yes, it may be said that he (peace be upon him) did not regard that as fitting for his station, so he followed it with drawing near (to Allah) by means of the horses through which he had been preoccupied; and that indicates repentance with strong indication. Nor would the matter of jihad have been disrupted by it, for he (peace be upon him) had been given other things besides that. Moreover, the mention of what was mentioned as a testimony to His words, ﴿Indeed he was a frequent returner (awwab)﴾, indicates that it includes turning back, even if we go to the view that the clause ﴿when there were displayed before him﴾ is connected to "awwab"; this almost does not refute this speech at all.

And as for his saying: the fourth is that he addressed his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, with a word that is unsuitable, the reply is that if it is valid at all, it applies only to the view that the pronoun in ﴿Return them﴾ refers to the sun, and we do not hold that; so we are not obliged to answer it. What we say is that the pronoun refers to the horses, and the address is to his attendants, and even so he did not say that word out of recklessness or tyranny, as is imagined.

And as for his saying: the fifth is that he followed these sins with hamstringing the horses, and the prohibition has been reported etc., the reply is that he (peace be upon him) did not commit a sin, so that it could be said he followed these sins; and that the horses were hamstrung as an offering, and bringing them near was prescribed in his religion, so it is an act of obedience. From the totality of what we have mentioned, what is in his saying, the sixth, etc. is known. Moreover, you have already been shown the connection of these stories with what precedes them, and that does not depend on committing to what he said in this story and what he claimed to be correct. In his view there is a return of the pronoun in "hidden" to the horses, and it is not hidden from anyone of sound taste and upright nature that the hiding of the horses by the veil is a crude expression which the firm Book is too exalted for. Also, it hardly comes to mind what the referent of "until it was hidden" is, which he indicated in establishing what he claimed to be correct and its connection, according to what his quoted words at the end indicate, which is very far-fetched. The apparent meaning is that the saying "until it was hidden by the veil" is part of the reported speech, like what precedes it, and what follows it is not part of the narration. Also, that the return of the reference to the wiping he mentioned is contrary to what came in the fair report, and is itself far-fetched, and the purposes he mentioned in it are not hidden in their weakness. His claim that this interpretation is the one to which the Qur'an fits has no sound proof, and perhaps the proof of non-fit is evident.

As for his saying: "I am extremely astonished at people," etc., I say: my astonishment at him is greater than his astonishment at people, since the goodness of the view which the majority have judged good was hidden from him, and he did not become aware of the fair reports that came concerning it, and he thought that holding it contradicts the belief in the infallibility of the prophets, peace be upon them, until he said what he said and hurled arrows at the majority. And as for his saying, in preferring the return of the pronoun in "hidden" to "the swift horses" over its return to the sun, that they are mentioned explicitly while the sun is not, this is nothing, for its return to the sun makes the speech crude, so it should not be resorted to merely because the pronoun returns to an explicitly mentioned referent. Moreover, its return to the explicitly mentioned swift horses is itself open to examination. Nor does the majority face the objection of disagreement of pronouns in their referents, which is confusion, for disagreement with a qarinah is not harmful. And more surprising than what has been mentioned is his claim that it follows, on what the majority said, that Solomon (peace be upon him) repeated his saying, "Indeed I loved the love of good out of remembrance of my Lord," from the afternoon until sunset; for the majority did not approach anything from which this would follow at all, since none of them said that "until" (ḥattā) is connected to "said," as he claimed; rather, according to them it is connected to "I loved," in the sense we have already set out. Whoever is fair would not accept either the claim that he (peace be upon him) repeated that saying until the horses went out of his sight, as this imam said. And his saying, rebutting those who hold the return to the sun, that they hold he abandoned the afternoon prayer, which the saying "Indeed I loved..." rejects, because if that love were out of remembrance of Allah he would not have forgotten the prayer: the majority do not say that "ʿalā" is for causation, and the rejection mentioned, even granting it, cannot be made except on that basis; and what they say, which we have already set out for you, is far removed from it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 33 (part 3 of 3):

In sum, the statements of this imam (al-Razi) on this point are inconsistent, and he was not fair to the majority of scholars, who knew the transmitted reports better than he did. Yes, what he mentioned regarding the verse is a possible reading of it, but a remote one, if one sets aside the reports and the traditions that came from the early generation (al-salaf). A similar view was mentioned by Abd al-Wahhab al-Sha'rani in his book (al-Yawaqit wal-Jawahir). In truth, and God Most High knows best, it comes from the words of the Greatest Shaykh, Muhyi al-Din (Ibn al-Arabi), may his secret be sanctified. He opposed the majority, as the imam did. In the one hundred and twentieth chapter of the (Futuhat al-Makkiyya), he said: "The exegetes who took al-tawari (the concealment of the sun behind the veil of night) as evidence have no proof, for the sun is not mentioned here, nor is the prayer they claim. The context of the verse does not indicate what they said in any apparent way at all. As for their reliance on the words of God Most High, ﴿And We did test Solomon﴾, the trial meant there is only the testing with the horses: whether he loved them for the remembrance of his Lord Most High through them, or loved them for their own sake. So he (peace be upon him) informed about himself [p. 198] that he loved them for the remembrance of his Lord, glorified is He, through them, not for their beauty, their perfection, or his need for them," and so on to the end of what he said.

Ibn al-Arabi was a contemporary of the imam, and he wrote to him a letter encouraging him to take the path of the Sufis, but they never met. It is most likely that neither took from the other what he said about the verse; rather, neither heard it from the other. The knowledge of each of them cannot be denied, and the Shaykh is an ocean whose depth cannot be reached. As for what he mentioned in the reliance (on the trial of Solomon), I have not found it attributed to any exegete, and God Most High knows best.

Ibn Kathir read ﴿بِالسُّؤْقِ﴾ (bis-su'q, "with the shanks") with a silent hamza (sukun). Abu Ali said: this reading is weak, but its justification in analogy (qiyas, reasoning by analogy with established usage) is that since the damma came after the waw, it was regarded as if it were on the waw, just as they do with a damma-marked waw, where they replace it with a hamza. Its justification by analogy is that Abahiyya al-Numayri used to pronounce a hamza for every silent waw preceded by a damma, and he would recite:

"I love those who come to Musa (Moses)."

Abu Hayyan said: it is not weak, because the root of al-saq contains a hamza, so its pattern is fa'l with a silent 'ayn, and this reading came in accordance with this dialect. It has been objected that the hamza in al-saq is a substitution contrary to analogy, since there is no doubt that it is hollow (ajwaf, with a weak middle radical), so the justification must be by what was mentioned before.

Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿بِالسُّؤُوقِ﴾ (bis-su'uq) with a damma on the hamza, followed by a silent waw, on the pattern of al-fusuq. Bakkar transmitted it from Qunbul, and it is also the plural of saq.

Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, read ﴿بِالسّاقِ﴾ (bis-saq) in the singular, dispensing with the plural because there is no ambiguity.

﴿وَلَقَدْ فَتَنَّا سُلَيْمَانَ وَأَلْقَيْنَا عَلَى كُرْسِيِّهِ جَسَدًا ثُمَّ أَنَابَ﴾ Among the most apparent of what has been said about his trial, peace be upon him, is that he said: "Tonight I will go in to seventy women, and each one will bear a horseman who will fight in the way of Allah, the Exalted." He did not say, "If Allah wills." So he went in to them, but only one woman became pregnant, and she bore half a man. This was narrated by al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others, from Abu Hurayrah, as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet ﷺ), and in it: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, had he said, 'If Allah wills,' they would have fought as horsemen."

But in Sahih al-Bukhari the number is "forty" instead of "seventy," and that the angel said to him, "Say: If Allah wills," but he did not say it.

The most that this involves is leaving what is better (tark al-awla), so it is not a sin. Even if he himself counted it a sin, the "body" (jasad) refers to that half-child who was born to him. The meaning of "casting it upon his throne" is that the midwife placed it upon his throne so that he would see it.

The Imamiyya (Twelver Shi'is) narrated from Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, that a son was born to Sulayman, and the jinn and the devils said: "If a son of his survives, we will surely suffer from him what we suffered from his father of trials." So he, peace be upon him, feared them, and he made the child and his wet-nurse among the clouds, where they could not know. Then he noticed nothing except that the child had been cast upon his throne dead. This is a warning that caution does not save one from destiny, and he was rebuked for abandoning the trust in God (tawakkul) that is fitting for the elite, which is to abandon engaging with the means (asbab). This is also narrated from al-Sha'bi, and some narrated it from Abu Hurayrah in a manner whose fabrication no one doubts except one who doubts the infallibility (isma) of the prophets, peace be upon them. As for me, I am not certain of the authenticity of this report. Rather, the apparent sense of the verse is that the subjugation of the wind came after the trial, and this is apparent in the report's being unsound, because the placing in the clouds requires that (i.e., that he was placed in the clouds, which contradicts the verse).

Abd ibn Humayd and al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated through 'Ali ibn Zayd, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, that Sulayman, peace be upon him, secluded himself from people for three days. So Allah, the Exalted, revealed to him: "O Sulayman, you have secluded yourself from people for three days, so you have not looked into the affairs of My servants, and you have not given justice to the wronged against the wrongdoer." His kingdom was in his ring, and whenever he entered the bathhouse he would place his ring under his bed. The devil came, took it, and people gathered around the devil, and Sulayman said, "O people, I am Sulayman, the prophet of Allah, the Exalted." But they pushed him away, and he wandered for forty days. He came to the people of a ship, who gave him a fish, and he split it open, and there was the ring in it. So he put it on, then came and seized the devil by its forelock, and at that he said: "My Lord, grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me."

al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated, and Ibn Hajar and al-Suyuti said, with a strong chain, from Ibn 'Abbas: Sulayman, peace be upon him, wanted to enter the privy, so he gave his ring to Jaradah, who was his wife and the dearest of his wives to him. Then the devil came in the form of Sulayman,
[Page 199]
and said to her, "Give me my ring." So she gave it to him. When he put it on, mankind, the jinn, and the devils submitted to him. When Sulayman came out, he said to her, "Give me my ring." She said, "I have already given it to Sulayman." He said, "I am Sulayman." She said, "You are lying; you are not Sulayman." So he began to come to no one and say to him, "I am Sulayman," without being denied. Finally the children began to pelt him with stones. When he saw this, he realized that it was a matter from Allah, the Exalted. The devil stood judging among the people. When Allah, the Exalted, wanted to restore his authority to him, He cast into the hearts of the people the denial of that devil. They sent to the wives of Sulayman and said, "Do you deny anything about Sulayman?" They said, "Yes, he comes to us while we are menstruating, and he did not used to come to us before that." When the devil saw that he had been detected, he thought his affair had ended. So he ordered the devils, and they wrote books containing sorcery and deceit, and they buried them beneath the throne of Sulayman, then unearthed them and read them to the people, and said, "By this Sulayman used to prevail over people and overpower them." So the people disbelieved in Sulayman. That devil sent the ring and threw it into the sea, and a fish swallowed it. Sulayman, peace be upon him, used to work for wages on the seashore. A man came and bought fish, among which was that fish. Sulayman was called, and he carried the fish to the door of the man's house. The man gave him that fish, and he split its belly, and there was the ring in it. He took it and put it on, and mankind, the jinn, and the devils submitted to him, and he returned to his former state. The devil fled to an island in the sea, and Sulayman sent after him. He was rebellious, so they could not catch him until they found him asleep. They built a structure of lead over him, and he awoke, and they bound him and brought him to Sulayman. He gave an order, and a chest of marble was hollowed out for him, and he was placed inside it. Then it was sealed with copper, and he ordered that it be thrown into the sea.

It was mentioned as the cause of that: Sulayman, peace be upon him, had raided Sidon in the islands, killed its king, and captured his daughter, who was this Jaradah mentioned above, and he loved her. Her tears never dried from grief for her father. So he ordered the devils, and they fashioned for her an image of him, and this was permissible in his law. She used to go to it and return with her attendants, and they would prostrate to it as they were accustomed to do in his kingdom. Asif informed him, so he broke the image and struck the woman, and he was rebuked for this, because he had been heedless of the condition of his household.

There is disagreement about the name of that devil. According to al-Suddi, it is Haqiq; according to most, it is Sakhr, and this is the well-known one. Allah, glorified is He, only said "a body" (jasadan) because it had only taken the form of another, namely Sulayman, peace be upon him. That fashioned form had none of the spirit of its true owner, but that devil dwelt within its mold. Therefore it was called "a body." The phrasing of al-Qamus is explicit that "jasad" applies to a jinn.

Abu Hayyan and others said: This view is among the fabrications of the Jews and the sophistical zanadiqa (heretics), and no intelligent person should believe in the soundness of what it contains. How is it permissible for a devil to take the form of a prophet, so that his affair becomes confused for people, and they believe that this one who appears is the prophet? If this were possible, one could not trust the sending of any prophet. We ask Allah, the Exalted, for the safety of our religion and our minds. Among its most repugnant claims is the assertion that the devil was empowered over the wives of his prophet until he had intercourse with them while they were menstruating. Allahu Akbar! This is a monstrous slander and a grave matter. Attributing this report to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, cannot be accepted as sound, and likewise the claim of the strength of its chain back to him is not accepted, even if whoever you heard say so has said it.

And there came from Ibn 'Abbas, through the narration of 'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir, what is clearly indicative that this is from the reports of Ka'b (al-Ahbar). It is known that Ka'b narrates it from the books of the Jews, which are not trustworthy. Moreover, the implication of what comes later, that the subjugation of the devils after the trial, rejects the soundness of this account, as is not hidden. Furthermore, the matter of Sulayman's ring, peace be upon him, is extremely well known among the elite and the common people, and it is highly improbable that Allah, the Exalted, tied the kingdom He gave His prophet, peace be upon him, to that ring. In my view, if that ring contained the secret they claim, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, would have mentioned it in His Book. Allah, the Exalted, knows best the reality of the matter.

Some people said: Sulayman, peace be upon him, fell ill with an illness like fainting, until he was on his throne as if he were a body without a spirit. Their saying about the weak was common: "flesh on a sickbed" and "a body without a spirit." So the body cast upon the throne was himself, peace be upon him.

This was narrated from Abu Muslim, who said regarding Allah's words, ﴿ثُمَّ أَنَابَ﴾: that is, he returned to health. He made ﴿جَسَدًا﴾ a circumstantial state (hal) of the omitted object of "alqayna" (we cast), as if it were said: "And We indeed tried Sulayman," that is, We tested him and made him ill, and We cast him upon his throne weak, as if he were a body without a spirit, then he returned to his health. Its weakness is not hidden. The truth is what was mentioned first in the marfu' hadith. ﴿أَنَابَ﴾ is connected with "thumma" (then), whereas the apparent form would have been "fa" (so), as in Allah's words: ﴿فَاسْتَغْفَرَ رَبَّهُ﴾ (and he asked his Lord for forgiveness). It was said: this indicates the continuation and extension of his turning (in repentance), for what extends in time is joined with "thumma" by regarding its final parts, unlike seeking forgiveness, which should be hastened, and there is no extension in its time. It was also said: the connection with "thumma" here is because he, peace be upon him, did not know the cause prompting the turning right after it occurred. This differs from the story of Dawud, peace be upon him, where the connection there was based on the supposition of the trial, and what is fitting for him is not to delay seeking forgiveness from it. It was also said: the connection with it here is because there was a long period between the time of his turning and the first time of what happened from him, peace be upon him, of omitting the exception (in saying "if Allah wills"), which was the period of the pregnancy. There is no such period between the time of Dawud's seeking forgiveness, peace be upon him, and the first time of what happened from him in that manner.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 35:

﴿Said﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿repented﴾ and an explanation of it, according to what is in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim (Abu al-Su'ud's commentary), and this is the apparent reading. It is also possible that it is a explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani) arising from the narration of what preceded, as if it were said: "Did he have a state in which stroking the horses, their shanks and necks, did not harm him? And was he in a condition that wisdom required his trial?" So it was answered with what was answered. Its sum is yes: he had a state in which stroking did not harm him, and he was in a condition that wisdom required his trial. For he called for a great kingdom and it was granted to him. It is also possible to establish the resumption in another way. Likewise, it is possible that it is a grammatical resumption (isti'naf nahwi) relating some of his states, peace be upon him, so reflect. ﴿My Lord, forgive me﴾: (this is) what I would not like to have proceeded from me.

﴿And grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me﴾: that is, it will not be proper for anyone other than me, because of its greatness. Thus "after" (ba'd) here is like its use in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Who then can guide him after Allah?﴾, meaning other than Allah, Exalted is He. It is more general than that the other be in his own era. The intended meaning is describing the kingdom with greatness by way of metonymy (kinayah), like your saying: "So-and-so has what no one has of virtue and wealth," though there may be among people those similar to him, and you mean that he has a great share of that, not that no one else is given the like of it, so that it would be a rivalry. Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in Nawadir al-Usul, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed an 'ifrit (a powerful jinn) began to slip in upon me last night, to cut off my prayer. But Allah, Exalted is He, enabled me to overcome him. I was about to tie him to one of the pillars of the mosque until you all woke up and looked at him, but then I remembered the words of my brother Solomon: ﴿My Lord, forgive me, and grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me﴾, so Allah, Exalted is He, sent him back dejected." This does not contradict that, because he (peace and blessings be upon him) intended to perfectly observe the supplication of his brother Solomon (peace be upon him) by leaving aside something included in that great kingdom. Otherwise, the great kingdom is not merely tying an 'ifrit to a pillar, but rather all that is included in His saying, Exalted is He, which follows: ﴿So We subjected to him the wind﴾, etc. It was said: the absence of contradiction is because metonymy is compatible with intending the literal meaning, just as it is compatible with intending its negation. Perhaps he (peace be upon him) only sought that so that it would be a sign of the acceptance of his request for forgiveness and a consolation of heart for what he had missed by leaving the exception (istithna'), or so that through it he might increase his obedience to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the good worldly blessing for a righteous servant. So there is no difficulty in seeking the kingdom in this context, if we follow what the sublime wording apparently requires, namely that both requests proceeded together.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Solomon (peace be upon him) grew up in a house of kingship and prophethood and inherited both. He wanted to ask his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, for a miracle, so he asked, according to his familiarity, for a kingdom exceeding the kingdoms, with an increase that is extraordinary, beyond the customary, reaching the limit of miraculousness, so that it would be a proof of his prophethood, overpowering those sent to. It would not be a miracle until it breaks customs, and that is the meaning of ﴿that will not befit anyone after me﴾. So His saying "after me" means "other than me and besides me," as in the earlier interpretation. The goodness of asking for that as a miracle, apart from familiarity, is that he (peace be upon him) was in the time of tyrants who boasted of kingship, and every prophet's miracle is of the kind that is famous in his era. Do you not see that when magic was famous and prevalent in the time of Moses (peace be upon him), he brought them what swallowed up what they had produced? And when medicine was famous in the time of the Messiah (peace be upon him), he brought them the healing of the blind and the leper and the raising of the dead? And when eloquence was famous in the time of the Seal of the Messengers (ﷺ), he brought them a speech of which they could not produce the shortest section of its sections. It was objected that what is fitting for a request for a miracle is that it occur at the beginning of prophethood, and the apparent sense of the sublime wording is that this request was after the trial and the repentance. How not, when His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿He said﴾ etc., is a substitute for ﴿repented﴾ and an explanation of it, and the trial did not occur at the beginning as the wording indicates. It was answered: we do not concede that what is fitting for a request for a miracle is that it be at the beginning of prophethood; and even if conceded, there is nothing in the verse that negates its occurring, and likewise the occurrence of the trial at its beginning, especially if we say that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿He said: My Lord, forgive me﴾ etc., is not an explanation of ﴿repented﴾. It was answered, on the view that the trial was the removal of kingship, that his return after it is like the beginning.

Some of those who went to this view mentioned that he (peace be upon him) remained in his kingdom before this trial for twenty years, and remained after it for twenty years also. They said regarding this verse: the object of the supplication is the attribute, so the meaning of the verse is: "Grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone other than me among those in my time, by his being deprived of it by me as this deprivation (of Solomon)."

This meaning was related from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and Qatada, and its sum is the supplication that his kingdom not be taken away from him during his life. What is understood from the context of the consequence is the answering of his supplication (peace be upon him), and that what was granted to him is not taken away from him afterwards. It is permitted that this is a supplication for non-deprivation even if no deprivation had preceded it. The continuance of Allah's blessing, Mighty and Majestic, is among what is good to supplicate for, and the traditions are full of that. So this view does not necessarily depend on interpreting the trial as the removal of kingship, as reported earlier.

Al-Jubba'i said: he (peace be upon him) sought a kingdom that would never belong to anyone else, and he did not seek that except after permission, for prophets (peace be upon them) only seek what they are permitted to seek. It is possible that Allah had informed him that if he asked for that it would be more suitable for him in religion, and informed him that there is no good for anyone else in it. This is like the saying of a speaker: "O Allah, make me the wealthiest of the people of my time, if You know that this is better for me," for it is good and its speaker is not attributed to stinginess. It was said: the meaning of the verse on this view may be: "Grant me a kingdom that is fitting for me in wisdom, and that is not fitting in wisdom for anyone other than me," and by this he intended to seek that he (peace be upon him) be worthy of the blessings of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. And this, as you see, is (weak). It was said: other than that. Among the most astonishing things I have seen is what al-Sayyid al-Murtada said: it is permissible that he only asked for the kingdom of the Hereafter and the reward of Paradise, and the meaning of His saying: ﴿that will not befit anyone after me﴾ is that it is not deserved by anyone after reaching it, from the standpoint that it is not valid to do what earns that, because obligation has ended. It is not hidden that this is something the taste does not accept, and the following consequence (of the verse) rejects it entirely.

Some scholars used the verse, on some of the views mentioned in it, to declare takfir (ruling of disbelief) upon whoever claims to employ the jinn and their obedience to him. This is supported by the earlier hadith. The truth is that the employment of jinn established for Solomon (peace be upon him) did not occur through the mediation of names and spiritual exercises, but was a divine subjugation without any intermediary. It was also in a more complete manner, and despite that it was only part of the kingdom he asked to be granted. So the exclusivity, on the assumption that the verse indicates exclusivity, is the whole of what His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So We subjected﴾ etc., includes. Therefore the apparent position is not to declare disbelief upon whoever claims the employment of some of the jinn. We have indeed witnessed many times someone claiming that, and we have witnessed evidences of the truth of his claim in a manner that none denies except a sophist or an obstinate person.

Among the remarkable coincidences: on the day I was explaining this verse I met a man from Mosul who claimed that, and I tested him with something that would confirm his claim before a great assembly. He did it and brought wonders, and the proofs excluding the possibility of sleight of hand and the like were evident to people of understanding. However, I have a difficulty in this matter: the jinn servant may bring a dense thing, such as a locked box, among a group in a room whose doors have been shut and whose openings sealed, and no one perceives it. The difficulty is that the jinn is subtle, so how did he conceal the dense (object) so that it was not seen on the way, and how did he take it out of the box and place it into the room, while the openings were sealed? And to refine the dense and then condense it again afterwards is something only a dense or foolish (being) accepts. Similarly, is the aforementioned bringing like the bringing of the throne of Bilqis, by annihilation and recreation, as the Shaykh al-Akbar (Ibn Arabi) says, or by another way, as others say? Perhaps the Law also rejects this. As for the swiftness of passage, if it helps, then what about not seeing (the object) on the way? The most that can be said is that perhaps the jinn has a sorcery or the like by which he took away perception, so he manipulated the box and the openings of the room as he wished, and brought the dense object carrying it, and no one among the people perceived it. If this is established, then well and good; otherwise the matter is problematic. The apparent indication of making the sentence ﴿He said: My Lord, forgive me﴾ an explanation of the repentance requires that seeking forgiveness is intended for its own sake and not merely a means to seeking the gift. Regarding whether seeking the gift is also intended for its own sake, there are two possibilities.

Mentioning seeking forgiveness first, supposing both are intended for their own sake, is for greater concern with the matter of religion. It may also be made, together with this, a means to the intended seeking of the gift, for beginning the supplication with something like that is more hopeful for acceptance. It was permitted, with some remoteness, after holding to resumption in general, that seeking the gift is what is intended for its own sake and seeking forgiveness is a means to it. What has been said regarding seeking companionship for him will come, if Allah, Exalted is He, wills.

It is read: "min ba'di-ya" (with a fatha on the ya'), and its reading with it in li is related. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾ is a reason (ta'lil) for the supplication for forgiveness and gift together, not for the supplication for the latter alone, for forgiveness is also certainly among the effects of the attribute of bestowing. Whoever permitted that seeking the gift is what is intended took it as support for this reason, supposing that it is only for the supplication for the latter alone; and likewise by the absence of mention of answering the supplication for the former, for the apparent view is that His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 36:

﴿So We subjected the wind to him﴾ to the end of the verse is a consequence (tafri') of his request for a kingdom that should not belong to anyone after him. Had forgiveness also been intended, it would have said: "So We forgave him and subjected the wind to him," and so on. It has been answered that it is permissible to say that forgiveness for one who seeks it, especially the prophets (peace be upon them), being a matter well known, was not stated explicitly, unlike the granting of a kingdom to one who asks for it. What is mentioned in the place of the fa' (consequence particle), together with what follows in the verse, is sufficient to indicate that. This indication is strengthened on the assumption that the request for kingdom is a sign of the acceptance of his seeking forgiveness and the answering of his supplication, so reflect. Taskhir (subjection) means tadhlil (making submissive), i.e., We made it submissive to his obedience in response to his supplication. It has also been said: We kept its submission constant as it was. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatadah and Abu Ja'far read "al-riyah" (the winds) in the plural. It has been said: this is more in accord with what is widespread, that al-rih (the wind) is used for evil and al-riyah (the winds) for good; and you know that this is not a consistent rule. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿flowing by his command﴾ is an explanation of its subjection to him, peace be upon him, or a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning flowing by his command; ﴿gently﴾, i.e., soft, from rakhawah (softness), not stirring up by its violence. This has been raised as an objection: it contradicts His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and to Solomon the wind, violent﴾, since there it is described as violent and here as gentle.

It has been answered that it was in its original creation violent, but it became gentle and easy for Solomon; or that it grows violent when carrying and becomes gentle when moving, so it was described according to two states; or that it is violent in itself, and when Solomon, peace be upon him, wished it to be gentle, it became gentle, as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿by His command﴾ indicates; or that it is gentle and violent according to the requirement of the situation. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: "gentle" means obedient, not opposing his will, like a commanded and compliant servant; so the meaning of its gentleness is its compliance with him, and this does not contradict its violence. Gentleness (lin) may mean obedience, and likewise hardness (salabah) may mean disobedience.

﴿Wherever it struck﴾, i.e., it intended and aimed, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and Qatadah. Al-Zajjaj related from the Arabs: "asaba al-sawab fa-akhta' al-jawab" (he hit the correct point but missed the answer). And from Ru'bah: two men of the people of language intended him to ask him about this word; he came out to them and said: "Ayya tusibani?" (What do you hit?). They said: "This is our aim," and they returned. It is also said: "Asaba Allahu bika khayran" (may God make you reach good through you). Al-Tha'labi recited:

Asaba al-kalam fa-lam yasta'i' fa-akhta al-jawab ladaa al-mu'dil
(He hit upon the speech but could not, and missed the answer at the difficult point.)

And from Qatadah that asaba in the sense of arada (intended) is the dialect of Hajar; it has been said it is the dialect of Himyar. It is also permitted that asaba be from saba yasub in the sense of "to descend," the hamza being for causation, i.e., "wherever he caused his troops to descend." And "wherever" (haythu) is related either to sakhkharna or to tajri.

﴿And the devils﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf, grammatical coordination) with "the wind". ﴿Every builder and diver﴾ is an apposition (badal, grammatical substitution) for "the devils". It is a badal kull min kull (apposition of the whole to the whole) if what is meant is the known subjected ones, or if what is meant is those who possess the capacity for building and diving and the ability to carry them out. If that is not intended, it is a badal baʿḍ (apposition of part to whole), and a pronoun is then to be understood, meaning "of them". Diving is for extracting ornaments. He, peace be upon him, according to what is said, was the first to extract pearls. ﴿And others bound together in fetters﴾ is coordinated with ﴿every﴾, not with "the devils", because they are among them, unless what is meant is the specific known group. It is also not coordinated with what ﴿every﴾ is annexed to, because only annexation to an indefinite singular or a definite plural is appropriate there. "Asfād" is the plural of "ṣafad", which in the well-known sense means a shackle. It is also said to mean the collar (al-jāmiʿa), that is, the iron that joins the two hands to the neck. It is said that this is the most suitable meaning with "bound together" (muqarrinīn), because binding with it is common. The word is also used for a gift, because it binds the one who is favoured. From this is the saying of ʿAlī, may God honour his face: "Whoever shows you kindness has taken you captive, and whoever turns away from you has set you free."

And the saying of the poet: "He shackled a hand, whose owner releases it, and freed a neck, whose owner emancipates it." Abū Tammām said:

"My aspirations hang their necks upon you, shackled; indeed, giving is a captivity."

Al-Mutanabbi followed him in his saying:

"I have bound my soul in your shelter out of love, and whoever finds kindness as a fetter becomes bound."

They distinguished between the two verbs. They said: "ṣafadahu" means he shackled him, and "aṣfadahu" means he gave to him, the opposite of his promise and his threat. On this they have a lengthy discussion, in which al-Khafājī said what he said. Then he said: "The verification, in my view, is that here there are two roots, in each of which there is something harmful and something beneficial, both short and long in wording. In one of them the harmful is mentioned with the first wording and the beneficial with the longer wording later, and in the other the reverse. The reason in the first is that it is an actual matter, because it was coined for the fetter, and then applied to the gift, because it binds its owner. He used the shorter form for the fetter because of its narrowness, which suits the fewness of its letters, and the longer form for the gift because it is in the nature of generosity. He put the first first because it is the basic and lighter root. The reverse applies to waʿada and awʿada: he used the shorter form for the beneficial and put it first, and put the harmful later and multiplied its letters, because it is in the future and not yet actual. The promised good is praised for the speed of its fulfilment and the shortness of the time before it occurs, for the sweetest of goodness is what comes quickly, and this suits the fewness of its letters. In the threat, delay is praised, because of the goodness of forgoing it and pardoning it, so the multiplication of its letters is appropriate." Then he said: "This is a verification of the utmost excellence, and whatever is other than it is a futile illusion, so understand it."

By these bound ones (al-muqarrinīn) are meant the rebellious ones (al-maradah). The verse therefore indicates a division of the devils into workers, whom he, peace be upon him, employed in arduous tasks such as building and diving, and rebels, whom he bound together with chains, so that they would refrain from evil. Its apparent meaning is that there is actual restraint, and this is problematic, because the devils are either subtle fiery bodies capable of taking various forms, or pure wicked spirits. In either case it is not possible to bind them, nor to hold a fetter on them. It is answered by choosing the first option, which is the correct one.

The fetters are not the well-known kind. Rather, they are fetters by which the subtle can be bound in a way that prevents them from acting freely, and the matter from its very start is a departure from the normal custom. It is also said that the subtlety of their bodies, in the sense of their transparency, does not preclude solidity, as in glass and the celestial sphere according to the philosophers. Their bodies could therefore be transparent and solid, so they are not seen because of their transparency, and their binding is possible because of their solidity. Some denied solidity, because the penetration of the devils is established in places where solid matter cannot penetrate, and because they are not perceived by touch, whereas solid matter is perceived by touch.

It is also said: there is no objection to his, peace be upon him, binding them in a solid form, so that he binds them then with fetters. When a devil appears in a certain form, he may be bound by it, and he cannot take any other form or return to what he was. The Greatest Shaykh Muḥyī al-Dīn, may his secret be sanctified, has stated explicitly that a person's gaze binds the devil to the form in which he sees him. Whenever a person sees a devil in a form and does not turn his gaze away from it completely, the devil cannot hide from him, nor take another form, until he finds an opportunity to turn the gaze away, even for the blink of an eye.

Al-Jubbāʾī claimed that the devil had a dense body in the time of Solomon, peace be upon him, and people could see him. Then, when he, peace be upon him, died, God, Mighty and Majestic, caused those jinn to die and created another kind with a subtle body, such that they are not seen and cannot perform arduous tasks. This is not accepted at all except on a sound transmission, and where is it? It is also said: the closest view is that the intended meaning is an image of restraining their evils by being joined together in shackles, and there is no actual fetter or binding in reality.
