This is the gift of Ours, so bestow [it] or withhold [it], without reckoning.

Either it is a narration of what Sulayman (peace be upon him) was addressed with, showing the greatness of the kingdom he was given and that it was entrusted to him in a comprehensive delegation; or it is a speech attached to an implied saying, which is coordinated with (sakhkharna, "We subjected"), or a circumstantial clause (hal) from its subject, meaning: "and We said," or "saying to him: this..." and so on. The demonstrative refers to what he was given of the things mentioned before, meaning: this which We have given you of the great kingdom, the ability, and the authority over what none other than you was given authority over, is Our gift specific to you, so give to whom you wish and withhold from whom you wish, without being called to account for anything of either, and without being held responsible for it in the Hereafter, because the disposal of it has been entrusted to you absolutely. (Fa-bi-ghayr hisab) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun concealed in the imperative, and the fa' is a consequential fa' (fa' jaza'iyyah). "This is Our gift" is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar), and the predication conveys what we pointed out regarding the consideration of specificity, i.e., Our gift specific to you. Or it may be said that its mention is not for the purpose of informing about it, but so that what follows is consequent upon it, like the poet's saying:

"These are their dwellings, and you are longing for them; how long will tears remain on the eyelids?"

It is also permitted that (bi-ghayr hisab) be a circumstantial clause from the gift, as in: "And this, my husband, is an old man" (Q. 11:72), meaning: this is Our gift, clothed in being without reckoning upon it in the Hereafter; or: this is Our gift, very abundant, which cannot be counted or reckoned because of its great abundance. It is also permitted that it be a complement (silah) of the gift; some have considered it a qualifier of it, so that the benefit is complete and there is no need to consider what was previously mentioned. On both assessments, what intervenes is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD), so the separation by it does no harm, and the fa' is parenthetical (i'tiraDiyyah). The combination of the parenthetical insertion with the fa' occurs just as it occurs with the waw, like the poet's saying:

"Know that the knowledge of a man benefits him, that everything decreed will surely come."

It has been said: the demonstrative refers to the subjugation of the devils, and by bestowing and withholding is meant their release and their being kept in chains; and bestowing may mean release, as in the Exalted saying: "Then either a favour afterwards or a ransom" (Q. 47:4). The preferable reading of the Exalted saying "without reckoning" in this case is that it is a circumstantial clause from the concealed pronoun in the imperative. This view was transmitted by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim from Ibn 'Abbas. What is related from him that it refers to the wives granted to him (peace be upon him) and the power to have intercourse with them can hardly be sound, since no mention of that has occurred in the verse. The majority took the first view, and it is the more apparent. Ibn Mas'ud read: "This, so bestow or withhold, is Our gift, without reckoning."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 40:

﴿And indeed, for him with Us is a nearness⦆ — a closeness and honour, along with the great kingdom he possesses. This is an indication that his kingdom does not harm him, nor does it diminish him in the least from his station.

﴿And a good return﴾ — a good place of return in Paradise. It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "nearness" (zulfā). Al-Ḥasan and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read "wa-ḥusnu" with a nominative (raf') ending, in which case it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is omitted, meaning: "for him." According to these two readers, the pause (waqf) is at "la-zulfā." This matter of Sulaymān (peace be upon him) is among the greatest of affairs. Despite the great kingdom that Allah Most High gave him, he would weave palm fronds with his own hand, eat barley bread, and feed the Children of Israel white bread (al-ḥuwwārā).

Aḥmad transmitted it in al-Zuhd, from ʿAṭāʾ. Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted, from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Sulaymān (peace be upon him) never raised his gaze to the sky out of humility.'"

When Allah Most High gave him what He gave him—and among the kings of Persia in his era was Kaykhusrow—the jurist Abū Ḥanīfa Aḥmad ibn Dāwūd al-Dīnawarī mentioned in his history that he (peace be upon him) inherited his father's kingdom in the era of Kaykhusrow ibn Sabāwush. He travelled from Syria to Iraq, and news of him reached Kaykhusrow, who fled to Khurasan. He did not remain long before he died. Then Sulaymān travelled to Marw, then to the lands of the Turks, penetrated deeply into them, then crossed the lands of China, then turned back until he arrived at the lands of Fars, where he stayed for some days. Then he returned to Syria, then ordered the building of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). When he had finished, he travelled to Tihama, then to Sanaa, and among the account of him with its queen was what Allah Most High mentioned. He also campaigned in the Maghrib lands of al-Andalus, Tangier and others. Then the carpet was folded up, and among the armies of the dead a tent was pitched for him. Glory be to the Eternal King whose kingdom never ceases and whose authority never ends.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 41:**

﴿And remember Our servant Ayyub (Job).﴾ Ibn Ishaq said: The correct view is that he was from the Children of Israel, and nothing authentic has been transmitted about his lineage except that his father's name was Amus. Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) said: He is Ayyub son of Amus, son of Rum, son of Is, son of Ishaq, peace be upon him. Ibn Asakir reported that his mother was a daughter of Lut, and that his father was among those who believed in Ibrahim. Accordingly, he (peace be upon him) would have lived before Musa. Ibn Jarir also said he lived after Shu'ayb, and Ibn Abi Khaythama said he lived after Sulayman.

God the Exalted's words ﴿And remember﴾ etc. are a conjunction with "Remember Our servant Dawud (David)." The story of Sulayman (peace be upon him) is not introduced with this heading because of the complete connection between him and Dawud, peace be upon them both. "Ayyub" is either an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*, a noun clarifying the preceding one) to "Our servant," or a substitute for it in the sense of a substitution of the whole for the whole (*badal kull min kull*). God the Exalted's words ﴿when he called out to his Lord﴾ are a substitution of partial inclusion (*badal ishtimal*) from it, or from Ayyub. ﴿that﴾ means "with the fact that" (i.e., *anni* is *bi-anni*).

ʿIsa (ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar) read the hamza of "innī" with a kasra. ﴿The Satan has touched me﴾ (*massaniya*): it is also read with the *ya'* of "massani" sukun and with its omission. ﴿with hardship﴾: *nusb* with a damma on the *nun* and sukun on the *sad*, meaning fatigue, like *nasab* with two fathas. It is also said that it is the plural of *nasab*, as *watharn* and *wuthun* (idols). Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Abu ʿUmara from Hafs, al-Ju'fi from Abu Bakr, and Abu Mu'adh from Nafi' read it with two dammas, and this is a dialect. There is no obstacle to the second damma being a secondary one for assimilation (*ittiba'*). It is perhaps said that this indicates the heaviness and severity of his fatigue. Zayd ibn ʿAli, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Yaʿqub, and al-Jahdari read it with two fathas, which is also a dialect, like *rushd* and *rashad*. Abu Haywa, Yaʿqub in one narration, and Hubayra from Hafs read it with a fatha on the *nun* and sukun on the *sad*. Al-Zamakhshari said: according to the original form of the verbal noun. Ibn ʿAtiyya stated that this too is a dialect. After mentioning the recitations, he said: All of that has one meaning, which is hardship, and *nasab* is often used for the hardship of exhaustion.

Some people distinguished between these expressions, but the correct view is that they are dialects with one meaning, from the saying: *anṣabanī al-amr* ("the matter exhausted me") when it burdened me. End of quotation.

Page 206

The tanwin (nunation) here is for magnification, and likewise in God the Exalted's words ﴿and torment﴾. By it He meant pain, and this is what is meant by "harm" in His words ﴿Harm has touched me﴾.

It is also said: the *nusb* and the *darr* (harm) were in the body, and the *adhab* (torment) was in family and wealth. This is a quotation of his words (peace be upon him), with which he called out to his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, in his own expression. Otherwise it would have said "it touched him," in the third person. As for attributing the touching to the Satan, it is said that it is according to its outward meaning. That is because the accursed one heard the angels praising Ayyub (peace be upon him), so he envied him, and asked God the Exalted to empower him over his body, property, and children, and God the Exalted did so as a trial for him. The story is well known.

In some reports, the one who touched him was a devil called Musawwit. Al-Zamakhshari denied this, saying: It is not permissible for God the Exalted to empower the Satan over the prophets (peace be upon them) so that he may fulfill his desire of wearying and torturing them. If he were able to do that, he would not leave a righteous person without afflicting and destroying him. It is repeated in the Qur'an that he has no authority except whispering alone. He considered the attribution of the touching to him here to be figurative, saying: Since his whispering to him and his obedience to him in what he whispered was a cause of what God the Exalted touched him with of hardship and torment, he attributed it to him. He (peace be upon him) observed good manners in this, for he did not attribute it to God, glory be to Him, in his supplication, although He, the Majestic and Exalted, is the doer of it, and none is able to do it except Him. As for this whispering, it is said that his whispering to him (peace be upon him) was that he should ask God the Exalted for affliction, so as to test and examine his patience in what befalls him, as ʿUmar ibn al-Farid, the Sharaf al-Din, said:

*"Test me in whatever You wish for Your love, for my choice is what contains Your pleasure."*

His asking for affliction rather than well-being is a sin relative to his station, not a true sin, and the purpose of his calling out with that is the acknowledgment of the sin.

It is also said that a man sought his help against a tyrant, and the Satan whispered to him to abandon helping him, so he did not help him, and God the Exalted touched him for that reason with what touched him.

It is also said that his livestock were in the territory of a disbelieving king, and he flattered him and did not fight him, by whispering from the Satan. So God the Exalted rebuked him with affliction. It is also said that he whispered to him, so he was impressed by the abundance of his wealth and children, and God the Exalted tested him for that. All these views, in my opinion, contain what is not befitting the rank of the prophets (peace be upon them).

A group went to the view that the *nusb* and *adhab* were not the illness and pain he had, or the illness and the loss of family and wealth, but rather two matters that befell him while he was ill and had lost his family and wealth. It is said: they were the Satan's whisperings to him during his illness, about the great affliction and despair of mercy, and the incitement to impatience. The Satan would whisper this to him while he struggled to repel it, until he became exhausted and pained by what he was in of affliction, so he called out to his Lord, seeking to have it turned away from him and seeking help against it: ﴿The Satan has touched me with hardship and torment.﴾ It is also said that they were from the Satan's whispering to others. It is said that the Satan appeared to his wife in the form of a physician and said to her: "There is a afflicted man here; would you like me to treat him?" She said: "Yes, on the condition that when I cure him, he says: 'You cured me.'" She was inclined to that, and conveyed his words to Ayyub (peace be upon him), so he recognized that it was the Satan, and that was harder on him than what he was in. ﴿So he called out to his Lord: "Harm has touched me..."﴾ and so on. It is also said that the Satan asked her to slaughter for other than God the Exalted when he treated him and he was cured, and she was inclined to that. This weighed heavily on him (peace be upon him), so he called out. It is also said that three believers used to visit him, and one of them apostatized. He asked about him, and it was said to him: "Satan cast into him that God the Exalted does not afflict the prophets and the righteous." He was greatly pained by that and said what he said. In another report: some of the Children of Israel passed by him, and some of them said to others: "This did not befall him except for a sin he committed." This is a kind of whispering of the Satan, so that weighed heavily on him, and he said what he said. The attribution in all of what has been mentioned is with regard to whispering. It is also said otherwise. And God the Exalted knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 42:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Strike with your foot﴾ is either a narration of what was said to him before, or it is a quoted speech of an implied saying, coordinated with (nadā, "he called out"), meaning: so We said to him, "Strike with your foot," that is, strike with it.
Page 207
Similarly, His saying, the Exalted: ﴿This is a cool bath and a drink﴾, for it is also either a narration of what was said to him after his compliance with the command and the gushing of the water, or it is a quoted speech of an implied saying, coordinated with an implied matter that the discourse leads to. It is as if it were said: "So he struck it, and a spring gushed forth, and so We said to him: 'This is a bath you wash in, and you drink from it, and your outward and inward being will be healed.'" So "al-mughtasal" (the bath) is a passive participle with the object elided and the verb's effect transferred, and likewise "al-sharab" (the drink). It is reported from Muqatil that "al-mughtasal" is a noun of place, meaning "this is a place in which you wash," but this is nothing. The apparent sense of the verse is that the thing referred to by "bath and drink" is one and the same. It has also been said that he, peace be upon him, struck with his right foot and a hot spring gushed forth, and he washed in it, and with his left foot and a cold spring gushed forth, and he drank from it. Al-Hasan said: he struck with his foot and a spring gushed forth and he washed in it, then he walked about forty cubits, then he struck with his foot again and another spring gushed forth and he drank from it. Perhaps by the first he meant a hot spring. The apparent wording does not indicate multiplicity.

Describing it as "cold" on this basis applies to "drink," even though "bath" is mentioned before it as the thing described; and taking "this" as a reference to the genus of what gushes forth, or assuming "this is cold, etc." is a strained reading that does not escape weakness.

It has also been said: he was commanded to strike with his foot so that every disease would fall off his body.

This took place, according to what is narrated from Qatadah, al-Hasan and Muqatil, in the land of al-Jabiyah in Syria. There is also an elision in the discourse, that is: so he washed and drank, and thereby We removed the harm that was upon him,

And We gave him his family: by restoring them to life after their death, according to what is narrated from al-Hasan.

Al-Tabarsi narrated, from Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him, that Allah the Exalted restored to him the family members who had died before the trial, and his family members who had died while he was in the trial. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit): The majority hold that Allah the Exalted restored to him those of his family who had died, healed the sick, and gathered together those of them who had been scattered. It has also been said, and I incline to this, that He gave him those of them who were still alive, relieved them of their illnesses, and granted them a comfortable life, so they multiplied until their number reached those who had passed away, ﴿and the like of them with them﴾, so he had twice what he had before. The apparent meaning is that this gift was in this world. Some claimed that this is a promise, and that the gift will be in the Hereafter. ﴿As a mercy from Us﴾, meaning, as a great mercy to him from Our side.

﴿And a reminder for those of understanding﴾: and as a reminder to them of this, so that they may be patient in hardships as he was patient, and turn to Allah the Exalted in what afflicts them, just as he turned to Him, so that the Glorified will deal with them likewise. So do with him, [that is,] the good outcome. It is narrated from Qatada that he, peace be upon him, was tested for seven years and some months, and was thrown on the dunghill of the Children of Israel, with worms moving in his body. He was patient, so Allah the Exalted relieved him, greatly increased his reward, and bestowed good upon him. And from Ibn 'Abbas: that everything between his two feet up to his horn became one single sore, and he was laid upon ashes until the veil of his heart was revealed. His wife would go to him, and one day she said to him: "Do you not see, O Ayyub, what has befallen me? By Allah, from the hardship and destitution, I sold my hair for a loaf of bread so that I could feed you. So pray to Allah the Exalted that He may heal you and give you relief." He said: "Woe to you! We were in comfort for seventy years, so be patient until we are in adversity for seventy years." He remained in the trial for seven years. Then he prayed, and Jibril, peace be upon him, came and took him by the hand, then said: "Stand up." So he rose from his place, and [Jibril] said: ﴿Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and a drink﴾. He bathed and drank, and was healed. Allah the Exalted clothed him in a garment from Paradise, and he moved aside and sat in a corner. His wife came, but did not recognize him, and said: "O servant of Allah, where is the afflicted man who was here? Perhaps the dogs or the wolves have taken him." She kept speaking with him for a while. He said: "Woe to you, I am Ayyub. Allah the Exalted has restored my body to me, and has restored to me my wealth and my children, and the like of them with them. And He rained down upon me locusts of gold." He began taking the locusts in his hand and putting them in a garment, and spreading his cloak to receive them. Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "O Ayyub, have you not had enough?" He said: "My Lord, who could have enough of Your bounty and Your mercy?"

In al-Bahr: Anas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Ayyub remained in his affliction for eighteen years, his flesh falling away, until the people grew weary of him, and none remained patient with him except his wife."

The greatness of his trial, peace be upon him, is well known and widely spread, and no two people have disagreed about it. But regarding the extent of his condition, to the point that he was thrown on a dunghill and similar things, there is disagreement. Al-Tabarsi said: "The people of verification have said: it is not permissible that he be in a state that people find repulsive, because that would cause aversion. As for poverty, illness, and the loss of family, Allah the Exalted may test him with these."

In Hidayat al-Murid by al-Qani: "It is permissible for the prophets, peace be upon them, to suffer any human ailment that is not forbidden, not disliked, not a permissible thing that is degrading, not a chronic condition, and not something that souls loathe or that leads to aversion." Then, after two pages, he said: "By our words 'nor a chronic condition' and 'nor something that souls loathe,' we exclude what is of that kind, such as paralysis, leprosy, elephantiasis, blindness, and insanity." As for fainting, al-Nawawi said: "There is no doubt that it is permissible for them, because it is an illness, unlike insanity, which is a deficiency." Abu Hamid restricted fainting to that which is not prolonged, and al-Bulqini affirmed this. Al-Subki said: "It is not like the fainting of others, because it only veils their outer senses and not their hearts, since their hearts are protected from even light sleep." He said: "Insanity is impossible for them, even if slight, because it is a deficiency. Blindness is linked to it, and no prophet was ever blind. What is mentioned about Shu'ayb being blind has not been established. As for Ya'qub, he had a film over his eyes which then disappeared." End of quotation.

Some have distinguished regarding the occurrence of these conditions: between after the proclamation and the attainment of the purpose of prophethood, when it is permissible, and before it, when it is not permissible. Perhaps you will choose the view that they are protected from what souls loathe, and what leads to disgust and aversion absolutely. In that case, one must say that what Ayyub, peace be upon him, was tested with did not reach the level of disgust and aversion, as is indicated by what is narrated from Qatada and transmitted by the storytellers (qussas) in their books. Some have mentioned that his disease was smallpox, but I do not believe this to be correct. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

[Page 208]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 44:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And take in your hand a bundle [ḍighth]﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to ﴿Strike with your foot﴾, or to ﴿And We gave him﴾, with the implied meaning: "We said: take in your hand," and so on. The first is closer in wording (lafẓan), but this is more appropriate in meaning (maʿnan), for the need for this command does not arise except after recovery and the suitability of the time, since his wife — according to the differing reports — was Raḥmah daughter of Ifrāʾīm, or Mīshā son of Yūsuf, or Liyā daughter of Yaʿqūb, or Mākhīr daughter of Mīshā son of Yūsuf.

The subtlety of ﴿as a mercy from Us﴾ is not hidden. According to the first report, she went out for some need and was delayed; or she conveyed to Ayyūb from Satan that he should say a forbidden word, and he would be healed, and she advised him of this, saying to him: "How long will this affliction last? [Say] one word, then ask your Lord for forgiveness, and He will forgive you." Or she brought him something beyond what she usually brought of bread, so he thought she had committed a forbidden act in that, and he swore that if he recovered he would strike her one hundred blows. So God, exalted is He, commanded him to take the ḍighth, which is a small bundle of grass or basil or twigs. It was also said: a large handful of twigs. From it comes the expression ḍighth ʿalā ibbāla (a bundle upon a faggot), where the ibbāla is a bundle of firewood and the ḍighth is a handful of firewood upon it too. From it is the poet's saying:

"And below me a fine-bodied mare, which I had tethered, and I cast upon her a bundle of perfumed fresh grass."

Ibn ʿAbbās said here: the ḍighth is the stalk of a palm cluster (ʿuthkūl al-nakhl). Mujāhid said: it is the tamarisk (athl), a plant with thorns. Ḍaḥḥāk said: a bundle of mixed grass. Al-Akhfash said: green trees. And it is reported from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab that when he (peace be upon him) was commanded, he took a ḍighth of reed (thumām) containing one hundred stalks. Qatāda said: it is a single stalk containing ninety-nine stalks, and the original (intended) is the completion of one hundred. If this is considered essential to the concept of ḍighth — and I do not think so — then well; otherwise the speech is taken to mean one hundred, as if it were said: "Take in your hand a ḍighth in which there are one hundred stalks." ﴿Then strike with it﴾, that is, with that ḍighth, ﴿and do not break your oath﴾, for righteousness (al-barr) is fulfilled by it. God, exalted is He, prescribed this as a mercy to him and to her, for the goodness of her service to him and his pleasure with her. It is a concession that remains in force regarding the ḥudūd (prescribed punishments) in our sharia, and in other matters as well; but other than the ḥudūd is known from it by the stronger inference (al-ṭarīq al-awlā).

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Abū Umāma ibn Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, who said: "A slave-girl among the Banū Sāʿida became pregnant from fornication. She was asked: 'By whom is your pregnancy?' She said: 'By so-and-so the paralysed.' The paralysed man was asked, and he said: 'She has spoken the truth.' This was brought to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he said: 'Take a cluster containing one hundred stalks, and strike him with it one blow.' And they did so."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Thawbān: "A man committed an immoral act in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he was ill, near death. His family informed (the Prophet) of what he had done, so the Prophet ﷺ commanded a palm-spathe containing one hundred stalks, and he was struck with it one blow."

Al-Ṭabarānī reported from Sahl ibn Saʿd: "The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) was brought an old man whose veins had become prominent, who had committed fornication with a woman, and he struck him with a ḍighth containing one hundred stalks, one blow."

These reports do not indicate the generality of the ruling for everyone who can endure the customary flogging. However, whoever holds that the ruling of the verse remains holds it in general, but they stipulated that each one of the hundred should reach the one struck, either with its tips upright or with its stems spread out in the manner of striking.

Al-Khafājī said: they stipulated in it the causing of pain; as for when there is no pain at all, then no. So if one strikes with a single whip that has two branches fifty times, one who swore to strike him a hundred times is righteous (yabarr) if he feels pain; but if he does not feel pain, he is not righteous, even if he struck him a hundred times, because striking is designed for an action painful to the body by an instrument of discipline. It was also said: he breaks his oath in every case, as is detailed in the commentaries on al-Hidāya and others. End of quotation.

Ibn ʿAsākir reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: "It is not permitted for anyone after Ayyūb to do this, except the prophets, peace be upon them." In the Aḥkām al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm of al-Jalāl al-Suyūṭī, from Mujāhid, he said: "This was specific to Ayyūb." Al-Kiyā said: al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfa and Zufar held that whoever does this has fulfilled his oath; Mālik disagreed and considered it specific to Ayyūb, peace be upon him. Some said: the ruling was general and then abrogated (nusikha); the correct view is that the ruling remains. The verse is cited as evidence that a husband may strike his wife, and may swear without adding an exception (istithnāʾ); and that the condition for istithnāʾ is that it be connected (ittiṣāl), for had it not been a condition, He, glory be to Him and exalted is He, would have commanded him to make the exception and would not have needed the striking with the ḍighth.

ʿAṭāʾ used it as evidence for another matter: Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr reported with a sound chain from him that a man said to him: "I swore that I would not clothe my wife with a garment until she stands at ʿArafa." He said: "Carry her on a donkey, then go and make her stand at ʿArafa with it." The man said: "I only meant the day of ʿArafa." ʿAṭāʾ said: "Ayyūb, when he swore that he would flog his wife a hundred lashes, intended to strike her with the ḍighth; God, exalted is He, only commanded him to take a ḍighth and strike her with it." Then he said: "The Qur'an is only lessons, the Qur'an is only lessons."

There is room for discussion on this matter. Many people have used this verse as evidence for the permissibility of legal stratagems (ḥiyal) and made it a foundation for their validity. In my view, every stratagem that results in nullifying a legal wisdom of the Sharia is not accepted, such as the stratagem for avoiding zakat and the stratagem for avoiding the waiting period (istibrāʾ). This is like a middle position on the question, for among the scholars there are those who permit stratagems absolutely and those who do not permit them absolutely; and the scholar Ibn Taymiyya discussed this at length. ﴿Indeed We found him patient﴾ in what afflicted him in his person, his family, and his wealth.

He, peace be upon him, used to say whenever a calamity befell him: "O God, You took, and You gave," and he would praise God, mighty and majestic. His complaint to God, exalted is He, about Satan does not detract from this, because patience is the absence of impatience (jazaʿ), and there is no impatience in what was mentioned, such as wishing for well-being and seeking healing; and he said that, as it was said, out of fear of temptation in religion, as you have heard above.

It is also reported that he said in his supplication: "My God, You know that my tongue never contradicted my heart, my heart never followed my sight, I was never distracted by what my right hand possessed, I never ate without an orphan with me, I never spent the night sated while a hungry or naked person was with me." Then God, exalted is He, relieved him.

﴿How excellent a servant﴾, that is, Ayyūb, ﴿indeed he was one who turns back (awwāb)﴾, a justification for his praise
Page 210
The meaning of awwāb has already been mentioned,

﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob﴾. "Al-thalatha" (the three) is either an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to "ʿibādanā" (Our servants), or a substitution (badal) for it.

It was also said that it is in the accusative by an implied "aʿnī" (I mean). Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Kathīr, and the people of Makkah read "ʿabdanā" (Our servant) in the singular. In that case, "Ibrāhīm" alone is a substitution, an explicative apposition, or the object of "aʿnī," and he is singled out by the title of servanthood for the greater honor he holds. What follows him is coordinated with "ʿabdanā." It is also permissible that the intended meaning of "ʿabdanā" is "ʿibādanā," with the singular noun used in the generic sense (lil-jins) in place of the plural, so that the two readings coincide.

﴿possessors of strength and insight﴾: "ūlī al-aydī" means those possessing strength in obedience, and "al-abṣār" means those possessing insight in religion. Here "al-aydī" is a metonymy (majāz mursal) for strength, and "al-abṣār" is the plural of "baṣar" in the sense of "baṣīrah" (insight). This is also a figurative usage, but it is the well-known one for that word. Alternatively, "ūlī al-aʿmāl al-jalīlah wa al-ʿulūm al-sharīfah" means those possessing noble deeds and exalted knowledge. In this reading, mention of "the hands" is mention of the cause with the effect intended, and "al-abṣār" in the sense of "al-baṣāʾir" is a figurative reference to the knowledge that branches from them, as with the first interpretation. On both readings there is an implicit rebuke of the ignorant and idle, that they are like those who have lost their hands and eyes, and a reproach for their neglect of striving and reflection although they are able to do both.

It was also said that "al-aydī" means the blessings, i.e., those upon whom God Most High bestowed prophethood and high station, or those who bestowed blessings and kindnesses upon people by guiding and teaching them. There is much to be said about this.

It was read as "al-ayādī" in the plural of plural, like "awṭuf" and "awāṭif." ʿAbdullāh, al-Ḥasan, ʿĪsā, and al-Aʿmash read "al-ayd" without the yāʾ. It was said that the intended word is "al-aydī" with the yāʾ, which was dropped by relying on the kasrah in its place. Since "al" (the definite article) replaces tanwīn, the yāʾ was dropped along with it, just as it is dropped with tanwīn. Abū Ḥayyān related this, then said: "This explanation is not admissible, because dropping this yāʾ in the presence of "al" is something Sībawayh mentioned among the poetic licenses (ḍarāʾir)." It was also said that "al-ayd" means strength in obedience to God Most High, similar to what preceded. Al-Zamakhsharī, after explaining the omission by reliance on the kasrah, and interpreting it as "al-ayd" from "al-taʾyīd" (support), said: "It is unsteady and not well established."

It was justified by the fact that this reading entails the loss of the parallelism (muqābalah) and the loss of the rhetorical nuance (al-nukta al-bayāniyyah). So do not be heedless.

Indeed, We purified them with a pure [quality]: the remembrance of the Abode." This is a reason for what they were described with. The bāʾ (ب) indicates causality (al-sababiyyah, the sense of "because of"). The word "khāliṣah" is an active participle (ism fāʿil, a participial noun), and its tanwīn (the nunation ending) serves to magnify it. His words, exalted is He, "the remembrance of the Abode," explain it after its vagueness, for magnification. It is also permissible for it to be a predicate of its implied pronoun, meaning: it is the remembrance of the Abode. In either case, "dhikrā" is a verbal noun (maṣdar) with its object added to it (muḍāf li-mafʿūlihi), and the definiteness of "al-Dār" is by prior reference, meaning the Abode of the Hereafter. This implies that it is the true abode, while this world is a metaphor. That is, We made them sincere to Us because of a pure quality of great standing, unmixed with anything: their constant remembrance of the Hereafter. Their sincerity in obedience results from their remembering it, because the aim of their gaze and the object of their thoughts in all that they do and leave undone is the neighbourhood of God, mighty and majestic, and attaining the vision of Him, and this cannot be achieved except in the Hereafter.

It has also been said: We purified them by granting them success in it (the Hereafter) and by kindness toward them in choosing it. The bāʾ, as in the first reading, indicates causality, and the statement is like your saying: "I honoured him with knowledge," meaning: because he is knowledgeable, I honoured him; or: I honoured him because you made him knowledgeable. In the second, it may be imagined that it is a connective (ṣilah). The first interpretation is supported by the reading of al-Aʿmash and Ṭalḥah: "bi-khāliṣatihim" (with their pure [quality]).

Ibn al-Mundhir reported, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, that "the remembrance of the Abode" means their reminding people of the Hereafter, encouraging them toward it and discouraging them from this world, in a manner pure of selfish appetites, as is the practice of the Prophets, peace be upon them. It has also been said: the intended Abode is this world, and its remembrance is good praise and the truthful tongue that belongs to no one else. This is attributed to al-Jubbāʾī and Abū Muslim, and Ibn ʿAṭiyyah mentioned it as a possibility. The meaning of the verse according to this, as al-Ṭabarsī said, is: We singled them out for good mention in the generations after them.

Abū Jaʿfar, Shaybah, al-Aʿraj, Nāfiʿ, and Hishām read "khāliṣah" in the genitive construction with "dhikrā" (idāfah), as an explanatory construction, meaning: "with that which is purified from the remembrance of the Abode," in the sense that they do not mix its remembrance with anything else at all. Or it may carry other meanings. On this reading it is also permissible for "khāliṣah" to be a verbal noun like "al-ʿāqibah" and "al-kādhibah," added to its agent, meaning: We purified them in that the remembrance of the Abode became pure for them. The apparent sense of Abū Ḥayyān's words is that the possibility of it being a verbal noun is also valid in the first reading, but he said: "The more apparent is that it is an active participle."

[Page 211]
—

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 47:

﴿And indeed they are, with Us, among the chosen ones﴾, i.e., those selected from among their kind. Here there is a well-known grammatical point of i'lal (morphological alteration).

Regarding it, it is permissible that it (the phrase ﴿عِنْدَنا﴾ "with Us") be a complement of the predicate (khabar), and that it be a complement of an omitted element indicated by ﴿among the chosen ones﴾, i.e., "and they are chosen with Us." They did not permit it to be a complement of the mentioned ﴿al-mustafayn﴾ ("the chosen ones"), because the alif-lam in it is a relative (mawsulah) and ﴿mustafayn﴾ is a relative clause (silah), and what is within the scope of a relative clause does not have its complement precede the relative pronoun, lest it entail the precedence of the relative clause over the relative pronoun. It has been objected that we do not concede that the alif-lam in it is relative, since it is not intended to denote occurrence (hudūth). Even if it is conceded, the preceding element is an adverbial (ẓarf), and this is given a latitude not given to other things. The apparent view is that the sentence is coordinated (ʿatf) with what precedes it, and its emphasis serves to add greater concern for their being, in His presence, among the chosen from among mankind.

﴿al-akhyar﴾ ("the good ones"), i.e., those who surpass others in goodness. It is the plural of khayr (good), the opposite of sharr (evil), which in origin is an elative form (af'al tafdil). The analogical rule for the elative form is that it should not be pluralized into af'al, but because of the obligation to lighten it, to the extent that it is not said akhyar except as an anomaly or in poetic necessity, it has been treated as though it were an original pattern. It has also been said that it is the plural of khayyir (with doubled letter) or of khayr (without doubling), derived from it, like amwat as the plural of mayyit (with doubling), or mayt (without doubling).

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah 38, verse 48:

﴿And mention Isma'il﴾. He is mentioned separately from his father and brother, showing concern for his status, in that the Arabs share him with no one else. Or it is to indicate his firmness in patience (sabr), which is the purpose of the mention here. ﴿And al-Yasa'﴾. Ibn Jarir said: he is the son of Akhtub, son of al-'Ajuz, and he mentioned that Ilyas appointed him as his successor over the Children of Israel, and then he was given prophethood. The lam in it is an extra lam (al-lam al-za'ida, the lam of addition), which is constant because it accompanies the naming. This does not contradict his being non-Arab, for it has remained in some non-Arabic proper names, such as al-Iskandar (Alexander). Al-Tibrizi considered it a grammatical error for someone to say "Iskandar" without it. My own view is that, if it is a non-Arabic name and the definite article (al-) is part of the naming, it should not be said that the lam is an addition to it. It was also said that it is an Arabic name, derived from yasa', the present tense of wasi'a, related by al-Jalal al-Suyuti in *al-Itqan*. In the *al-Qamus* it says: "Yasa', like yada', is a non-Arabic name to which al-(the definite article) was added, and it is not added to its counterparts such as Yazid."

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿wa-al-Layasa'﴾ with two lams and with shaddah (doubling). It is as if its original form were *Liyasa'*, on the pattern fiy'al, from al-lasa' (the sting). The definite article was added to it, by analogy with the transferred noun (al-manqul) which takes it in order to mark its original form. Some scholars were certain that in this reading too it is a non-Arabic proper name to which the lam was added.

﴿And Dhul-Kifl﴾. It was said he is the son of Ayyub. It is reported from Wahb that God Most High sent, after Ayyub, Sharaf, the son of Ayyub, as a prophet, and named him Dhul-Kifl, and commanded him to call to His tawhid (oneness). He remained in al-Sham (Syria) throughout his life until he died, and he lived seventy-five years.

In *al-'Aja'ib* by al-Kirmani: it was said he is Ilyas; it was said he is Yusha' ibn Nun; it was said he is a prophet whose name is Dhul-Kifl; it was said he was a righteous man who undertook (takaffala) affairs and fulfilled them; it was said he is Zakariyya, from the words of God Most High: ﴿And Zakariyya was made her guardian﴾ (3:37). End of quotation. Ibn 'Asakir said: he is a prophet for whom God Most High guaranteed, in his work, double the reward of the work of other prophets. It was said: he was not a prophet, and al-Yasa' appointed him as successor, and he undertook for him that he would fast by day and stand in prayer by night. It was said: that he would pray one hundred rak'ahs every day. It was said: he was a righteous man among the righteous who lived in his time, when there were four hundred prophets from the Children of Israel, whom a tyrannical king killed, except for one hundred of them who fled from the killing. He sheltered them, concealed them, and took care of their needs, so God Most High named him Dhul-Kifl. It was said: he is al-Yasa', and that he had two names; but the apparent sense of the text rejects this.

﴿And all of them﴾, that is, all of them ﴿are among the chosen ones﴾, the well-known for goodness. This refers to the verses preceding, which speak of their virtues. ﴿Such is the mention﴾, that is, honour for them. The word *dhikr* has become common in this sense, because honour necessarily entails fame and being mentioned among people, so it is used figuratively for it by the relation of necessary connection (ʿalaqat al-luzum). What is meant by the mention of their stories and God Most High's praise of them is a great honour for them. Or the meaning is: this which has been mentioned of the verses is a kind of the mention which is the Qur'an. He mentioned that for the transition from one type of speech to another, as al-Jahiz says in his books: "This is a chapter," and then he begins another chapter; and as the writer says when he finishes a section of his book and wishes to begin another: "This, and it was such and such." It is said that the predicate is often omitted in such cases, and upon this reading is ﴿This; and indeed for the transgressors is the worst place of return﴾ (38:55). You will hear, God willing, the discussion about it, so it should not be said that there is no benefit in it, since it is known that it is from the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas said: "This is the mention of the prophets who passed before, peace be upon them,"

[p. 212]

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, for the righteous is a good place of return﴾, i.e., a place to return to. This begins the statement of their great reward in the Hereafter, after the statement of their good remembrance in this world. By "the righteous" (al-muttaqin) is meant either the genus, into which they enter as a first instance, or the very people previously mentioned, who are described by this term to praise them for taqwa (God-consciousness), which is the utmost degree of perfection. In my view, the sentence is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence before it, as if it were said: "This is their honour in this world, and that for them and their likes, or indeed for them in the Hereafter, is a good place of return." Or it is of the type of coordinating one narrative with another narrative.

Al-Shihab al-Khafaji, may God have mercy on him, said: "It is a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyya)," but he did not specify the subject of the circumstantial clause. It is unlikely that it refers to *dhikran* (ذِكْرًا), because it is an indefinite noun that comes first, nor that it refers to *hadha* (هَذا), because it is a subject (mubtada'). Moreover, the meaning under the assumption of a circumstantial clause is obscure.

Some of the eminent scholars of the modern age said: he intended that the speech has the sense of "and the situation is thus," i.e., the matter and the state of affairs are thus. He did not mean that the sentence is a circumstantial clause in the well-known sense, which requires a bearer of the circumstance and an operator acting upon the circumstance, and so on. He claimed that the matter is the same in every sentence that is said to be a circumstantial clause and in which there is no pronoun referring back to what precedes it, such as: "Zayd came while the sun was rising." He said: "This is what should be relied upon, even though the grammarians have not mentioned it." And the circumstantial clause is not hidden from anyone who has discernment.

The annexation (iḍāfa) of *husna* (حُسْنَ) to *ma'ab* (مَآبٍ) is an annexation of the adjective to the noun it qualifies. This is either by interpreting it as "a place of return that possesses goodness," or "a good [place of return]," or, without such interpretation, deliberately for the sake of emphasis (mubalagha).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 50:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ is a badal al-ishtimal (a substitution of inclusion). It is also permissible that it be in the accusative on the basis of praise. Al-Zamakhshari made it an 'atf al-bayan (explicative apposition) to ﴿a good place of return﴾. ʿAdn (Eden) is said to be among the proper names that have become predominant by a presumed predominance (ghalaba taqdiriyya). The obligatory presence of an idafa (genitive construction) in it, or its being made definite with the article, is the more common case, as Ibn Malik explicitly stated in al-Tashil (his work on grammar). ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ is like the city of Taba (Madinat Taiba), not like "the human being of Zayd," for the latter is ugly. It has also been said: the proper name is the plural ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾. This too is not of the predominant type, because the idafa intended, which the proper name replaces through predominance, is an idafa that gives it definiteness. On both views, it is specific, so it is fit to serve as an explicative. However, Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that the grammarians have two positions regarding 'atf al-bayan. One of them holds that it occurs only with definite nouns (ma'arif), so that an 'atf al-bayan follows only a definite noun. This is the position of the Basrans. The second holds that it may occur with indefinite nouns (nakirat), so that an 'atf al-bayan may follow an indefinite noun, just as a definite noun may follow a definite noun. This is the position of the Kufans, and al-Farisi followed them. As for their disagreement regarding definiteness and indefiniteness, no one held that except al-Zamakhshari, as Ibn Malik explicitly stated in al-Tashil. So it is a construction of the matter according to his position.

Others held that ʿadn is a verbal noun (masdar) of "ʿadana bi-makan kadha" (he settled in such a place), and from it comes al-maʿdin (the mine), the place where gems settle. There is no proper-name status here, and no transfer. The meaning of ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ is gardens of settlement and permanence. If it is an 'atf al-bayan, then it is according to the position of the Kufans and al-Farisi.

Among the strange reports is what Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: I asked Kaʿb about His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾, and he said: "Gardens
صفحة 213
of vines and grapes in Syriac." In the tafsir of Ibn Jarir it is said to be in Greek (Rumiyya). His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿with doors opened for them﴾ is either an adjective of ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾, which is the view of Ibn Ishaq and followed by Ibn ʿAtiyya, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from its implied pronoun in the predicate of inna, the governing element being the presumed settledness (al-istiqrar al-muqaddar) or the adverbial phrase itself, because it includes its meaning and substitutes for it. This is the view of al-Zamakhshari and his summarizers. Or it is a circumstantial clause from its deleted pronoun together with the governing element, the meaning indicating it, the estimate being "he wishes its being opened"; this is the view of al-Hufi. "The doors" is the deputy subject of ﴿opened﴾ according to the majority, and the connecting pronoun referring back to the gardens is deleted, its estimate being "the doors of them." The Kufans dispensed with that by the article (alif-lam), since it stands in place of the pronoun, as if it were said: "opened for them are its doors." Abu ʿAli held that the deputy subject of ﴿opened﴾ is a pronoun for the gardens, and "the doors" is a badal al-ishtimal from it, as is apparent in al-Zamakhshari's words. It cannot be a badal al-baʿd min al-kull (partitive substitution), because the doors of the gardens are not a part of the gardens, according to what Abu Hayyan said. Zayd ibn ʿAli, ʿAbdullah ibn Rafiʿ, and Abu Haywa read ﴿Gardens of Eden opened﴾ with both in the nominative, on the basis that they are two predicates of an omitted subject, meaning: it, i.e. the return, is Gardens of Eden whose doors are opened for them; or it is Gardens of Eden, they are opened with their doors for them; or they are a subject and predicate.

The connection of the sentence with what precedes it is that it explains ﴿a good place of return﴾, because its substance is gardens whose doors are opened as an honour to them. Or it is a parenthetical sentence (mu'taridha).

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿reclining therein﴾, and His saying: ﴿calling therein for abundant fruit and drink﴾. It has been said that these are two circumstantial clauses (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in ﴿for them﴾, and they are anticipated circumstantial clauses (ḥāl muqaddara), because reclining and what follows it do not occur at the time the doors are opened, but after it. It has also been said that the first is an anticipated circumstantial clause from the pronoun mentioned, and the second is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in مُتَّكِئِينَ (muttakiʾīn). It has been permitted to make both of them circumstantial clauses of ﴿the God-fearing﴾, but this is not valid unless we say that the intervening element is not foreign, and the apparent meaning is that it is foreign. Some of the eminent scholars said: The more evident view is that مُتَّكِئِينَ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in يَدْعُونَ, placed first out of consideration for the rhyme-ending (fāṣila), while يَدْعُونَ is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf) explaining their state, as if it were said: What is their state after entering it? So it is said: they call therein for abundant fruit and drink, reclining therein. The restriction to fruit is to indicate that their eating is purely for enjoyment and pleasure, not for nourishment, since nourishment is for replacing what is lost, and there is no loss there. Since fruit comes in varieties, He, Exalted is He, described it as abundant, and its abundance results from the variety of its kinds and the abundance of each kind. As for drink, since it is a single kind, namely wine (al-khamr), it was stated in the singular. It has been said: fruit was described as abundant, and drink was not described, to indicate that there will be a great quantity of drink, whether its kinds are many or one. It may be said, and God knows best: the estimated reading is "and abundant drink," but "abundant" was omitted because of what came before it and out of consideration for the rhyme-ending.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 52:

﴿And with them will be women restraining their glances, (desiring only their husbands)﴾, i.e., they do not look at other than their husbands; or, they are restrained in their glances toward them, so that they (the men) do not look at other than them, because of the intensity of their beauty. The completion of the statement has already passed and is sweet. ﴿Of equal age﴾, i.e., of the same age, likened in equality and similarity to the *tara'ib* (the breastbones, i.e., the ribs of the chest), or because they all fell to the ground together at the time of birth and touched its dust. Thus *tarb* is in the sense of *mutarib* (one of the same age), just as *mithl* is in the sense of *mumathil*. Apparently this description pertains to them (the women among themselves), and so it indicates the love of some of them for others and their friendship with one another, for women of equal age love and befriend one another. In this there is great comfort for their husbands, just as in the hostility of co-wives there is great toil and a grave calamity for them. This has been tested and proven true; we ask God Most High for pardon and well-being.

It has been said that this description pertains to them and their husbands, i.e., their ages are like the ages of the men, so that complete mutual love may be achieved. This was preferred on the grounds that a man's concern for love between himself and his wife is greater than his concern for love among his wives, though this requires consideration. Then, the first description, on the first meaning, is sufficient to indicate their love for their husbands, and on the second meaning it is sufficient to indicate the love of their husbands for them. When love arises from one side, it generally arises from the other side as well, and it has been said: "From heart to heart there is a path." The matter in what is observed is that the wives being younger than the husbands is more beloved to them, not equality. Some chose that this description pertains to them and their husbands, which entails the equality of some of them with others. This holds when the intended meaning of the Most High's words ﴿And with them﴾ etc. is "and with each one of them." But if the intended meaning were "and with them collectively," and the plurality were distributed such that each individual of the people of Paradise has one of the restraining-glanced, equal-aged women, then considering the description as pertaining to them and to the husbands would seem required. However, this supposition contradicts what the reports have stated, whether we say, following what was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that the verse concerns human women, or we say, following what the author of *al-Faynan* stated, that it concerns the *hur* (the maidens of Paradise). It has also been said: based on what is apparent in the description, that equality in age exists among the *hur* and among the women of Paradise, so the verse applies to both.

This is the stated fact of the matter: "This is what you are promised for the Day of Reckoning" (hadha ma tu'aduna li-yawm al-hisab). That is, li-ajl yawm al-hisab, "on account of the Day of Reckoning." What they were promised is on account of their obedience and their righteous deeds, and these become manifest through the reckoning. So the reckoning is made as though it were the cause for the delay in fulfilling the promise. Therefore the attribution to the Day and to the reckoning is metaphorical (majaz).

It is also permitted that the lam (li-) carries the meaning of ba'da ("after"), as in the example: "It was written for five nights having passed (li-khams khalawna) of Jumada al-Akhirah," for instance. And this is less burdensome (aqall mu'unah).

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited yu'aduna with the ya' of the third person (yaa al-ghaybah). According to the recitation of the majority (al-Jumhur), with the ta' of address (ta' al-khitab), there is in it an iltifat (shift of grammatical person).

﴿Indeed, this﴾ — i.e., what has been mentioned of the various kinds of blessings and honors — ﴿is indeed Our provision﴾, which We have given you, ﴿which has no end﴾, meaning no cessation, ever. (Regarding "this" [hadha]), al-Zajjaj said: that is, "the matter is this," taking it as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence). Abu Ali said: that is, "this is for the believers," taking it as a subject whose predicate is omitted. Some scholars estimated it as mentioned.

Abu al-Baqa permitted the possibility that it is a subject with an omitted predicate, and the possibility that it is a predicate with an omitted subject. Some permitted that it is the agent (fa'il) of an omitted verb, meaning "this has passed," and that it is the object (maf'ul) of an omitted verb, meaning "take this." It was also permitted that the word is an ism al-fi'l (a noun functioning as a verb, here meaning "take") with dha as its object without any need for an estimated element. Its written form as a connected word makes this unlikely, and the estimation is easier than it. As for His Exalted saying, ﴿And indeed, for the transgressors is the worst of final destinations﴾, it is coordinated (ataf) with what precedes it. The problem of coordinating a declarative sentence (khabar) with an imperative/performative one (insha') under some of these possibilities has an easy answer. Al-Khafaji also pointed to the ḥāliyya (circumstantial clause) here, and perhaps its matter, according to some of the stated opinions, is minor.

"The transgressors" here means the disbelievers, as indicated by the statement of Ibn Abbas, who said: that is, those who transgressed against Me and denied My messengers. Al-Jubba'i said: the people of major sins, whether they were disbelievers or not. The attribution of "worst" (sharr) to "destination" (ma'ab) is like the attribution of "good" (husn) to it mentioned earlier. The apparent antithesis would require saying, "the ugliness of destination" here, or "the good of destination" earlier, but this is like that: it is not to be considered when the meanings are opposed, because it is a case of excessive artificiality in the rhetorical ornamentation (badi') science, as al-Marzuqi explicitly stated in his commentary on al-Hamasa, so it is said. It was also said that it is from the rhetorical device of ihtibak (omitting from each of two parallel parts an element mentioned in the other), and its original form is: "Indeed, for the righteous is the best destination and the good destination; and indeed, for the transgressors is the ugliest destination and the worst destination." Al-Khafaji found this good, but there is a degree of remoteness in it.

﴿Indeed, this﴾ — i.e., what has been mentioned of the various kinds of blessings and honors — ﴿is indeed Our provision﴾, which We have given you, ﴿which has no end﴾, meaning no cessation, ever. (Regarding "this" [hadha]), al-Zajjaj said: that is, "the matter is this," taking it as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence). Al-Khafaji also pointed to the ḥāliyya (circumstantial clause) here, and perhaps its matter, according to some of the stated opinions, is minor.

"The transgressors" here means the disbelievers, as indicated by the statement of Ibn Abbas, who said: that is, those who transgressed against Me and denied My messengers. Al-Jubba'i said: the people of major sins, whether they were disbelievers or not. The attribution of "worst" (sharr) to "destination" (ma'ab) is like the attribution of "good" (husn) to it mentioned earlier.
