Al-Khafaji found this good, but there is a degree of remoteness in it.

Al-Alusi's commentary on Surah 38, verse 56:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Jahannam﴾ (Jahannam, the Fire), its i'rab (grammatical case and function) is known from what has preceded. His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿yaslawnaha﴾ means they enter it and suffer its heat. It is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause, "state") either from Jahannam itself, or from the hidden pronoun in the predicate of inna (indeed), which refers back to (﴿evil place of return﴾), and which is intended to mean it (Jahannam). The ḥāl is muqaddarah (anticipated, i.e., its state is one that is yet to come about). ﴿So evil is the resting-place﴾, meaning: it, namely Jahannam, is [the evil resting-place]. Thus the one to whom dispraise applies is omitted. Al-mihad is like al-firash (bedding) both in wording and meaning, and it is used metaphorically for what a sleeper spreads out for himself. Al-mahd is like al-mihad, though it may be restricted to the resting place of an infant.

[Page 215]

﴿This﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada', subject), meaning "the punishment is this." His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿so let them taste it﴾ is a clause that follows the clause before it, so it has the status of the answer to an omitted conditional clause. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿scalding water and ghassaq﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is scalding water and ghassaq." The demonstrative *dha* may be used to refer to a plurality. Or it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning "from it is scalding water, and from it is ghassaq," as in the verse:

*Until, when the dawn lights up in the darkness,*
*and the herbs are left, some wilted and some reaped.*

Meaning: from it is something wilted, and from it is something reaped. Or *hadha* is a subject whose predicate is ﴿scalding water﴾, and the clause ﴿so let them taste it﴾ is a parenthetical insertion, like your saying: "Zayd, understand, is a righteous man." Or *hadha* is a subject whose predicate is ﴿so let them taste it﴾, according to the view of al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash, a grammarian) who permitted this, as in "Zayd, strike him," citing the verse:

*And many a woman said, "Khawlan, marry their girl!"*

Or *hadha* is in a position of accusative case governed by a hidden verb which ﴿so let them taste it﴾ explains, meaning: "let them taste this, so let them taste it." Perhaps you will prefer the view that *hadha* is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is (scalding water), and what lies between is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad). Al-Zamakhshari (author of al-Kashshaf) gave precedence to this view. The *fa'* in ﴿so﴾ is explanatory and sequential, and it indicates that they will have a tasting after a tasting. In ﴿scalding water and ghassaq﴾, on these two readings, the two possibilities mentioned first apply.

*Hamim* is water of extreme heat.

*Ghassaq*, with the doubled *sin* (ghassaq), is as Ibn Abi Ishaq, Qatadah, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, al-Fadl, Ibn Sa'dan, and Harun recited it from Abu 'Amr. With the single *sin* (ghasaq), as the rest of the seven readers recited it, it is a name for what flows from the pus of the people of Hell, as reported from 'Ata', Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd. From al-Suddi: it is what flows from their tears. Ibn Jarir reported from Ka'b that it is a spring in Hell into which flows the venom of every venomous creature, such as snakes, scorpions, and others, in which the unbeliever is dipped so that his skin and flesh fall off. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the zamharir (extreme cold). It was also said: it, whether doubled or single, is an adjective from *ghasaqa*, like *daraba* and *sami'a*, in the sense of "to flow." One says, "the eye ghasaqat" when its tears flowed. According to what is in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, by Abu Hayyan), it would then be an adjective whose noun has been omitted, meaning "and a drink that is ghassaq," and it is intended to mean what flows from the skins of the people of Hell, for example. The adjectival use is more apparent in the doubled form, because *fa''al* with doubling is rare among nouns. From it comes *al-ghayyad* (the male owl), *al-khattar* (a type of oil made from olive oil), and *al-'aqqar* (what is used for treatment from plants). Among the curious views is that of al-Jawaliqi and al-Wasiti that *ghassaq* is what is cold and foul-smelling in the language of the Turks. The truth is that it is Arabic. Indeed, foulness is a description of it in reality, but it is not included in its meaning.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Hibban, and a group of others reported, and al-Hakim authenticated it, from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If a bucketful of ghassaq were poured out in the world, it would make the people of the world stink."

It was also said: *ghassaq* is a punishment which none knows but Allah, Mighty and Majestic. But this report refutes it,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 58:

﴿And other [punishment of] its kind⁠﴾, i.e., and another kind of drink (madhuq, "that which is tasted"), which Ibn Mas'ud explained, as related from him by a group of narrators, as zamharir (extreme cold); or [it means] "and another punishment."

Al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, Ibn Jubayr, 'Isa, and Abu 'Amr read "ukhar" (in the plural), i.e., "and other kinds of drink" or "other kinds of punishment." ﴿Of a similar kind﴾, i.e., of the likeness of this drink, or of the punishment in its severity and dreadfulness. The pronoun is given in the singular rather than the dual in consideration of the hamim (boiling water) and the ghassaq (intensely cold liquid), taking it as referring to what has been mentioned; or it refers to the drink, which comprises both the hamim and the ghassaq; or it refers to the ghassaq. Mujahid read "shiklihi" with a kasra on the shin, and this is a dialectal form of "mithl" (like). When it means "charm/attractiveness" (ghanj), it is only with the kasra. ﴿Pairs﴾, i.e., kinds. And "akhar," according to both readings, may be the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "this is a drink or another punishment," or "these are other kinds of drinks or punishments," and the clause is conjoined to "hamim" [in this sense]. If you wish, you may supply "huwa" or "hiya" and conjoin the clause to "huwa hamim." It may also be a subject whose predicate is omitted, i.e., "and of it is a drink or another punishment," or "and of it are other drinks or kinds of punishment," and the conjunction is with "minhu hamim." It is also permitted to supply the predicate as "for them," i.e., "and for them is a drink or another punishment," or "and for them are other drinks or kinds of punishment," and the conjunction is with ﴿this, so let them taste it﴾. In all of these, "wa min shiklihi" and "wa azwaj" are two attributes of "akhar" or "ukhar." Although "akhar" is singular in form, it is plural in meaning and applies to multiple things.

It is also possible that "akhar" or "ukhar" is a subject, with "min shiklihi" as its attribute and "azwaj" as the predicate. The answer regarding the lack of agreement under the singular reading is what you have heard. It may also be that this is a conjunction with "hamim," the conjunction of a singular to a singular, with "min shiklihi" as its attribute and "azwaj" as an attribute of the three conjoined items. It is also permitted that "akhar" be the subject, "min shiklihi" its predicate, and "azwaj" the subject of the adverbial phrase. It may also be that the first is the subject, "min shiklihi" a fronted predicate, and "azwaj" the subject, with the clause being the predicate of the first subject, namely "akhar." Beginning with it is valid because it belongs to the category of "daif 'adha bi-qarmalah" (a weak one sought refuge in a bush); so the true subject is the omitted described noun, i.e., "a kind of other" or "a drink of other." It has been said that it is used for detailing. Among the justifications mentioned for an indefinite noun being used for detailing is the example: "The people are two: a man whom you honored and a man whom you humiliated." Ibn Hisham examined this in al-Mughni. They made the pronoun of "shiklihi" in both cases refer to "akhar," and these two would hardly be coherent under the plural reading, so reflect carefully, and do not be heedless.

﴿هَذا فَوْجٌ﴾ ("This is a host"): a large multitude of your followers in misguidance.

﴿مُقْتَحِمٌ﴾ ("plunging"): one who rides into hardship and enters it, or one who is in the midst of a terrifying severity. ﴿مَعَكُمْ﴾ ("with you"): the meaning is "This is a host that enters the Fire along with you, suffering what you suffer." This is a report of what the angels of punishment say to the leaders of misguidance upon their entry into the Fire, as a rebuke to them. Accordingly, the sense is: "It is said to them upon entry, 'This is...'" and so on.

In al-Kashshaf, which Abu Hayyan also favoured, it is a report of the speech of the tyrants among themselves, one of them addressing another concerning their followers, saying: "This is a host plunging with you." The adverbial phrase (al-ẓarf, adverbial of place) is connected to ﴿مُقْتَحِمٌ﴾. It was permitted that it be a second qualifier (al-naʿt, adjective) of ﴿فَوْجٌ﴾, or a circumstantial qualifier (al-ḥāl, circumstantial accusative) of it, since it has already been described, or of the hidden pronoun (al-ḍamīr al-mustatir) within it. Abu al-Baqa prohibited its being an adverbial phrase, saying: "It would entail corruption of the meaning." Al-Kawashi and the author of al-Anwar followed him. The author of al-Kashf objected to him, saying: "If the corruption lies in its indicating that they crowded one another to enter, and the meaning is not one of crowding between the two groups, the followers and the followed, since after entering they say that not in a state of crowding, then this is not necessary, because plunging does not indicate crowding, nor is it necessarily linked to it. It is rather like: 'I struck him along with Zayd (ḍarabtu maʿahu Zaydan),' which indicates participation in the striking and simultaneity. Likewise, the plunging of the followed into the Fire along with the followers indicates participation in each of the two groups' undergoing the plunge into the Fire and enduring its severity within a time that is conventionally close. If one said, 'This is a host with you, plunging,' it would not convey that the addressees are likewise, and the intended meaning would be corrupted. It is strange that one who permitted it to be a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in ﴿مُقْتَحِمٌ﴾ did not permit it to be an adverbial phrase. If there is a different objection, let him state it first, and then let him raise the objection." End of quotation. Some of them said: "The reason the adverbial sense is corrupt while the circumstantial sense is not, is that the meaning is not that they plunged into companionship and entered into it, but rather that they plunged into the Fire while accompanying you and being simultaneous with you." This is a corrupt statement with no real substance. The meaning conveyed by ﴿مَعَ﴾ (maʿa, "with"), which is expressed by companionship, is togetherness in being qualified by the meaning of its complement. It thus conveys that the two groups share in the plunging, not in companionship, as he imagined. Nor does it indicate that their two times are identical, as is explicitly stated in al-Mughni. Even if it were granted, its closeness makes it counted as unified, as was indicated in the wording of al-Kashf. So the truth is that there is no corruption.

The words of the Exalted, ﴿لا مَرْحَبًا بِهِمْ﴾ ("No welcome to them"), are an invocation (duʿaʾ) from the followed against their followers, whether the speaker of what precedes is the angels, peace be upon them, or some of the leaders to others. Whether it is a qualifier of ﴿فَوْجٌ﴾, or a circumstantial qualifier of it because of its description, or of its pronoun, in any case it is interpreted as a statement said to them: "No welcome," because it is an invocation, and an invocation is a performative utterance (inshaʾ) which is not described by it. Likewise it cannot be a circumstantial phrase without interpretation. The meaning is that they deserve to be told this, not that it was actually said to them. In the case of its being a qualifier or circumstantial phrase, it is part of the speech of the angels, peace be upon them, if they are the ones speaking, or part of the speech of some of the leaders. It was also permitted that it be the beginning of a speech from them. "Marḥaban" (welcome) comes from "al-ruḥb" with a ḍammah on the rāʾ, which is spaciousness; from it comes "al-ruḥba," an open wide space. It is a direct object (mafʿūl bihi) of a verb that must be omitted. "Bihim" ("to them") is an explanation of those cursed. The bāʾ here is for explanation, like the lām in the phrase "suqyan lahu" ("water to him"). The claim that the lām, rather than the bāʾ, is like this is an assertion without evidence. The meaning is: "They did not bring them spaciousness and room." It was said that the bāʾ is for transitivity, so its object is a second direct object of "ataw" (they brought), and this is based on the assumption that the lām cannot be for explanation. The statements of al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan are sufficient evidence against this. It is said: "Marḥaban bika," meaning "Your land has become spacious for you," just as it is said meaning "You came to a spacious land, not a narrow one." It is understood from the words of some of them that "marḥaban" may be an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) of an omitted verb, meaning "May the abode not be spacious for them, a spaciousness." The majority hold the first view. In any case, the intended meaning of this, when affirmed, is an invocation for good, and when negated, an invocation for evil.

﴿إنَّهم صالُو النّارِ﴾ ("Indeed they are the ones who burn in the Fire"): a reason given on the part of the angels for their deserving the invocation against them, or a description of them with what has been mentioned. Or it is a reason given by the leaders for this. The statement in this case implies that they will not benefit from them, as if it were said: "They enter the Fire by their deeds just as we do, so what benefit is there for us from them? So, no welcome to them."

﴿They said﴾, that is, the followers, who are the group that rushes in upon the leaders.

﴿Nay, but you! No welcome to you!﴾ That is, rather you are more deserving of what was said to us, or of what you said to us. Perhaps they addressed them with this on the assumption that the speaker was the angel guardians (the Khazanah), peace be upon them, although the apparent meaning is that they would say, by way of an apology to those speakers: "Rather, they are not welcome!", intending thereby to show their sincerity in contending with the leaders and in appealing to the guardians, hoping for their judgment to lighten their punishment or to double the punishment of their adversaries.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit): they addressed them so that the confrontation would be directed at those whom they could not confront in the world with something ugly, which would soothe their hearts, since they were the cause of their disbelief, and would be more painful to the leaders. This also is by way of interpreting the saying, on the basis that an inshaʾ (performative utterance) does not become a report (khabar); that is, "Rather, you are the ones about whom it is said," i.e., more deserving that it be said of you: "No welcome to you!" ﴿You brought it upon us﴾ is an explanation of their being more deserving of that, and the pronoun of absence in ﴿brought it upon us﴾ refers to the punishment, because it is understood from what precedes it, or to the verbal noun that it implies.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 61:

﴿They will say﴾ — and this is al-Saliy — meaning: you have brought forward the punishment, or the burning, and the entry into the Fire, upon us, through your misleading us and enticing us toward the corrupt beliefs and evil deeds that we had put forward, not that we ourselves undertook them of our own accord.

In the speech there are two rational metaphors (majazan 'aqliyyan, metaphors of attribution). The first is the attribution of the "bringing forward" to the leaders, because they were the cause of it through their misleading. The second is the attribution of it to the punishment or the burning, although the thing brought forward is not that, but rather the evil deed which is its cause. It has been said: the pronoun, which refers to the punishment or the burning caused by the deed, was applied to the deed as a linguistic metaphor (majaz lughawi). It has also been said: there is no need to resort to a metaphor here, so the bringing forward of the punishment or the burning is by way of the delay of mercy from them ﴿So evil is the abode﴾ — meaning: evil is the place of settling, Jahannam. This is from the speech of the followers, and it seems they intended by it to gratify themselves and to inflict harm, and that this abode is shared. It has also been said: by the aforementioned censure they intended to aggravate the crime of the leaders against them.

﴿They will say﴾ — meaning the followers as well. The saying of Ibn al-Sa'ib, that the speaker is all the people of the Fire, is highly contrary to the apparent meaning, so one does not turn to it. The insertion of the verb between their two speeches is due to the difference between them in essence and address, meaning: they said, turning away from disputing with their leaders, humbling themselves before Allah, Mighty and Majestic — ﴿Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, increase him in punishment, a double punishment in the Fire﴾ — meaning doubled, and its meaning is "possessing a double," i.e., a like amount: he is to have added to his punishment its like, so that with that increase he becomes twice the punishment of another. The term "double" is also applied to an unrestricted increase.

Ibn Mas'ud said here: "The double is serpents and scorpions." The apparent sense of some of their expressions is that ﴿whoever﴾ (man) is a relative pronoun, but al-Khafaji stated explicitly that it is a conditional. In al-Bahr: ﴿whoever brought forward﴾ refers to the leaders. Al-Dahhak said: it is Iblis and Qabil, and this is more fitting, contrary to the apparent sense reported from Ibn al-Sa'ib,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 62:

﴿And they said﴾ The pronoun refers to the tyrants (al-taghun) collectively. That is, the tyrants said to one another, in wonder and regret: ﴿What is wrong with us that we do not see men whom we used to count among the wicked﴾ in the world ﴿?﴾ That is, the lowly people who have no good in them and no benefit. By this they mean the poor among the believers. They used to belittle them and mock them because of their poverty and because they differed from them in religion. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the leading men of Quraysh, such as Abu Jahl and Umayya ibn Khalaf, and the People of the Well (Ashab al-Qalib). The men would then be Ammar, Suhayb, Salman, Khabbab, Bilal and their like, may God be pleased with them all. This is based on what is narrated from Mujahid, that the verse was revealed concerning them. The author of al-Kashf considered this weak, and the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul, the specific event that prompted a verse) does not serve as proof of restriction to that case. Some have inclined to the view that the pronoun refers to the followers, because the preceding words, God's saying ﴿They will say: Rather, you…﴾ and so on, are also addressed to them. They too used to mock the poor among the believers, following their leaders. Whatever the case, the clause ﴿we used to count﴾ and so on describes ﴿men﴾.

The words of His, may He be exalted, ﴿Did We take them as objects of ridicule?﴾ with an interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifham), because of which the connecting hamza (hamzat al-wasl) was dropped, as the two Hijazi readers, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, al-Hasan and Qatadah recited it. It is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) with no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis). They said this when they did not see them with them, as a denial against themselves and a rebuke to themselves for mocking them. His, may He be exalted, saying ﴿Or have our eyes turned away from them?﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿What is the matter with us that we do not see...﴾ etc., and the am (or) here is continuative (muttasilah). The preceding of what carries the meaning of the hamza makes its own preceding unnecessary, as the words of al-Zamakhshari imply. The meaning is: What is the matter with us that we do not see them in the Fire? Are they not in it, and is that why we do not see them? Rather, our eyes have turned away from them, so we do not see them, while they are in it. Or it is connected to His saying ﴿We took them...﴾ etc., and the am in it may also be continuative, the contrast being in terms of what follows necessarily. The meaning is that we did both things to them: mocking them, or disdaining and belittling them, and that our eyes rise above them and pass them over. This is in the sense of denying both matters together against themselves. From al-Hasan: all of that they did. They took them as objects of ridicule, and their eyes turned away from them, belittling them. Or it is disjunctive (munqati'ah), as if they had turned away from denying the mockery and denied against themselves something worse than it, namely that they made them people of no account to whom no regard is paid in any way. The use of ﴿zaghat﴾ instead of azaghna carries great emphasis, as if the eye by itself rejects them because of the ugliness of their appearance. How far is this from mockery, for the one mocked may be beloved and honoured.

It is permitted that the meaning of (or have our eyes turned away) be disjunctive: rather our eyes have turned away, and our understandings have failed, so that their place was hidden from us, and that they were upon the clear truth. The two Nahwi readers (al-Kisa'i and Hamzah... ) and Hamzah recited ﴿We took them﴾ without a hamza. It is permitted that it be understood as implied, with am indicating it, so the two readings coincide. And it is permitted that it not be so, and the statement is an announcement. Ibn al-Anbari said: the sentence is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: and We had taken them. It is also permitted that it be a resumptive sentence explaining what precedes it. Al-Zamakhshari and a group said: it is a second attribute of rijalan (men), and ﴿Or have our eyes turned away﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿What is the matter with us that we do not see...﴾ as you heard at first.

It is permitted that am here be disjunctive, as if they turned away from what came before and denied against themselves what is worse than it, or turned away from that to explain that what had happened to them on their account was due to the deviation of their eyes and the weariness of their understanding in perceiving that they were upon the truth, because of the shabbiness of their condition. ʿAbd Allah and his companions, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, al-A'raj, Nafi' and Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited sukhriyyan with a damma on the sin (sukhriyyan), meaning, as in the Bahr, the subjugation (sukhrah) and employment (istikhdam). The meaning of sikhriyyan with a kasra, according to the well-known usage of sakhar, is mockery (huzw), and this is the meaning of what is related from Abu 'Amr, who said: whatever is like servitude is sukhriyy with a damma, and whatever is like mockery is sikhriyy with a kasra. It was also said: with a kasra it means from taskhir (subjugation).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 64:

﴿Indeed, that﴾, i.e., what was related about them,
Page 219
﴿is the truth﴾ that they will necessarily speak. So what is meant by its being true is its being realised in the future.

Allah's words ﴿the dispute of the people of the Fire﴾ are the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., it is a dispute (takhāṣum). The sentence is an explanation (bayān) of that. The initial vagueness followed by the clarification gives further affirmation of it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a substitute (badal, apposition) for ﴿ḥaqq﴾ (truth), and the substituted element (al-mubdal minhu) does not in reality drop out of effect. It was also said: it is a substitute for the position (maḥall) of the noun of inna (indeed). By "dispute" (takhāṣum) is meant mutual speech (taqāwul). It is also permitted to take it in its literal sense, since the saying of the leaders, ﴿Welcome to them﴾ no, ﴿and the saying of the followers, "Nay, you — no welcome to you"﴾ are of the kind of dispute. So the whole exchange is called a dispute because it includes this. It was said: this is evident where the speech is between the leaders and the followers. But if the whole is taken as the speech of the guards (khazana), then it is not so. And if ﴿no welcome﴾ is taken as the speech of the leaders, while ﴿this is a company﴾ is the speech of the guards, then it is correct to make it a dispute in a figurative sense (majāz).

Ibn Abi 'Abla read ﴿takhāṣuma﴾ with a fatḥa (in the accusative), so it is a substitute for ﴿that﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a qualifier (ṣifa) of it. This was criticised on the ground that describing a demonstrative noun (ism al-ishāra) with a non-derived word is permissible only if the qualifier is defined with the article ʾal- (alif-lām), as he mentioned in al-Mufaṣṣal (a grammar book by al-Zamakhshari) without reporting any disagreement on this. Thus there is a contradiction between his position and what the view that it is a qualifier requires, together with the separation (faṣl) that this entails, which is either impermissible or ugly. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) replied: analogy requires the permissibility, because the demonstrative noun needs something to remove its vagueness, which denotes a specific entity, whether or not it is specific to one reality or to several realities. This degree does not take the noun out of denoting the reality of the specific entity, by which it may validly be a qualifier of the demonstrative noun. As for usage, it is opposed by the basic usage in qualification: just as the majority interpreted ﴿this man﴾ as a qualifier despite the possibility of apposition or explanation (bayān), so al-Zamakhshari interpreted it as a qualifier despite the possibility of apposition, because he took the sense into account. It does not contradict what is in al-Mufaṣṣal, because he mentioned that only in the context of the vocative (nidāʾ), on the assumption that the demonstrative noun is not independent. And because the case of independence is less common, he did not address it. It has been explained in its place that in the vocative alone it is impermissible to qualify a demonstrative noun when it is not independent, joined to a noun preceded by ʾal-. Moreover, the two books, al-Kashshaf and al-Mufaṣṣal, often differ from each other, and the objection that it entails separation is not a decisive one, for it is permissible, especially on the assumption that the demonstrative noun is independent. End of quotation. It is not free from some issues.

Ibn al-Sumayqa read ﴿takhāṣama﴾ as a past-tense verb, with ﴿ahlu﴾ in the nominative (marfūʿ), as its subject (fāʿil).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 65:

﴿Say﴾, O Muhammad, to the polytheists of Makkah: ﴿"I am only a warner"﴾. I warn you of the punishment of God the Exalted for the polytheists. The statement is a rebuttal of their saying: "This is a sorcerer, a liar," for warning is incompatible with sorcery and lying.

It may also be said that the meaning is: "I am only a messenger who warns, not a sorcerer or a liar." This has its own beauty, for each of the two attributes of messengerhood and warning is incompatible with each of the two attributes of sorcery and lying. However, the incompatibility of messengerhood with sorcery is more evident, and between them there is antithesis (tibaq). Likewise, warning is incompatible with lying. To this is added God's saying: ﴿"There is no god except God"﴾, to convey that he, peace and blessings be upon him, also has the attribute of calling to the Oneness of God, may He be glorified and exalted. Thus both matters independently convey meaning.

The "min" in ﴿"min ilah"﴾ is superfluous (za'idah) for emphasis, meaning: there is no god at all except God, ﴿"the One"﴾, meaning the One who does not admit plurality in His essence in terms of individuals, such that He would have a universal quiddity (mahiyyah kulliyyah), nor in terms of parts, ﴿"the Subduer"﴾ over every thing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 66:

﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ of the existing things. From Him, glorified is He, they were created, and to Him belongs the management of all their affairs. ﴿The All-Mighty (al-Aziz)﴾ who overcomes and is not overcome in any of His affairs, exalted is His majesty, and retribution is included in this. ﴿The Oft-Forgiving (al-Ghaffar)﴾, the one who is intensive in forgiveness, forgiving whom He wills of whom He wills. It is an affirmation of tawhid (oneness of God). As for the first attribute, it is evident in this and does not need explanation. As for ﴿the Subduer (al-Qahhar)﴾

page 220

over everything: because if there were a god other than Him, glorified is He, He would not be the subduer of it, since it would not then be subject to Him; rather it might necessarily be subdued, and that is incompatible with divinity. Exalted is Allah far above that, a great exaltation. As for ﴿Lord of the heavens﴾ etc., it is because if another were possible alongside Him, exalted is His majesty, the proof of mutual restraint referred to by His words, glorified is He: ﴿If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾, so the heavens and the earth and what is between them would not have come into being. It was also said: because the meaning of ﴿Lord of the heavens﴾ etc. is Lord of every existing thing, so everything other than Him is included in it, and so it cannot be a god. As for al-Aziz, it requires that He overcome others and not be overcome, and with partnership that cannot be complete.

As for al-Ghaffar, it requires that He forgive whom He wills whatever He wills, so perhaps He wills forgiveness for one person while the other wills punishment for him. If the will of the one is fulfilled, then the other is not a god; and if the will of the other is fulfilled and his will is not fulfilled, he is not a god either. Exalted is Allah far above that, a great exaltation. Whatever is said regarding the proof of mutual restraint, in questions and answers, applies here too. In these attributes there is clear indication of promise and threat. Because the description of warning was explicitly mentioned earlier, the attribute al-Qahhar was placed before al-Ghaffar here. It is also permissible that the intended purpose is to confirm the warning, and the second (attribute) is brought as a completion of it and as a clarification of what is general in it. That is, say to them: "I am only a warner to you by what I know, and I have warned you of the punishment of one with these attributes, for one such as Him is worthy of being feared for His punishment, just as He is worthy of being hoped for His reward." The first aspect is more suitable to the context, because the concluding with those attributes, in indicating that calling to tawhid is an end in itself, is in a place that cannot be denied; and because this, in relation to what has passed from the beginning of the surah until here, is like the one who argues saying after completing his demonstration: "So the conclusion is..." so it should be in the same pattern as what was expounded. In it is His words, exalted is He: ﴿Has he made the gods into one god?﴾ So understand.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verses 67–68:**

﴿Say﴾: The repetition of the command (qul) signals that what is to be said is a weighty matter of great importance, which must be taken seriously, both in obeying it and in acting upon it. ﴿It﴾, that is, what I have informed you of, namely that I am a warner-messenger and that God Most High is One with no partner, ﴿is a momentous news﴾: a report of very great benefit, about which there is no doubt at all. ﴿From which you turn away﴾: you persist in turning away from it because of the persistence of your heedlessness. This clause is a second qualifier (sifah, descriptive attribute) of "news." The whole statement is a rebuke to them, an alert to where the error lies, and a display of the utmost compassion and tenderness that the situation of the call (da'wah) requires.

Some eminent scholars have inclined to the view that ﴿it﴾ refers to the Qur'an, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatadah. They cited the end of the surah and said that this reference includes what has been mentioned in the first instance. He preferred that this sentence be an independent resumptive statement (isti'naf, a new sentence beginning without grammatical dependence on what precedes), censuring them for their poor condition in relation to it, and for their failure to appreciate its exalted worth despite its great magnificence, which should have moved them to turn toward it and receive it with good acceptance. It seems that the discourse here looks back to what is said at the beginning of the surah: ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾, ﴿But those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾. It was brought in this way so that it may be inferred that it descends from God Most High, by means of what points to it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verses 67–68:**

﴿Say﴾: The repetition of the command (qul) signals that what is to be said is a weighty matter of great importance, which must be taken seriously, both in obeying it and in acting upon it. ﴿It﴾, that is, what I have informed you of, namely that I am a warner-messenger and that God Most High is One with no partner, ﴿is a momentous news﴾: a report of very great benefit, about which there is no doubt at all. ﴿From which you turn away﴾: you persist in turning away from it because of the persistence of your heedlessness. The whole statement is a rebuke to them, an alert to where the error lies, and a display of the utmost compassion and tenderness that the situation of the call (da'wah) requires.

They cited the end of the surah and said that this reference includes what has been mentioned in the first instance. He preferred that this sentence be an independent resumptive statement (isti'naf, a new sentence beginning without grammatical dependence on what precedes), censuring them for their poor condition in relation to it, and for their failure to appreciate its exalted worth despite its great magnificence, which should have moved them to turn toward it and receive it with good acceptance. It seems that the discourse here looks back to what is said at the beginning of the surah: ﴿By the Qur'an, full of reminder﴾, ﴿But those who disbelieve are in arrogance and opposition﴾. It was brought in this way so that it may be inferred that it descends from God Most High, by means of what points to it.

The commentary of the verse, "He said, 'I had no knowledge of the exalted assembly when they were disputing'" (﴿ما كانَ لِيَ مِن عِلْمٍ بِالمَلإ الأعْلى إذْ يَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾) etc., in which it includes the mention of one of the reports of the earlier communities in detail without any prior knowledge of it, nor any direct engagement with its usual causes such as studying the divine books or hearing from the People of the Book. This is a clear proof that it comes by way of revelation from God Most High, and that all of His other reports are likewise. According to what we have said, it is a reminder to establish prophethood through a brief mention of it, as a preface to guiding the path, a reminder for the rest, and a ladder to listening to what is mentioned, which is a kindness to those being addressed and an honouring of the caller. Not touching on the like of this in the matter of tawhid is because its proofs are manifest, although mentioning some of them is fresh and new, and this is what the attributes mentioned just above point to. So it should not be said that focusing on establishing prophethood without tawhid is evidence that the intended purpose of the information is prophethood, and that the second was brought as a completion of that.

You know that prophethood and the Qur'an being a revelation from God Most High are mutually implicated: whenever one of them is established, the other is established. However, it has been preferred to take the verse as being about prophethood, and to establish it, since it is closer, and to introduce this verse with the like of what introduced the verse before it that contains the claim of prophethood, namely His words (say) (﴿قُلْ﴾). So if this preference is accepted for you, then so be it; otherwise do not deviate from what has been related from Ibn ʿAbbas and those with him, and from al-Hasan, that it refers to the Day of Resurrection, as in His words: ﴿About what are they asking one another? About the great news﴾ (78:1–2). It has also been said that it refers to the reports of the prophets, peace be upon them, that preceded, and it has been said that it refers to the disputing of the people of the Fire. Knowledge is construed with the preposition bi (ba') in view of the meaning of encompassment. Al-mala' (the elite; literally, "the assembly that fills the eyes with splendour and the souls with majesty and radiance") is a collective noun (ism jam', a noun denoting a group), and for this reason it is described by the singular, namely al-a'la (the exalted). The intended meaning is the assembly of the angels, Adam, and Iblis, upon him be the curse, and they were in the heavens, so the height is literal. The discussion among them was as you will know, God willing. The phrase (when) (إذْ) is connected to an omitted element required by the context, since the intended meaning is the negation of his, upon him be prayer and peace, knowledge of their states, not of their essences. The estimated meaning is: "I had no knowledge in any way of the state of the assembly in the past, except at the time of their disputing." This is better than estimating the sentence as the majority have held, i.e., "I had no knowledge of the speech of the assembly except at the time of their disputing," because his knowledge (ﷺ) is not restricted to what passed between them of statements only, but is general to them and also to the actions, such as the prostration of the angels, peace be upon them, and Iblis's refusal and arrogance, as the revelation expresses. So it is better to consider the generality in its negation too. It has also been said that (when) is a badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion) from (the assembly), or an adverbial complement (ẓarf) of knowledge, but there is a discussion about this. The disputing concerns what He indicates by His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿when your Lord said﴾ etc. The expression with the present tense yakhtasimun (they dispute) is used because it is a strange matter, so it is brought to make it present in the mind as a narration of the situation. The plural pronoun refers to the assembly. Abu Hayyan related that it refers to the Quraysh and found this unlikely. It seems that in ﴿they dispute﴾ there is then a shift (iltifat, a change of grammatical person) from the address in ﴿you turn away from it﴾ to the third person. The disputing concerns the matter of his prophethood, upon him be prayer and peace, or the matter of the Qur'an, or the matter of the Return. This involves a departure from what has been transmitted, and a resort to what can hardly be understood from the verse without any need for it. Even with this, a sound taste does not accept it.
