Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 70:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: It is revealed to me only that I am a plain warner﴾ is a parenthetical statement placed between the general summary of their disputing and its detail, to confirm the establishment of his knowledge (peace and blessings be upon him) and to specify its cause. However, the explanation of its negation in what preceded, since it was indicative of its establishment now, and it is evident that his (ﷺ) not being associated with any of its familiar beginnings determines that it is none other than by way of revelation (wahy), necessarily. Thus that was made a matter of established certainty, needing no direct informing about it, and the purpose of the benefit was made his being informed of what calls to revelation and validates it. So the substitute for the subject (in "yuha", "it is revealed") is either a pronoun referring to the state implied earlier, as was indicated before, or something that includes it and other things. The meaning is: "What is revealed to me is the state of the Highest Assembly," or "What is revealed to me is what is revealed of the unseen matters, of which their state is one, for a matter of the matters, except that I am a plain warner from Him, exalted is He." For his (peace and blessings be upon him) being so is among the incentives for revelation to him and its validators. It is also permitted that the pronoun substituting for the subject refers to the verbal noun understood from ﴿yuha﴾, i.e., "what is done as revelation to me is concerning the state of the Highest Assembly, or concerning something of the unseen matters of which their state is one, for a matter of the matters, except that I..." etc.

It is also permitted that the prepositional phrase be the substitute for the subject, with "innama" taken as "anna" with the lam omitted. Al-Kashshaf says: The meaning of the restriction is that he (ﷺ) was not revealed to for any matter except that he is a plain warner, and what a plain warner! Like your saying: "You were not appointed as a judge, O so-and-so, except because you are a learned, practicing, guiding person." Al-Zamakhshari permitted that, after deleting the lam, the substitute for the subject be the phrase itself, and the meaning of the restriction is: "I was commanded with this matter alone, and nothing other than that, because it is the matter that includes all commands, either implicitly or by necessary implication; or: I was commanded only to warn you, not to guide you or to restrain you from obstinacy, for that is not up to me." What was mentioned first is more suited to the situation of the parenthetical statement, as is not hidden from one who is not a stranger to the perception of subtleties.

Abu Ja'far read "innama" with a kasra, on the basis of direct quotation, i.e., "What is revealed to me is only this statement," and its being revealed to him is his being commanded (peace and blessings be upon him) to say it. The essential meaning of the restriction is close to what was mentioned just above. It is also permitted that the meaning be: "I was commanded only to say this statement to you, rather than to say, for example, 'I know the unseen without revelation.' So reflect, and do not be heedless."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 71:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When your Lord said to the angels﴾ etc. This begins the detailed account of what was left general in the "dispute" (ikhtisam), which is the mutual speaking that took place among them. It is a substitution (badal) for ﴿when they dispute﴾, a substitution of the whole for the whole (badal kull min kull). It has also been permitted that it is a substitution of a part (badal ba'd). The attribution of the dispute to the angels is valid, even though the speaking took place between them and God exalted, as His saying ﴿when your Lord said﴾ etc. indicates, because His speaking to them is each through an intermediary angel (malak). So the meaning of the exchange of speech among the Exalted Assembly (al-mala' al-a'la) is the exchange of one angel with the rest of the angels, peace be upon them, concerning the matter of the vicegerency (istikhlaf), and with Iblis concerning the matter of prostration, and with Adam in His saying ﴿inform them of their names﴾. The meaning of the exchange being between the angels, Adam and Iblis is that its existence is among them in general. There is no requirement of combining the literal and the metaphorical in the attribution, so everything is literal, because the Exalted Assembly includes the intermediary angel, who is the actual speaker, while He, Mighty and Majestic, is the speaker in a metaphorical sense. Do not say "the disputant" (al-mukhasim), so that the matter is reversed. As for what is said, that His saying ﴿when your Lord said﴾ requires that His speaking to them be without an intermediary, this is rejected, because it is the substitution of the time of a narrative for the time of the discussion within it. The purpose is that the narrative be known, not that every part correspond to every part, and that is neither required nor intended. Furthermore, there is in it a sublime benefit: that the angel's speaking to them, or to the two of them, is on behalf of God exalted, so they are also speaking to Him, exalted. This meaning is intended from this, but not from the wording itself, so that the aforementioned combination is avoided. And God, Mighty and Majestic, is counted among the Exalted Assembly by taking it to refer to what is other than humankind, so that the dispute is established with Him and with them, in the sense that He, glorified, dispute with them in their presence and they dispute with Him, along with what it contains of implying a direction for Him, Mighty and Majestic, which the context clearly rejects. He, glorified, did not mention the angels' reply, peace be upon them, so that the exchange would be completed concisely by what has been repeated many times. For this reason He, majestic is His affair, did not say: "Indeed I am creating a creature of such and such a description, making it a vicegerent."

This arrangement has been observed here for a secret reason: that the aim of the narrative should end with the account of Iblis, to suit what the people of Makkah were engaged in. By his refusal to comply with one command, what happened to him happened, so how will their state be, when they are immersed in disobedience? In it also is that he was the first to establish disobedience, so he is their leader and guide to the Fire. He mentioned the account of the prostration of the angels and omitted their exchange concerning the vicegerency, in order to distinguish between the two exchanges, and that a question before the command is not like a question after it, for the latter entails delay. Then there is in it, implicitly, the account of the honouring of Adam, peace be upon him, a sign that the teacher and the advisor is to be honoured, and that this is an ancient law from Him, exalted. It was incumbent upon the people of Makkah to treat the Prophet ﷺ in the manner of the angels' treatment of Adam, not in the manner of Iblis' treatment of him. This is said by the author of al-Kashshaf (Sahib al-Kashf), and it is good. However, what the abbreviation was attributed to, namely the repetition of that many times, is not complete unless that was in a Meccan surah revealed before this surah. Some have attributed the omission of the mention to being sufficient with what is in al-Baqarah. But in this there is: that its revelation came later than the revelation of this surah, because it is Madani, and this is Makki, so it is not valid to rely on it by reference before its revelation. As for the meaning being that the hearers of the Qur'an are sufficed after that, its state is not hidden. Perhaps the narrative was known by hearing it from the Prophet ﷺ, and he was knowledgeable of it through revelation,

223

even if it was not at that time revealed as Qur'an, so it was abbreviated here, for what is mentioned in al-Kashf, being sufficed by that. He also said in it: That is, you say: the exchange between the angels and Adam, peace be upon them, when He said: ﴿Tell Me their names﴾, as a rebuke to them for what they attributed to him from their saying: ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption in it and sheds blood?﴾ And between him and Iblis, either because he was included in the denial and the rebuke, indeed he was the most severe of them in that. But God overcame the angels, because he was too base to be mentioned alongside them individually, or because he was commanded to prostrate to his teacher and refused, and He made him hear what he heard.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When your Lord said﴾ etc. is for the purpose of introducing an introductory part that includes the narrative of the exchange and depicts its origin. So it does not follow from it that the Lord, exalted is His affair, is one of the speakers, even though there is between Him, glorified, and them an exchange which God exalted has related. This is less strained than what contains the claim that His speaking, exalted, to them was through an angel, for the one who prevents may prevent intermediation according to our principle, and according to the principle of the Mu'tazilah as well, especially if the rebukers are taken to be all the angels. On both views the benefit of substituting ﴿when your Lord said﴾ for ﴿when they dispute﴾ is clear. The objection that if it were a substitution it would have been "when my Lord said," to match His saying ﴿I had no knowledge﴾, is answered: the context does not require the shift, and the shift is not harmful, for it is in the style of His saying exalted: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say: "They were created by the Mighty, the All-Knowing"﴾ "Who made the earth for you." So the address "for you" is according to the view that it is the speech of God exalted completing their speech. Its tail-end here is likewise from the speech of God exalted, to complete the speech of the Prophet ﷺ. This is like what your interlocutor says: "The Amir came to me," and you say: "The one who honoured and favoured you," or he says: "I saw the Amir on Friday," and you say: "On the day he bestowed upon you such-and-such robe of honour." From this it is known that it is not a case of shift at all, and that this substitution in this style is for greater beauty. End.

It has also been permitted to say that ﴿when﴾ ('idh) in ﴿when your Lord said﴾ is an adverbial complement of ﴿they dispute﴾, and the Exalted Assembly means the angels, and their dispute means their saying to God exalted: ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption in it and sheds blood?﴾, in response to His saying exalted: ﴿Indeed I am placing in the earth﴾, and so on. The validity of intending this does not depend on God exalted being counted among the Exalted Assembly, nor on His having spoken to them through an angel, nor has the detailed account of the dispute been mentioned at all. Rather it suffices to mention it after the revelation, whether it is mentioned as Qur'an or not. The interpretation of the Exalted Assembly as the angels is preferred over its interpretation as including Adam, peace be upon him, because that, as you have heard, requires the claim that Adam was in heaven, and this is evident that he, peace be upon him, was created in heaven, or was raised up to it after his creation on earth. Both of these matters are not accepted by many people. Ibn al-Qayyim in his book Miftah Dar al-Sa'adah transmitted from a group that Adam, peace be upon him, was only created on earth, and that the Garden in which he was settled after what happened had happened was also on earth. He brought many strong proofs for this and did not answer any of them, so reflect. Some have gone to the view that the Exalted Assembly is the angels, and that their dispute was about degrees and expiations.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated it and authenticated it, and al-Tabarani and others, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ was delayed from us one morning at the dawn prayer until we nearly saw the sun's eye. Then he came out quickly, and the call to prayer was given, and the Messenger of God ﷺ prayed. When he had finished the salam he called out in a loud voice and said: 'Remain in your rows.' Then he turned to us and said: 'Behold, I will tell you what held me back from you this morning. I stood up during the night, and stood and prayed what was decreed for me, and I dozed in my prayer until I became heavy with sleep. Then behold, I saw my Lord, blessed and exalted, in the most beautiful form. He said: "O Muhammad." I said: "At Your service, my Lord." He said: "About what does the Exalted Assembly dispute?" I said: "I do not know." So He placed His palm between my shoulder blades, and I found the coolness of His fingertips between my breasts, and everything was made manifest to me, and I knew. He said: "O Muhammad." I said: "At Your service." He said: "About what does the Exalted Assembly dispute?" I said: "About the degrees and the expiations." He said: "What are the degrees?" I said: "Feeding the food, spreading the greeting of peace, and praying at night while the people are asleep." He said: "You have spoken truly. What are the expiations?" I said: "Completing the ablution in difficult conditions, waiting for the prayer after the prayer, and walking on foot to the congregations." He said: "You have spoken truly. Ask, O Muhammad." I said: "O God, I ask You for doing good deeds, and abandoning wrong deeds, and love of the poor, and that You forgive me and have mercy on me, and when You intend a trial for Your servants, take me to You without being tried. O God, I ask You for Your love, and the love of one who loves You, and the love of a deed that brings me closer to Your love." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Learn them, and study them, for they are true.'"

The meaning of their dispute in this, according to what is in al-Bahr, is their difference over the amount of its reward. It is not hidden that carrying the dispute in the verse to what has been mentioned is far removed from the context, for it is among what the People of the Book did not know, so the polytheists would not accept it from him, upon him be blessings and peace, at all. Yes, it is another dispute with no connection to the present context. Those who take ﴿when﴾ in ﴿when He said﴾ as governed by an implied ﴿remember﴾ (udhkur), and likewise everyone who says that the dispute is not concerning the matter of Adam, peace be upon him, make it so.

Al-Shihab al-Khafaji said: "The more evident view, that is, absolutely, is that ('idh) is attached to the implied udhkur, as is customary in such cases, so that ﴿when they dispute﴾ remains in its generality, and so that there is no separation between the substitute and what it substitutes, and so that it includes what is in the authentic hadith about their dispute concerning the expiations and the degrees, and so that there is no need to explain the change from ('my Lord') to ﴿your Lord﴾." End. In it there is something that is not hidden.

Among the strange things said about their dispute is what al-Kirmani related in his 'Aja'ib: that it is an expression for their debating among themselves about deriving knowledge, like the debate of the people of knowledge on earth. This is refuted by one who claims that all their knowledge is actual. What is known from the early generations (al-salaf) is that it was the speaking about the matter of Adam, peace be upon him, and the refutation by it is also achieved. The intended meaning of "the angels" in ﴿When your Lord said to the angels﴾ is what includes Iblis, because at that time he was immersed among them. Perhaps the expression with them rather than a pronoun referring back to the Exalted Assembly, on the view of identity, is due to the commonness of associating the speech with them among the People of the Book under this title, or due to the fame of the contrast between angel and human, so that His saying, glorified, is very subtle: ﴿When your Lord said to the angels: "Indeed I am creating a human from clay."﴾ It was said: He expressed it thus to show total absorption in the one addressed, and the intended meaning is: "Indeed I am creating, in what is to come." In the expression with what has been mentioned there is something that the expression with the present-tense form does not have, in indicating that He, exalted, is the doer absolutely, without any diverting factor. "Human" (bashar) means a dense body that touches and makes contact, or one whose skin is manifest, not covered with hair, wool, or fleece. The intended one is Adam, peace be upon him. Here it is mentioned: his creation from clay (tin); in Al 'Imran: his creation from dust (turab); in al-Hijr: from clay of sounding dry earth (salsal), from black mud moulded (hama' masnun); in al-Anbiya': from haste ('ajal). There is no contradiction. The only point is that it was mentioned regarding some of the nearer stages of the material and some of the more remote stages. Furthermore, what was applied at the time the narrated event occurred is not the name "human," since the thing named by it had not yet been created at that time, let alone being named by it. Rather it is an expression revealing his state, and he was only referred to by this name at the time of the narration.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 72:

﴿Then when I have fashioned him﴾ — i.e., I have formed him in the human form and the human creation, or I have fashioned the parts of his body by balancing his natural constitution. ﴿And breathed into him of My spirit﴾ — this is a metaphor for the bestowing, in actuality, of that by which life exists upon the matter receptive to it, so there is no actual blowing nor anything blown. That is: when I have completed his readiness (isti'dad) and bestowed upon him that by which he lives, namely the pure spirit which is of My command. ﴿Then fall down to him﴾ — an imperative from waqa'a (to fall), and in it is evidence that what is commanded is not mere bowing, as has been said; that is: fall prostrate to him. ﴿in prostration﴾ — as a greeting to him and an honouring of him.

﴿فَسَجَدَ المَلائِكَةُ﴾ means: so He created him, fashioned him, and breathed into him the spirit, and so the angels prostrated to him. ﴿كُلُّهُمْ﴾ means in such a way that none of them remained who did not prostrate. ﴿أجْمَعُونَ﴾ means by way of accompaniment (ma'iyyah), such that none of them lagged behind any other. So "kull" (all) indicates comprehensiveness, while "ajma'" indicates togetherness. There is no restriction in its meaning to the circumstantial sense (hal), contrary to some scholars. Its verification, according to al-Kashshaf (Zamakhshari's commentary), is that the clear derivation indicates that it carries the meaning of gathering and joining. The basic principle in discursive usage (al-itlaq al-khitabi) is to interpret a thing in its most complete state, and there is no doubt that gathering at one time is the most complete of its kinds. However, since its use as an emphasis became widespread, it was made to stand in place of "kull" in conveying comprehensiveness, without regard to completeness. Thus, when comprehensiveness is understood through another expression, it is necessary to observe the basic meaning, to preserve speech from being rendered meaningless. Even if this is granted, the emphasis on totality is achieved by removing it from its apparent meaning toward the texts, and "ajma'un" is an emphasis of that emphasis, so it conveys the most complete kind of comprehensiveness, which is comprehensiveness at one time. Deriving this benefit from making it like placing the apparent noun in place of the pronoun does not appear to be sound. The objection based on His saying, glorified is He: ﴿لأُغْوِيَنَّهم أجْمَعِينَ﴾ ("I will surely mislead them all") stems from a failure to grasp how the indication works. The apparent meaning of this verse and of the verse in al-Hijr is that their prostration was consequent upon the conditional command that is related, and many noble verses, like those in al-Baqarah and al-A'raf and others, apparently indicate that it was consequent upon the immediate (tanjizi) command. The verification of this has already passed, so let it be referred to.

(Page 225)

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 74:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except Iblis﴾, this is an exception of the connected type (istithna' muttasil), because he, although he was a jinn, was counted among the host of the angels, described with their attributes, neither standing nor sitting except with them. So the angels encompassed him by way of taghlib (the dominance of the greater group in inclusion, a rhetorical device), and then one of them was singled out for exception. Or [it is connected] because among the angels there is a kind of beings who reproduce, and he was among them. Or it is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'). His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿was arrogant﴾, according to the first view, is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining how the prostration was abandoned, which is understood from the exception. For his abandoning it could be from deliberation and careful consideration, and by this it becomes established that it was out of refusal and arrogance. According to the second view, it may be connected to what precedes it, meaning: but Iblis was arrogant and magnified himself. ﴿And he was among the disbelievers﴾, meaning: and he became one of them by his arrogance and his magnifying himself against the command of God Exalted. The omission of the fa' (then/so), which indicates causation, is a leaving it to the perceptiveness of the listener, or because the intended meaning is manifest.

That magnifying oneself against His command, Mighty and Majestic is He, especially verbal command, causing disbelief, is something about which there should be no doubt. Moreover, this arrogance involved deeming the command repugnant and considering it oppression. It is also possible that the meaning is: and he was among the disbelievers in the knowledge of God Exalted, because of His knowledge, Mighty and Majestic is He, that he would disobey Him, and that there would proceed from him what would proceed by his own choice, the corruption of his inner disposition, and his readiness for it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 75:**

Allah, exalted and majestic is He, says, in rebuke and reproach: ﴿O Iblis, what prevented you from prostrating﴾ (i.e., from prostrating), ﴿to what I created﴾ (i.e., to the one I created). Here "mā" is taken as a relative pronoun, with an omitted returning pronoun. This has been used as evidence for the permissibility of applying "mā" to individuals who have reason. Those who did not permit this said that "mā" is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), and that the verbal noun is meant in the sense of the object: "to prostrate to a created being." ﴿With My two hands﴾. According to some of the people of ta'wil (figurative interpretation), this is one of the metaphors of the khalaf (later scholars). It is a representation of Him, peace be upon him, being особенно cared for in His creation, since it is the nature of one who is cared for that he is worked on with both hands. Among its effects is his creation without the intermediary of a father or mother; his being a small body in which the greater world is contained; his being fit to receive what is not bestowed upon others; and other of the distinctions of humanity.

According to another group among them, "the hand" means "power," and the dual form is for emphasis, indicating the greatness of His power, exalted is He. This is because the dual is used for mere repetition, as in His saying: ﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾. So what is meant is its necessary implication, which is emphasis. This is because Allah, in His creation, performed various acts: from making him clay that had been left to ferment, to making him a body of flesh and bone, to breathing the spirit into him, to giving him the capacity for knowledge and action, and similar things, all of which indicate the greatness of the power of the Creator of powers and capacities. It has also been allowed that this is due to the variation in Adam's actions, for he sometimes performs angelic acts, as if they were from the effects of the right hand, and sometimes performs animal acts, as if they were from the effects of the left hand. Yet both of His hands, glorified is He, are right hands.

According to some: "the hand" means "blessing," and the dual is either for the reason already mentioned, or to mean the blessing of this world and the blessing of the Hereafter.

The Salaf (early generations) say: the hand, singular and dual, is affirmed for Allah, exalted and majestic is He, in the meaning befitting Him, glorified is He, and they do not say in such a context that it means "power" or "blessing." The apparent meaning of the reports is that the created being has a distinction over others through it. It is established in the authentic collection (al-Sahih) that He, glorified is He, said in answer to the angels: "Give them the world, and to us the Hereafter; by My might and My majesty, I will not make him whom I created with My two hands like him to whom I said 'Be,' and he was."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh in al-ʿAẓamah, and al-Bayhaqi, related from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: Allah created four things with His hand: the Throne, the Gardens of Eden, the Pen, and Adam. Then He said to everything: "Be," and it was.

It has come in more than one report that He, exalted is He, wrote the Torah with His hand. In the hadith of the debate between Adam and Musa, peace be upon them both, there is what indicates that being created by it is a description of honor, where Musa said to him: "You are Adam, whom Allah created with His hand." Likewise in the hadith of intercession, that the people of the Standing (on the Day of Judgment) come to Adam and say to him: "You are Adam, father of mankind, whom Allah created with His hand." From this it is known that the order of the rebuke in "What prevented you from prostrating" is based on Allah's creating him with His two hands, for the emphasis of the reproach and the intensification of the censure, as if it were said: "What prevented you from honoring with prostration the one who deserves honor, because of the divine care that surrounded his existence?"

Al-Zamakhshari claimed that "I created with My two hands" is of the type "I saw him with my eye," so "with My hands" is for emphasizing that he is a created being, about which there is no doubt. Since Iblis abandoned prostration to Adam, peace be upon him, out of the suspicion that it was prostration to a created being, and this was combined with the fact that Adam was created from clay while he himself was created from fire, and he forgot that Allah, glorified is He, when He commanded one who is greater than him and closer to Him among His servants, namely the angels, they obeyed and did not look at the disparity between the one prostrating and the one prostrated to, out of glorification of His command and reverence for His address. He (Allah) mentioned to him what he clung to of the doubt, and presented the speech in the form of "agreeing with the implication" (qawl bi-l-mujib), while alerting him to the slip of the foot. So it is as if it were said to him: "What prevented you from prostrating to something which, as you say, is a created being that I created with My two hands, with no doubt that it is created, in obedience to My command and exalting My address, as the angels did?"

It is not hidden that the context is far removed from what he mentioned, and making that of the type "I saw with my eye" only results in emphasizing createdness. Presenting the speech in the form of "agreeing with the implication" is something that is hardly accepted, for the way of "agreeing with the implication" is that one concedes to the other party, then objects to him, not that the objection is introduced at the outset and presented as a riddle, rather as an enigma. Furthermore, the authentic reports are clear that this is a description of honor, not as he claimed. Also, making the prostration of the angels to Adam a matter of mere obedience, without regard to Adam's honor, peace be upon him, is refuted by what has been conceded in many places, that it was a prostration of honor. How could it be otherwise, when it is opposed by ﴿Will You place in it﴾? Likewise His teaching him the names; so let the side of the Commander, exalted is His state, and the side of the one prostrated to, upon whom be blessings and peace, be taken into account, to fulfill both rights. It is as if He said what He said, and presented the verse in a way that did not occur to Iblis, to avoid breaking his school of thought. He is not obliged to concede that the verse indicates honor, and to restrict it to one aspect; and then it does not indicate superiority absolutely, so that breaking his school of thought would follow.

By my life, this man (al-Zamakhshari) wronged his father Adam, peace be upon him, in this discussion in his al-Kashshaf, where he cited, in it, an example for what he established in the verse: he made the fall of the nobles an example for Adam, peace be upon him. And he showed kindness to the enemy of Allah, Iblis, when he upheld his excuse and validated his belief that he is superior to Adam because he is from fire and Adam is from clay. His error is from another side, namely that he did not compare himself to the angels, since they prostrated to him while knowing that, in relation to them, he is of lowered rank and fallen station. How many a slip he has, for which the one who committed it is not said to have stumbled, along with the prophets, may the blessings and peace of Allah, exalted is He, be upon them, in this station. We ask Allah, exalted is He, to protect us from the precipices of desire and to keep our feet firm.

And it was read "bi-yadayya" with the ya' of the dual pronoun vowelled with a kasra, like "muṣrikhiyya," and "bi-yadi" in the singular. ﴿Have you become arrogant﴾ with the interrogative hamza of denial and dropping the hamzat al-wasl, meaning: "Did you act arrogantly without right?" ﴿Or were you among the high ones﴾, or: "Or were you deserving of exaltation, surpassing in it?" It was also said: the meaning is "Has arrogance arisen in you, or have you not ceased, since you existed, to be among the arrogant?" The opposition in the first reading is in terms of entitlement and its absence, while in the second it is in terms of occurrence and eternity. For this reason it was said "were you among the high ones" rather than "are you among the high ones." It was also said: the high ones are a category of angels called "al-muhaymun" (the bewildered), who are absorbed in contemplating the beauty and majesty of Allah, exalted is He, and none of them knows that Allah created anything other than himself. They were not commanded to prostrate to Adam, peace be upon him. Or they are the angels of the heaven, who were not commanded to prostrate, and what was commanded was the angels of the earth. So the meaning is: "Did you abandon prostration out of arrogance, or did you abandon it because you are one of those who were not commanded to it?" There is no hiding what is in this. In all of these, "am" (or) is connective. Ibn 'Atiyyah related from many grammarians that it is not connective in this way when the two verbs differ, as in: "Did you strike Zayd, or did you kill him?" Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying it is an incorrect view, and that Sibawayh expressly stated the opposite.

A group, including Ibn Kathir according to what has been said, read "istakbarta" with the alif of connection (i.e., "is-takbarta") — and this is the reading of the people of Makkah, though it is not among the well-known readings of Ibn Kathir. It is possible that the interrogative hamza was omitted, because "am" indicates it, as in the poet's saying: "With seven did we throw the pebbles, or with eight?"

It is also possible that the speech is a statement, with "am" being disconnective, and the meaning: "Rather, you are among the high ones," and what is meant is His belittling of him, glorified is He.

قال الألوسي في *روح المعاني*:

﴿قالَ أنا خَيْرٌ مِنهُ﴾ قِيلَ: هو جَوابٌ عَنِ الِاسْتِفْهامِ الأخِيرِ، يُؤَدِّي مُؤَدّى أنَّهُ كَذَلِكَ، أيْ هو مِنَ العالِينَ على الوَجْهِ الأوَّلِ، وأنَّهُ لَيْسَ مِنَ الاسْتِكْبارِ سابِقًا ولاحِقًا في شَيْءٍ على الوَجْهِ الثّانِي، ويَجْرِي مَجْرى التَّعْلِيلِ كَوْنُهُ فائِقًا، إلّا أنَّهُ لَمّا لَمْ يَكُنْ وافِيًا بِالمَقْصُودِ، لِأنَّهُ مُجَرَّدُ دَعْوى، أُوثِرَ بَيانُهُ بِما يُفِيدُ ذَلِكَ وزِيادَةً، وهو قَوْلُهُ: ﴿خَلَقْتَنِي مِن نارٍ وخَلَقْتَهُ مِن طِينٍ﴾. أمّا الأوَّلُ فَظاهِرٌ، وأمّا الثّانِي فَلِأنَّهُ ذَكَرَ النَّوْعَيْنِ تَنْبِيهًا على أنَّ المُماثَلَةَ كافِيَةٌ فَضْلًا عَنِ الأفْضَلِيَّةِ، ولِهَذا أبْهَمَ، وفَصَّلَ، وقابَلَ، وآثَرَ: (خَلَقْتَنِي وخَلَقْتَهُ) دُونَ: أنا مِن نارٍ، وهو مِن طِينٍ، لِيَدُلَّ على أنَّ المُماثَلَةَ في المَخْلُوقِيَّةِ مانِعَةٌ، فَكَيْفَ إذا انْضَمَّ إلَيْها خَيْرِيَّةُ المادَّةِ؟ وفِيهِ تَنْبِيهٌ على أنَّ الآمِرَ كانَ أوْلى أنْ يَسْتَنْكِفَ، فَإنَّهُ أعْنِي السُّجُودَ حَقُّ الآمِرِ، واسْتَلْطَفَهُ صاحِبُ *الكَشْفِ*، ثُمَّ قالَ: ومِنهُ يُعْلَمُ أنَّ جَوابَ إبْلِيسَ مِنَ الأُسْلُوبِ الأحْمَقِ. وجَعَلَ غَيْرُ واحِدٍ قَوْلَهُ: ﴿أنا خَيْرٌ مِنهُ﴾ جَوابًا أوَّلًا، وبِالذّاتِ، عَنِ الِاسْتِفْهامِ بِقَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿ما مَنَعَكَ أنْ تَسْجُدَ﴾، بِادِّعاءِ شَيْءٍ مُسْتَلْزِمٍ لِلْمانِعِ مِنَ السُّجُودِ على زَعْمِهِ، وقَوْلُهُ: ﴿خَلَقْتَنِي﴾ إلَخْ، تَعْلِيلًا لِدَعْوى الخَيْرِيَّةِ.

وأيًّا ما كانَ، فَقَدْ أخْطَأ اللَّعِينُ (Iblis)، إذْ لا مُماثَلَةَ في المَخْلُوقِيَّةِ، فَمَخْلُوقِيَّةُ آدَمَ (peace be upon him) بِاليَدَيْنِ، ولا كَذَلِكَ مَخْلُوقِيَّتُهُ، وأمْرُ خَيْرِيَّةِ المادَّةِ على العَكْسِ في النَّظَرِ الدَّقِيقِ. ومَعَ هَذا فَالفَضْلُ غَيْرُ مُنْحَصِرٍ بِما كانَ مِن جِهَتِها، بَلْ يَكُونُ مِن جِهَةِ الصُّورَةِ، والغايَةِ أيْضًا، وفَضْلُ آدَمَ (peace be upon him) في ذَلِكَ لا يَخْفى، وكَأنَّ خُطاهُ لِظُهُورِهِ لَمْ يَتَعَرَّضْ لِبَيانِهِ، بَلْ جَعَلَ جَوابَهُ طَرْدَهُ، وذَلِكَ قَوْلُهُ تَعالى:

﴿He said: "Then get out of it."﴾ The "fa" (فاء) indicates that the command follows from what appeared from the accursed one of opposition to the glorious command and of giving as its justification the most evident falsehoods. That is, "Then get out of Paradise." The implicit reference before its mention is due to its being well known that he was one of its inhabitants.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he was in 'Adn, not in Jannat al-Khuld (the Paradise of Eternity). Furthermore, for the command to be valid, it suffices that he was among those who had taken Paradise as a homeland and dwelling, and it does not depend on his being in it in actuality at the time of the address, as is common in discourse. A person who quarrels with his companion in the market, or with someone else in a house, says: "Get out of the house," even though at the time of the quarrel he is not actually in it. This applies if it is said that the dialogue did not take place in Paradise. It has also been said that "from it" means "from among the ranks of the honoured angels," and this is the intended meaning of the descent (al-Hubut), not a descent from the heaven as has been said. For his whispering to Adam, peace be upon him, took place after this expulsion, and it was, as is reported through the channel of the Hiss, a call from the gate of Paradise. Moreover, many scholars have entirely denied the descent from the heaven, on the basis that the Paradise in which Adam, peace be upon him, was made to dwell was on earth.

It has also been said: "Get out of the form in which you are, and strip yourself of it." The command here is one of creation (al-Takwin). The accursed one used to take pride in his form, so Allah the Exalted changed his form, so he became black after having been white, ugly after having been beautiful, and dark after having been luminous.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿for you are accursed (rajim)﴾ is the reason for the command to depart. That is, you are cast out from every good and honour. Thus "rajm" is a kinayah (metonymy, an indirect expression) for expulsion, because the one who is expelled is stoned with stones. Or it refers to a devil who is pelted with shooting stars, so they have said. It may also be said that the intended meaning of "rajim" is "humiliated," for stoning entails abasement. This is further from the suspicion of repetition with the sentence that follows it from the first aspect, and more in agreement with what is in al-A'raf, in His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿So get out, for you are among the debased﴾.

Page 228

And indeed upon you is My curse (﴿وإنَّ عَلَيْكَ لَعْنَتِي﴾), meaning My removal from mercy. In al-Hijr the word "al-la'na" (اللعنة) appears. If the definite article (ال) in it is for previous reference (al-'ahd), or is a substitute for the pronoun it is attached to, then the lack of difference between what is there and what is here is evident. If it is meant to denote every curse, then that is because the curses of those who curse him, from among the angels and the two categories of jinn and humankind (al-thaqalayn), are also from Him, may He be exalted. They invoke upon him the curse of Allah, the Exalted, and his removal from His mercy. ﴿Until the Day of Judgment﴾ (﴿إلى يَوْمِ الدِّينِ﴾), the Day of Recompense and punishment. In this there is an indication that the curse, despite its complete grievousness, is not sufficient as the recompense for his crime. Rather, it is a model (unmudhaj) of what he will encounter, continuing until that Day. But this does not mean that it will end on that day, as the apparent meaning of the time limit may suggest. The view that it ends has been attributed to some of the Sufis. Rather, it means that on that day he will encounter, among the varieties of torment and the diverse forms of punishment, what will make him forget the curse and render it as though it had passed. Do you not see the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then a crier will announce among them that the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾, and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And some of you will curse others﴾?

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 79:

﴿He said: "My Lord, then give me respite"﴾ i.e., grant me a delay and postpone me. The fa' (the "then") is connected to an elided element that the speech implies, as though he said: "Since You have made me accursed, then grant me a delay and do not cause me to die." ﴿Until the Day they are resurrected﴾ i.e., Adam and his descendants, for recompense after death, and this is the time of the second blowing (of the Trumpet). The accursed one intended by this to find an opening to lead them astray and to take his revenge upon them, and to escape death, because it will not exist after the Resurrection. The matter of the Resurrection was well known among the angels, so he heard it from them and said what he said. It is also possible that he knew it by reason, since he recognized it through some signs, or through another of the ways of knowledge, that the individuals of this kind (of creation) cannot avoid committing injustice among themselves, that the abode is not an abode of permanence, rather death must occur in it, and that wisdom requires recompense.

﴿He said, "Indeed, you are among those given respite."﴾ The answer comes in a nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya, a sentence beginning with a noun), and it explicitly includes what the devil asked for along with the others, in a way that indicates that the questioner is following them in this. This is a clear statement that it is an informing about the respite that was decreed for them from eternity, not a new granting of a special respite for him that was given in answer to his supplication. His request for respite was a request to delay death, since by it he would be among them, and not a request to delay punishment, as some have said. That is known from the idafa (genitive construction) of "the Day" to "the Religion" (in ﴿the Day of the Religion﴾). That is, "You are one of those whose terms were delayed from eternity, in accordance with what the wisdom of creation requires."

﴿Until the Day of the Appointed Time﴾, which I have determined and specified for the annihilation of creation, and it is the time of the first blast, not until the time of resurrection, which is what he asked about. The fa' (the "fa" particle) is therefore not for linking the granting of respite itself to the request for respite, but for linking the emphasized informing to it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before﴾ (Qur'an 12:77), and in the words of al-Shafi'i: "So if you show mercy, you are deserving of it."

﴿He said, "Indeed, you are among those given respite."﴾ The answer comes in a nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya, a sentence beginning with a noun), and it explicitly includes what the devil asked for along with the others, in a way that indicates that the questioner is following them in this. Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 82–83:

﴿He said: "By Your might"﴾ It is an oath by the authority (sultan) of Allah, exalted and majestic is He, and His dominion (qahr). Just as it can be by His essence, it can also be by His attribute. So the ba' (bi-) is for the oath, according to the view of most scholars, and the fa' (fa-) indicates that the content of the sentence follows from the granting of respite; that is, "So I swear by Your might,"

﴿"I will surely mislead them all"﴾ that is, the individuals of this species, by making sins appealing to them,

﴿"except Your servants among them who are sincere"﴾ and they are those whom Allah, exalted is He, has made sincere for His obedience and protected from misguidance.

And it has been read as "al-mukhlisin" (with kasra, in the form of the active participle), meaning those who have made their hearts or their deeds sincere for Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verse 82–83:

﴿He said: "By Your might"﴾ It is an oath by the authority (sultan) of Allah, exalted and majestic is He, and His dominion (qahr). Just as it can be by His essence, it can also be by His attribute. So the ba' (bi-) is for the oath, according to the view of most scholars, and the fa' (fa-) indicates that the content of the sentence follows from the granting of respite; that is, "So I swear by Your might,"

﴿"I will surely mislead them all"﴾ that is, the individuals of this species, by making sins appealing to them,

﴿"except Your servants among them who are sincere"﴾ and they are those whom Allah, exalted is He, has made sincere for His obedience and protected from misguidance.

[Page 229]

﴿He said﴾, i.e., God, Exalted and Majestic, said: ﴿So the truth, and the truth I say﴾. The first word is read in the nominative, فالحَقُّ, as a subject (mubtada', "inchoative") whose predicate is omitted, or as a predicate (khabar) whose subject is omitted. The second word, والحَقَّ, is in the accusative as an object (maf'ul) of the verb that follows it, and it has been placed before that verb for restriction (qasr), meaning: I say nothing but the truth. The fa' (فـ) indicates that what follows it is a consequence of what precedes it, i.e., "so the truth is my oath": ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾. Whether al-Haqq is one of God's names or the opposite of falsehood (batil), God has magnified it by swearing by it. This is preferred because the name is repeated as a definite noun, or the meaning is "so I am the Truth," or "so my word is the truth." God's statement ﴿I will surely fill﴾ and so on is then the answer to an omitted oath, meaning: "By God, I will surely fill," and God's statement ﴿and the truth I say﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ) confirming the content of the oath clause according to the first two readings, and according to the third reading it confirms the content of the preceding clause, namely "so my word is the truth."

The statement فالحَقُّ is a subject whose predicate is ﴿I will surely fill﴾. This is because the meaning is "that I fill," which is not a valid construction at all. The majority of readers read فالحَقَّ والحَقَّ with both in the accusative. This is explained as follows: the second is a fronted object as stated above, and the first is an oath-object from which the particle of oath has been omitted, so it takes the accusative, as in the line from the Kitab (Sibawayh's book):

Indeed, upon you is God's oath that you pledge allegiance,
that you be taken unwillingly or come willingly.

Also like your saying: "By God, I will surely do it," whose answer is ﴿I will surely fill﴾, with what lies between them being a parenthetical clause. It has also been said that it is in the accusative as an incitement (igra'), meaning: "So hold fast to the truth." ﴿And I will surely fill﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath. Al-Farra' said: it has the meaning of your saying: "Truly, I will certainly come to you" (haqqan la-ata'annaka). Whether the definite article (al-) is present or omitted is the same, meaning: "I will surely fill Hell in truth." So according to him it is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid) for the content of the sentence. It is not hidden that this verbal noun may not be placed first according to the majority of grammarians, and that it is specific to a sentence whose two parts are purely fixed definite nouns. Sahib al-Basit (the author of al-Basit) said: "It may also be that the predicate is indefinite and the subject is a pronoun, as in: 'He is Zayd, known,' and 'He is the truth, clear,' and 'I am the commander, boasting,' and it may be a noun, as in: 'Zayd is your father, kind,' and 'Your brother is Zayd, well-known.'" End of quote. It seems that al-Farra' does not stipulate what they stipulate in this matter.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-A'mash read both with the nominative. The first is explained as above, and the second is explained as a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the clause that follows it, with an omitted pronominal link (rabit), meaning: "I say it," like the reading of Ibn 'Amir: (And to each God has promised the best [reward]), and like the line of Abu al-Najm:

Umm al-Khiyar has come to claim against me a sin, all of which I did not commit.

Kull (all) is in the nominative so as to produce the total negation that the poet intends. Al-Hasan, 'Isa, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hammad, from Abu Bakr, read both in the genitive. The first is explained as being governed by the omitted oath particle wa- (و), meaning: "So by the truth," and the second is governed by coordination with it, just as you say: "By God and by God, I will surely stand," and ﴿I say﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the oath and its answer. Al-Zamakhshari made it a fronted object, "li-aqulu" (for "I say"), and the genitive is due to reproducing the form of the word sworn by. He said: its meaning is emphasis and intensification, and this function is an addition to what the parenthetical clause itself conveys, because the departure from the grammatical case that it requires to the reproduction of form, when it is for preserving the original form, shows that this form has a special place of care. This applies to every reproduction of speech without a verb of saying or what stands in its place, and so in our case it indicates extraordinary care for the matter of the oath and conveys intensification and emphasis.

It is also read with the first word in the genitive by implying the particle of oath, and the second in the accusative as an object.

﴿From you﴾, i.e., from your kind, from the devils; ﴿and whoever follows you﴾ in misguidance and error; ﴿of them﴾, of the descendants of Adam, peace be upon him; ﴿all together﴾, an emphasis for the pronoun in ﴿from you﴾, and the pronoun governed by the second min (من). The meaning is: "I will surely fill Hell with the followed and the followers, all together, leaving none of them behind." Or it is an emphasis for the followers only. The meaning then is: "I will surely fill it with the devils and with whoever among all people follows them, with no difference between one person and another, even after there are followers among them from the children of the prophets and others." The emphasis is placed on the followers and not the followed because the condition of the followers, when it reaches the point of connecting to the children of the prophets, then what of the followed?

[Page 230]

Sahib al-Kashf (the author of al-Kashf) said: The proponent of this view considered proximity, and that the speech is between the Exalted Truth and the accursed one concerning the followers, so he emphasized what was intended and left out the emphasis of the other for sufficiency. Know that this story has been mentioned in several surahs, and some of what is mentioned in one has been omitted in another for brevity, relying on what has been mentioned about it. There may be two words in one place that are identical in meaning but differ in wording, for the sake of variety of expression. The difference may also be attributed to multiple occasions of utterance. For example, it is said that the accursed one swore once by His might, and that was related in Surah Sad with His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿He said: then by Your might﴾, and another time by God's misguiding him, which is one of the effects of His power and might, Exalted and Majestic, and a ruling among the rulings of His dominion, and that was related in Surah al-A'raf with His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿He said: because You have led me astray﴾. The difference may also be attributed to differences in context, such as the omission of the fa' in His statement ﴿Give me respite until the day they are raised﴾ and in His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed you are among those given respite﴾ in al-A'raf, while it is mentioned in both places in Sad. What must be considered in transmitting speech is only its original meaning and the very signification it conveys. As for the manner in which it conveys that meaning, this is not something that must be observed at all in transmission. Rather, it may or may not be observed according to what the context requires, and its omission does not harm the original speech. Indeed, when it is transmitted, features and particulars may be observed that the speaker himself did not observe at all, since the context of reporting required them, and they are the crux of the matter. This does not detract from the transmitted speech being the original meaning, as the Shaykh al-Mufti Abu al-Su'ud has verified and discussed at length, so let it be consulted.

﴿From you﴾, i.e., from your kind, from the devils; ﴿and whoever follows you﴾ in misguidance and error; ﴿of them﴾, of the descendants of Adam, peace be upon him; ﴿all together﴾, an emphasis for the pronoun in ﴿from you﴾, and the pronoun governed by the second min (من). The meaning is: "I will surely fill Hell with the followed and the followers, all together, leaving none of them behind." Or it is an emphasis for the followers only. The meaning then is: "I will surely fill it with the devils and with whoever among all people follows them, with no difference between one person and another, even after there are followers among them from the children of the prophets and others." The emphasis is placed on the followers and not the followed because the condition of the followers, when it reaches the point of connecting to the children of the prophets, then what of the followed?

[Page 230]

Sahib al-Kashf (the author of al-Kashf) said: The proponent of this view considered proximity, and that the speech is between the Exalted Truth and the accursed one concerning the followers, so he emphasized what was intended and left out the emphasis of the other for sufficiency. Know that this story has been mentioned in several surahs, and some of what is mentioned in one has been omitted in another for brevity, relying on what has been mentioned about it. There may be two words in one place that are identical in meaning but differ in wording, for the sake of variety of expression. The difference may also be attributed to multiple occasions of utterance. For example, it is said that the accursed one swore once by His might, and that was related in Surah Sad with His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿He said: then by Your might﴾, and another time by God's misguiding him, which is one of the effects of His power and might, Exalted and Majestic, and a ruling among the rulings of His dominion, and that was related in Surah al-A'raf with His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿He said: because You have led me astray﴾. The difference may also be attributed to differences in context, such as the omission of the fa' in His statement ﴿Give me respite until the day they are raised﴾ and in His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed you are among those given respite﴾ in al-A'raf, while it is mentioned in both places in Sad. What must be considered in transmitting speech is only its original meaning and the very signification it conveys. As for the manner in which it conveys that meaning, this is not something that must be observed at all in transmission. Rather, it may or may not be observed according to what the context requires, and its omission does not harm the original speech. Indeed, when it is transmitted, features and particulars may be observed that the speaker himself did not observe at all, since the context of reporting required them, and they are the crux of the matter. This does not detract from the transmitted speech being the original meaning, as the Shaykh al-Mufti Abu al-Su'ud has verified and discussed at length, so let it be consulted.

﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it﴾, that is, for the Qur'an, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, or for conveying what is revealed to me, or, as some have said, for calling people to God Most High. ﴿Any reward﴾, that is, any worldly reward, whether great or small. ﴿Nor am I of those who pretend﴾, that is, of those who affect and adorn themselves with what does not belong to them. You have never known me to be affected or to claim what is not mine, so that I would assume prophethood and fabricate the Qur'an. He, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him, was commanded to say this statement about himself to them, not to inform them of its content, but to call upon what they already knew of him, and to remind them of what they knew. In this there is a censure of pretence (takalluf).

Ibn 'Adi narrated, from Abu Barzah, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Shall I not inform you of the people of Paradise?' We said: 'Yes, O Messenger of God.' He said: 'They are the merciful among themselves.' He said: 'Shall I not inform you of the people of the Fire?' We said: 'Yes.' He said: 'They are the despairing, the hopeless, the liars, and the pretenders (al-mutakallifun).'"

The sign of the pretender, as narrated by al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman from Ibn al-Mundhir, is threefold: that he contends with one who is above him, that he reaches for what he cannot attain, and that he says what he does not know. In the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) it is reported that Ibn Mas'ud said: "O people, whoever knows something should say it, and whoever does not know should say: God knows best. God Most High said to His Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it, nor am I of those who pretend﴾."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 38, verses 87–88:

﴿It is nothing but a reminder⁠﴾, that is, what it is, namely the Qur'an, is nothing but a reminder of exalted status from God, Exalted is He.

﴿to the worlds﴾, to both groups of creation (jinn and humankind) entirely. ﴿And you will surely come to know its news﴾, that is, what it reports of promise and threat and other matters, or its report which is said concerning it in reality, namely that it is the truth and the sincere word. ﴿After a time⁠﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and Ibn Zayd said: it means the Day of Resurrection. Qatadah, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: after death. Al-Hasan used to say: O son of Adam, at death the certain news comes to you. The news (naba') has been explained as the promise and threat which occur in this world, and the meaning is: you will know that by its realization when the swords of the Muslims seize you, and that was the Day of Badr; al-Suddi also pointed to this. In any case, the verse contains a threat that is not hidden.

Page 231

This (and among what some of the Sufi masters said regarding some verses) they said concerning His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with him at dusk and sunrise﴾ and ﴿and the birds gathered; all were to him returning [in repentance]⁠﴾, that it apparently indicates that inanimate objects and animals, which in the view of the people of veils are not speaking, are living, perceiving beings who have knowledge of God, Mighty and Majestic. Al-Sha'rani related from his shaykh 'Ali al-Khawwas, may his secret be sanctified, the view that animals are charged with obligations in a manner the veiled ones do not perceive, and he allowed that their warner may be from themselves, or may be from outside them, of their own kind. He said: they were called "bahaim" (animals, lit. "the obscured ones") only because the matter of their speech and their conditions has been obscured to most of creation, not because the matter is obscure to them themselves. It is related from him that he used to treat every inanimate thing in existence as he would a living being, and he would say that it understands address and feels pain as an animal feels pain.

It has been said: concerning His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, many of the associates oppress one another, except those who believe and do righteous deeds⁠﴾, it is an indication that souls are disposed to injustice and the rest of the blameworthy traits, and that those whose souls have been purified are very few compared to others. ﴿O David, indeed We have made you a successor (khalifah) upon the earth⁠﴾. Al-Sha'rani related that his succession, peace be upon him, and likewise the succession of Adam, was in the world of forms and the world of the governed souls, not the luminous world; for each person among its people has a known station which his Lord, Glorified is He, has assigned to him. The Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, has a lengthy discourse on succession. It is related from some heretics that the successor has no sin recorded against him, nor is he within the bond of obligation, because his rank is a delegated rank; and this is outright disbelief. The scholars distinguished between the khalifah and the king (malik).

Al-Tha'labi related through the chain of al-'Awwam ibn Hawshab who said: a man of my people who witnessed 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, told me that he asked Talhah, al-Zubayr, Ka'b and Salman, may Allah be pleased with them all, what the khalifah is as distinct from the king. Talhah and al-Zubayr said: we do not know. Salman said: the khalifah is the one who is just among the subjects, who divides among them equally, who is compassionate toward them as a man is toward his family, and who judges by the Book of Allah, Exalted is He. Ka'b said: I did not think anyone other than me knew the difference between the khalifah and the king. His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So judge between the people with truth and do not follow [your] desire⁠﴾ serve as an explanation of this succession, and in it is an indication of the blame of desire. In some reports: no god was worshipped on earth more hateful to Allah, Exalted is He, than desire; it is the greatest of idols.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So he began passing his hand over the shins and the necks⁠﴾. In it there is an indication, based on the well-known version of the story, that every beloved thing other than Allah, Exalted is He, if it veils you from Allah, Exalted is He, for a moment, it is incumbent upon you to deal with it by the sword of the negation of "there is no god but Allah." I have heard al-Shibli's use of this as evidence for tearing his garments, and what has been said about it. He said: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom that will not belong to anyone after me⁠﴾. He intended by this request only what would bring increased nearness to Him, Mighty and Majestic, and there is nothing in it that would detract from his perfection, peace be upon him; otherwise he would have been rebuked for it. The discussion of this has already preceded. From this it becomes known that what is in al-Jawahir wa al-Durar, related from al-Khawwas, is false. He said: We have been told that the ant which spoke to Sulayman, peace be upon him, said: O Prophet of Allah, give me security, and I will advise you of something I do not think you know. He gave her security, and she whispered into his ear and said: I smell from your words: ﴿and grant me a kingdom that will not belong to anyone after me⁠﴾ the scent of envy. Sulayman changed, and his color grew dusty. Then she said to him: you have abandoned courtesy with Allah, Exalted is He, in several respects. Among them, your not leaving the stinginess of the soul which Allah, Exalted is He, forbade you, for the presence of generosity which Allah, Exalted is He, commanded you. Among them, your excessiveness in asking that this gift not belong to anyone of your Lord's servants after you, so you restricted the Truth, Exalted is He, from giving anyone after your death what He gave; all of that due to your excessiveness in intense greed. Among them, your seeking that your Lord's kingdom be yours alone: you say "grant me," and you forgot that you are a servant of His, and it is not valid for you to own anything together with Him; and your joy at the gift would not occur except with witnessing your ownership of it, and that suffices as ignorance. Then she said to him: O Sulayman, and what is the kingdom you asked Him to give you? He said: my ring. She said: Fie upon a kingdom contained in a ring. End of quotation. What reached him is also shown to be false by several aspects not hidden from the masters, and it is strange that these were hidden from the masters.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿O Iblis, what prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?⁠﴾ point to the excellence of Adam, peace be upon him, and that he is the most complete of manifestations. The two hands, in their view, are an indication of the two attributes of gentleness and majesty, and all attributes return to them. Without doubt, in our view, he is more excellent than the angels, peace be upon them. Al-Sha'rani mentioned that he asked the masters about the question of preference that we alluded to, and he said: What the group of Sufis has gone to is that preference is valid only among shared genera, as one says: the most excellent of gems is the ruby, and the most excellent of garments is the robe; but when the genera differ, there is no preference, so one does not say: which is more excellent, the ruby or the robe? Then he said: What we hold is that all spirits do not admit of preference, except by way of reports from Allah, Exalted is He. Whoever the Truth, Exalted is He, informs of that, he is the one who has attained complete knowledge. Spirits have been diversified into three kinds: spirits that govern luminous bodies, and these are the exalted assembly; spirits that govern fiery bodies, and these are the jinn; and spirits that govern earthly bodies, and these are humankind. So all spirits are angels in truth, one reality and one genus. Whoever prefers without divine knowledge has no verification. For if we consider preference from the standpoint of origin absolutely, reason would judge the preference of the angels; and if we consider the perfection of origin and its comprehensiveness, we would judge the preference of humankind. From where do we have grounds to lean toward favoring one side over the other, given that the angel is a part of the human being in respect of his spirit, since spirits are angels? So the whole is from the part and the part is from the whole, and one does not say: which is more excellent, the part of the human being or his whole? Understand. End of quotation. The discussion of the question of preference is lengthy, and its place is in the books of theology. Moreover, the portion of the knower from the stories mentioned in this glorious surah is not hidden except from those with dim sight. We ask Allah, Exalted is He, to grant us success in understanding His Book, by the sanctity of the master of His prophets and beloved ones, ﷺ, and may He honor, exalt and ennoble him.
